News.title: Boy, 15, charged with murder after ‘stabbing man, 22, to death in fight over a hat’
News.content:
STABBING HORROR Boy, 15, charged with murder after ‘stabbing man, 22, to death in fight over a hat’

A TEEN boy has been charged with murder after a man was allegedly stabbed to death in a shocking fight over a hat.

Zane Robson, 22, was found with horrific stab wounds on Mann Street in Gosford, on the NSW Central Coast, at about 7.30pm on Tuesday.



Paramedics rushed to treat him at the scene before he was taken to Gosford Hospital, where he tragically died.

Police swooped on a home in Lake Haven at about 1.30am on Saturday, arresting a 15-year-old boy and a 45-year-old woman.



Neither can be identified for legal reasons.

The teenager was charged with murder and sensationally refused bail, with the case due before a Children’s Bail Court later on Saturday.



The woman was charged with hindering the apprehension of a person accused of committing a serious offence and appeared before the NSW Bail Division Court.

During the hearing, her solicitor Javid Faiz told the court the deadly confrontation had allegedly erupted over a hat.

He said: “I spoke to the detective in relation to the [alleged] murder… police say that it is not a gang-related type but rather that it is something that has occurred over a hat.”

Mr Faiz said the woman would fiercely contest the charges against her.



He said: “There is nothing to suggest that [she] was aware that there was a warrant at the time.

“[Police] have observed a female, they’ve knocked on the door and observed a female.

“It’s not one [case] where the young person has then taken off, the young person was found under the bed.”

Mr Faiz also told the court CCTV captured evidence of “how it all started”.

The court heard the woman cares for an autistic child and had only recently secured stable accommodation after being left homeless following the death of her partner.



She was granted bail on the strict condition she remain at the Lake Haven address and report to police every week.

Her matter will return to Wyong Local Court on August 11.

Mr Robson was identified earlier this week after his devastated family shared a heartbreaking tribute through a GoFundMe campaign.

A relative said: “No family is ever prepared for a loss like this.

“On the evening of July 28, 2026, our family was devastated by the sudden and tragic loss of a much-loved son, grandson, brother, brother-in-law, uncle, and friend.



“At just 22 years old, his life was taken far too soon in an [alleged] senseless act of knife violence in Gosford.”

The family said they were eternally grateful to first responders and “complete strangers” who desperately helped Mr Robson during his final moments.

They said: “In the middle of such a heartbreaking tragedy, knowing that people showed him kindness, compassion, and courage brings us immense comfort during what would have been a scary and lonely time.”

The family remembered Zane as a “bubbly, happy and inquisitive child” who adored motorbikes and following his siblings around.

“While Zane had his own personal struggles in life, he was a remarkably kind person who always showed deep love, empathy and compassion toward his parents, big brothers, little sister, family and friends.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“[He] always said “I love you” at the end of a phone call. He will be missed more than words can say.”

His grieving family thanked those who donated to the fundraiser, which will help cover funeral costs and support his devastated loved ones.

News.title: Three dead after huge explosion rips through Moscow restaurant ‘where Russian general was celebrating his birthday’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

DEADLY BLAST Three dead after huge explosion rips through Moscow restaurant ‘where Russian general was celebrating his birthday’

AT least three people have died after a massive blast ripped through an elite Moscow restaurant near the Kremlin.

A Russian General was reportedly celebrating his birthday with high-ranking guests in a “private event” when the explosion occurred.



Another 17 attendees are reportedly in a serious condition, with witnesses describing horrific injuries at the scene.

Police and paramedics rushed to the Stalin-era high-rise building hosting the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square in central Moscow.



There were reports of “numerous cars with black license plates, used by the Russian armed forces and other security agencies” being at the restaurant.

An eyewitness said: “There were people lying on stretchers, a young woman was hysterical.”

The explosion was initially suspected to be caused by a gas leak in the kitchen, but cops are now probing whether it could have been a bomb.

It has not yet been confirmed whether a general’s birthday party was underway.



However prominent war propagandist Anastasia Kashevarova posted that the “elite” was celebrating at the Italian Balzi Rossi restaurant.

She wrote: “During another banquet, an explosion occurred. There are casualties and many wounded.

“They say it was a celebration, possibly a wedding, involving someone from the elite.”

One theory was a birthday party for Alexander Chayko, Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Aerospace Forces, who turned 55 five days ago.

Another suggested target is Major-General Vladimir Seliverstov, who turned 53 today and is a prominent paratroop commander.

News.content:

DEATH PROBE Man in his 40s found dead in hotel room in city centre as cops launch probe into ‘unexpected’ death

A MAN has been found dead in a hotel room, prompting cops to launch an investigation into his “unexpected death”.

The man, who was in his 40s, was discovered this morning at the Brownlows Inn on Mount Pleasant, in Liverpool, Merseyside Police confirmed.



Emergency services remain in the city centre, after being alerted to the death at around 11.15am.

Cops are saying the death is being treated as unexpected.



The man’s relatives have been informed and a post-mortem is currently underway to establish the cause of death.

Enquiries at the scene are ongoing.

News.content:

FIND HER Urgent search for missing schoolgirl, 12, who vanished from home as cops urge ‘call 999’ if you see her

COPS have launched an urgent search for a missing school girl who vanished from her home.

Officers are keen to find 12-year-old Ava after she went missing from Cradley Heath, in the Black Country.

The girl was last seen at 1.07pm on July 31.



If anyone thinks they have spotted her, they are urged to call 999 immediately.



She was last seen wearing a long sleeve black top, black shorts, white shoes and a black rucksack, police said.

The appeal was put out on social media late on Friday night, after she was reported missing to the police.

The Birmingham Police post said: “Missing: Have you seen Ava aged 12 from Cradley Heath?

“Ava was last seen at 13:07hrs on 31/07 wearing a long sleeve black top, black shorts, white shoes and a black rucksack.

“If you see Ava please call 999 quoting log number 4104-310726.”

News.title: Bio-hacker Bryan Johnson stores girlfriend’s menstrual blood in freezer as he admits to making her use ‘techno tampon’
News.content:
BIO-HACKER Byran Johnson has stored his girlfriends menstrual blood in a freezer after admitting to making her use a techno tampon.

The 48-year-old tech entrepreneur obsessed with reversing ageing, revealed he has stored around 10ml of his girlfriend’s menstrual blood at -80°C.



Bryan posted a picture of his 30-year-old girlfriend Kate Tolo on X alongside the bizarre revelation on Thursday.

He wrote: “Kate’s period blood is in my -80 °C freezer. Around 10 mL.”



The millionaire biohacker says the blood will be examined for everything from endocrine disruptors to microplastics.

“Menstrual blood is valuable and underutilized … It’s a non-invasive look into the uterus,” Bryan said.

“I like that Kate is a science experiment with me,” he added.

Kate appeared to back the controversial experiment, replying: “Thanks for looking after me bby.”

But the frozen blood sample is just one part of an extreme health programme Bryan claims will produce the most comprehensive data ever collected on a woman’s menstrual cycle.

He says Kate is collecting a staggering 14 million data points while completing more than 100 tasks every day.



The gruelling regime involves more than 50 devices and monitoring from a 12-person medical team.

Kate is required to provide regular urine samples, swallow a temperature pill and blow into a metabolism tracker.

And at exactly 9.42pm every night, she must “insert techno tampon device”.

When The Independent asked Bryan for details about the mysterious device, he said: “We will be sharing more on that soon.”

A Wall Street Journal report featured a picture of Kate examining a small tampon-shaped device.



The report described it as an acrylic device inserted into her vagina to track blood-flow variations.

Bryan has claimed the project is a “world first for female health”.

“This will be the most quantified menstrual cycle ever. And this is just to collect baseline measurement,” he wrote.



“Once we’re done with the 100 days, we’ll start trying interventions.”

Bryan has also promised to publish the results, including the “good, bad and ugly”.

The extraordinary project is expected to cost $2.6million a year and is being funded by Bryan and Kate’s company Immortals.

The company sells supplements and other products, offers access to prescription medicine and operates a concierge medical practice.

According to the Journal, Immortals is also preparing to launch products aimed at women.



Kate, who has a background in fashion, has defended the extreme monitoring as a way of improving understanding of women’s health.

“I’m really doing it because I think that this is our path toward women being understood in the world and being seen,” she told the Journal.

Bryan has similarly claimed: “Women are not well understood medically.”

Kate has said she has polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome and adenomyosis, while Bryan has also revealed she was diagnosed with endometriosis.

She has reportedly suffered severe pain during her periods and hopes the intensive monitoring could help identify treatments for her symptoms.



The couple’s controversial project comes after years of criticism over the lack of research into women’s health and menstruation.

Bryan own extreme attempts to combat ageing have also repeatedly sparked controversy.

The billionaire previously revealed that he had been infused with a litre of plasma from his teenage son Talmage.



Bryan has referred to Talmage as his “blood boy” after the teenager donated blood which was separated into plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

The plasma was then put into Bryan body in the hope that younger blood could rejuvenate him and repair cellular damage caused by ageing.

Bryan also donated a litre of his own blood to his father.

His obsession with tracking his body has extended to intimate measurements involving his son.

Last year, Bryan posted data comparing his nocturnal erections with those of Talmage.



He wrote on X, tagging his son: “Nighttime erection data from my 19-year-old son … and me.

“His duration is two minutes longer than mine. Raise children to stand tall, be firm, and be upright.”

Bryan has previously claimed he does not believe he will die.

Asked whether he thought he would die, he replied: “No.”

His extreme anti-ageing regime was documented in the Netflix documentary Don’t Die: The Man Who Wants to Live Forever.



Bryan has claimed to spend around $2million a year on his health in his bid to reverse ageing and extend his life.

His punishing routine includes red-light therapy, seven skin creams, tea-tree oil for his teeth and regular MRIs, ultrasounds, blood tests and colonoscopies.

He and Talmage have also followed a strict vegan diet capped at 2,000 calories, with their daily routine beginning at 5am and their final meal at noon.

Bryan has said his regime is designed to “build a family culture of health and hard work”.

He has faced fierce criticism over the extreme lifestyle, with critics comparing it to a “prison routine with more blood tests”.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Despite the backlash, Bryan claims his methods have reduced his biological age by five years and significantly slowed the ageing of his cells.

His latest experiment now sees Kate undergo an extraordinary 100-day monitoring programme, with her menstrual blood frozen at -80°C as Bryan attempts to gather unprecedented data on the female body.

News.title: Mum, 48, loses seven teeth after tripping over deep pothole in the dark as council refuses to pay compensation
News.content:
POTHOLE HORROR Mum, 48, loses seven teeth after tripping over deep pothole in the dark as council refuses to pay compensation

A MUM who lost seven teeth after tripping over a deep pothole has blasted the local council for not taking responsibility.

Business owner Alison Smith, 48, shattered nearly all of her front teeth after falling into the hole in a dark area in Ventnor, on the Isle of Wight.



Horrifying photographs show the extent of her devastating injuries, which left her face swollen and bruised.

The cafe owner had been on her way to meet her daughter when she fell at around 7.40pm in January 2025 on the dimly lit pavement.



Alison said that her daughter, who was 17, had been left “traumatised” after finding her mum covered in blood.

She added that she was not able to see her own mother, who’d recently had a brain tumour operation, as the sight of her injuries would be too distressing.



“I just tripped on the pothole, and my foot got caught in the pothole, in the lip on the edge, and I fell on my hand and knocked all my teeth out,” she said.

“My hand now isn’t fully recovered. I can’t lift myself up on it.

“I went to A&E because I thought I had smashed my cheekbone.

“I reported it and had a shameful response. They filled the pothole in within a few days, which says they are liable.”

She added that her daughter thought she had been stabbed or attacked given her horrific injuries.



Alison had extensive dental work done at her own expense, but could not afford implants because she’d received no compensation.

A plastic plate, inserted into the top and bottom of her mouth, makes it difficult for her to eat.

Serious hand injuries meant she had to close her beloved Gaslight Cafe in Sandown as she was unable to hold trays or lift heavy objects.

“I’m still so upset about it,” she said.

“Island Roads are saying they’ve done enough and have now filled the pothole in.



“But if it caused this much injury to me, old people could have died if they had gone flying like I did.”

She said she had considered the ‘no win no fee’ compensation claim but after recently losing both parents had decided to delay action.

“I just want someone to take responsibility for this,” she said.

“I’ve paid the price, and my daughter, who found me all bloodied after the fall, is still traumatised by it.

“It’s so unfair. Something that was not my fault has ruined my life, while Island Roads has just filled the holes and resurfaced the whole road and dismissed me.”



An Island Roads spokesperson said: “We have every sympathy for Ms Smith and for the injuries she has sustained as a result of this incident.

“The road was inspected in October 2024 as part of its routine six-monthly inspection and in line with accepted industry practice.

“No defects were identified that met the threshold for intervention either at that time or during our investigation following the incident.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They concluded that following an investigation, they were not able to accept liability in this case.

The pothole referred to in the claim – and another one nearby – were backfilled as part of the council’s “outgoing maintenance”.

News.title: Cops launch urgent manhunt for suspect, 22, who escaped a prison van moments after arriving outside court
News.content:
ON THE RUN Cops launch urgent manhunt for suspect, 22, who escaped a prison van moments after arriving outside court

COPS have launched a manhunt for a man who escaped from a prison van just moments after arriving outside court.

Stephen Grzyb, 22, from Liverpool, ran off from the Magistrates’ Court at around 10am having been transported from a police custody suite, Merseyside Police said.

Grzyb, who was charged with a domestic-related burglary, fled down Red Cross Street in the direction of The Strand, after being transported by prisoner transport contractor GEOAmey, the force added.



He is described as white, with short, dark hair and was last seen wearing a navy t-shirt and navy shorts.



Extensive inquiries are currently being taken by officers to locate him and patrols have also attended the home of the alleged victim in the case.

Inspector Bethan Hannon said: “We understand the concern this incident will cause, and it is vital the public can see Grzyb’s face so they can report any sightings and help us bring him back into custody as soon as possible.

“If you have heard from him or know where he is, please do the right thing and come forward.



“Assisting him in any way will bring police to your own door, so it is not an association worth keeping.

“If you see Grzyb, please call 999 immediately.

“We are carrying out extensive enquiries to find him with patrols on foot and CCTV enquiries being made right across the city centre so that we can return him to custody.”

Anyone with information is asked to get in touch with police quoting reference number 26000615520.

News.title: 109 toys you should NEVER buy your children – as fresh wave of squishy dumplings are seized in UK
News.content:
PARENTS should never buy these toys for their children as recalls continue to flag up dangerous substances and chemicals.

Last week, hundreds of squishy toys were seized after reports of strong chemical smells.

In the past seven months, 109 children’s toys have been urgently pulled from shelves over fears they pose a health risk to children.



Despite these toys having squishy, cuddly, and cute appearances, some have been found to contain dangerous substances, and should be avoided at all costs.



Squishy Dumpling (fakes)

Viral “Squishy Dumpling” toys have been gaining media attention, as children hunt down the glittery rare squishies hidden inside the basket-style boxes.

However, parents have been gradually noticing that a number of these dumpling toys have been omitting a distinct, and unnatural chemical smell.



In June, Cardiff-based wholesaler and website Samsons Cash and Carry Ltd saw its Squeezy Dumplings toy recalled over fear they pose a serious chemical risk.

Inside, the toy contained four times the legal quantity of the carcinogen benzene, which can irritate the eyes, nose, throat, skin, and digestive tract, and cause types of leukaemia after long-term, consistent exposure.

Experts have also urged parents to stop their children from microwaving squishy dumpling toys, after the trend caused a number of children to require skin grafts for life-changing burns.

To spot squishy dumpling fakes, it is important to look for clear safety instructions, a safety mark, and the name of a reputable importer or manufacturer on packaging.



Four details that tell you if a 'Squishy Dumpling' toy is genuine or fake According to Which?, anyone buying a dumpling toy should look out for the following: Clear safety instructions explaining what to do if the product leaks or is punctured.

explaining what to do if the product leaks or is punctured. A CE or UKCA mark that shows the item has been safety assessed.

, such as an importer or manufacturer. Be wary of products that give off a strong or unusual chemical smell. Swansea Trading Standards launched its investigation after concerns were raised about some dumpling toys emitting a noticeable odour.

Craft Kits (containing decorative sand)

Reputable names such as Crayola, Galt, and Hobbycraft, have all seen craft kits be pulled from shop shelves.

This comes as decorative sand contained inside the kits, whether it be inside small tubes or packets, were found to contain asbestos.

To safely store unused packets of decorative sand in these sets, place them in a heavy-duty plastic bag, double-tape it shut, and store it out of reach of children.



Sand-filled Stretchy Toys

74 sand-filled stretchy and squishy toys have been recalled this year due to asbestos contamination, including 40 from the HTI Stretcherz range.

Even though the sand is contained inside the product, repeated stretching increases the risk of it bursting.

The simplest solution is to follow the Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) disposal guidance to get rid of these toys, and to stop buying them.

Archaeological Dig and Science Kits



Earlier this year, Smyths Toys were forced to pull several of its “Dig Products” from shelves due to asbestos contamination in the excavation kits.

Safety watchdogs had found that the rock and mineral samples inside the kits posed a “serious risk” to children’s health.

Two science kits involving sand and slime were pulled by KTL Toys as well, with the educational kits also flagging asbestos contamination.

Like any toys including decorative sand, it is important to be wary of these excavation or archaeological dig sets, as a number have been flagged for contamination.

Sand art bottle craft sets and jars



A number of sand art bottles, as well as tubes of decorative sand, have also been recalled due to asbestos contamination.

The sets usually consist of a clear bottle or jar, with multiple bags of decorative sand to used to create layered rainbow patterns inside.

As expected, given decorative sand has provoked these recalls, avoiding large quantities, such as in these kits, should be avoided.

Wooden blocks containing sand

Wooden toys are often considered the safest for children, however, the sand contained inside these were contaminated with asbestos.

News.title: Prince Louis admits 'Charlotte says I'm not very good' at handstands as royal siblings name favourite sports
News.content:
Prince Louis admits 'Charlotte says I'm not very good' at handstands as royal siblings name favourite sports

Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis joined their parents Princess Kate and Prince William to watch a netball semi-final match at the Commonwealth Games at the Hydro arena in Glasgow

View 6 Images Prince Louis and Prince George chatted to athletes from Team Wales (Image: Getty Images)

Hints were shared today at what sports and exercises Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis enjoy as they sat and chatted with athletes from Team Wales.

‌



During on the final stop of their busy day at the Commonwealth Games, the children joined their parents, the Prince and Princess of Wales, to talk to the athletes. The family of five received a warm welcome as they arrived at Wales House in the centre of Glasgow.

‌



But when Welsh TV presenter Gethin Jones asked George if he wanted to see his parents team up on a tandem in the velodrome, the 13-year-old boy quickly replied “no”, seemingly embarrassed by the prospect.

‌



William and Catherine led their children over to speak to identical twin gymnasts Abigail and Emily Roper who won bronze medals within an hour of each other earlier in the week.

Prince Louis marks milestone at Commonwealth Games as he joins William and Kate in packed stadium READ MORE :

Meghan Markle will never leave California despite Harry reunion, royal expert claims READ MORE :

View 6 Images Catherine, Princess of Wales, also met athletes today (Image: Getty Images)

Balancing acts

The family chatted with the athletes and their proud parents for over five minutes, asking about their achievements and how they prepared for the Games. Catherine asked: "And what are you doing? As Charlotte was asking, are you doing a lot of stretching and conditioning?”

‌



They nodded and said they do a mix of both to ensure their strong and flexible. The future queen then turned to her youngest and said: “Louis, you’re perfecting your handstand at the moment.”

Though the youngster, with his arms crossed, said: "A bit, but Charlotte says I’m not very good.” The Roper twins then asked if Charlotte can do one, and she said “yeah”.

When they asked George the same question, he and Catherine laughed as the young prince told them: “I’m rubbish at anything that involves flexibility.”

‌



View 6 Images Princess Kate said Prince Louis has been perfecting his handstand (Image: Getty Images)

Princess Charlotte enjoys gymnastics

Charlotte then told them that her favourite part of gymnastics is the floor, with her mum added: “Charlotte likes her dancing.” Overhearing the conversation, William said: “She loves gymnastics and ballet.”

Having already learned that the young princess enjoys the sport, the Welsh gymnasts presented her with a Team Wales leotard that has been signed by the athletes. The family were then asked to update the medal table, as two more gold medals had been won by Team Wales, with William volunteering Louis for the task.

‌



The eight-year-old boy took the giant No 7 sticker and placed it on the board. He returned to his father’s side with his head bowed shyly, with William telling him well done and rubbing his back.

William, George, Charlotte and Louis then sat down with Para-athletes Aled Davies, and Olivia Breen, and 400m runner Charlotte Henrich, while mum Catherine stayed talking to the gymnasts.

View 6 Images The future queen spoke about Charlotte's love for gymnastics (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Prince Louis' for the high jump

The children were involved in the conversation, with Louis revealing that he recently participated in his first sports day at school and George telling them that his favourite event is the javelin.

Joining them at the table, Catherine was told: “Louis was saying he likes high jump.” She turned to her son and asked: “Louis, you like high jump?” He replied moodily: "Yeah," prompting several of the athletes to burst out laughing and William joking: “That’s news to us!”

Gethin then interrupted the conversation to announce that Wales had just won another gold medal, prompting the entire room to erupt into whoops and applause. Charlotte was then invited to update the medal tally to eight golds.

‌



Back at the table, Catherine said Laura Kenny was trying to get them involved in the velodrome, saying: “Come and give it a go!”

She added, laughing: "I did say be careful what you wish for as they want to put us on a tandem bike in the velodrome."

Gethin responded saying: "Oh please, please can we absolutely make that happen."

‌



Olivia joked it was that or the London marathon, after William told them that former cyclist Laura had just ran a sub-four marathon without any training. He said: "Fair enough. Well if that’s the ultimatum, riding a tandem bike, definitely."

View 6 Images William and Kate took their children to watch part of the Commonwealth Games (Image: Jane Barlow/PA Wire)

Playful Prince William

Each of the children were then handed a teddy bear of Gwen, the Welsh dragon, and a goodie bag featuring the Welsh cycling outfit, which were also handed to the Prince and Princess.

‌



Olivia joked that William and Catherine could wear the outfits when they ride the tandem, prompting the Prince to joke: “You know me and Lycra!”

View 6 Images Cheeky Prince Louis smiles as he wears a hat that reads Beicio Cymru - or Welsh Cycling (Image: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

As he pulled the top out of the bag he held up a tiny shirt, having accidentally been given one of the children’s tops, prompting hearty laughter from the table.

Article continues below

“I won’t whip the shorts out,” he joked.

The family then thanked their hosts before heading home after a busy day out.

News.title: King Charles pictured sipping dram of whisky at the Mey Highland Games
News.content:
King Charles pictured sipping dram of whisky at the Mey Highland Games

King Charles enjoyed the tipple as he took in the Mey Highland Games in Scotland, an annual sporting event held in Caithness, where he watched the traditional tug o’ war and other events

View 5 Images The King sipped a dram of whisky as he attended the Mey Highland Games (Image: Getty Images)

King Charles couldn't resist the local favourite as he kicked back with a whisky at the Mey Highland Games in Scotland.

‌



Wearing his traditional kilt as he took in a number of traditional sports in the north of the country, the Monarch greeted spectators and competitors enjoying the annual Caithness event.

‌



The sovereign has held the title of Chieftain at the Mey Highland Games since 2002, when he took it over from his mother, the late Queen. Today, he watched on as athletes participated in the traditional tug o’ war, with a group of firefighters taking part before shaking hands with the group after they won the competition.

‌



Other groups to meet the King included the Wounded Highlanders, a team of injured military veterans who regularly take part in the adaptive competitions in the Mey Highland Games.

Prince Louis marks milestone at Commonwealth Games as he joins William and Kate in packed stadium READ MORE :

Prince Harry sees rise in approval ratings after reunion with King Charles READ MORE :

5 View 5 Images Wearing his traditional kilt, the monarch couldn't resist the local favourite (Image: Getty Images) 5 View 5 Images The King enjoyed his drink as he watched the games in the very north of Scotland (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Charles, 77, also saw the tossing of the caber – which involves entrants carrying a long and heavy tree trunk and throwing it in an attempt to turn it end over end.

Troupes of Highland dancers and pipe bands also took part in the Highland Games. The Mey Highland Games takes place each year at the John O’Groats showground, traditionally on the first Saturday of August.

The first Mey Games was held in the nearby village of Mey in 1970 to celebrate the late Queen Mother’s 70th birthday. As guest of honour on the day, she declared the event a success and encouraged its organisers to make it an annual event.

‌



View 5 Images The King watches young Highland dancers perform (Image: Getty Images)

The event has grown considerably since it was founded in 1970 and around 2,000 people can turn out for it.

The King’s visit to the Mey Highland Games took place as his son William, who is known as the Duke of Rothesay while in Scotland, attended the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow along with his wife and children. Kate, the Duchess of Rothesay – along with Princess Charlotte, Prince Louis and Prince George – joined spectators watching netball at the Hydro arena.

‌



Last year, the King started flogging a bottle of whisky that might give buyers a headache.. it costs £3,200 a bottle.

View 5 Images Firefighters participate in the tug o' war (Image: Lesley Martin/PA Wire)

The tipple has been made to celebrate the monarch’s 75th birthday. Bosses at the Buckingham Palace shop reveal: “This Balmoral whisky comes from cask number 1838, distilled on November 7 1978, was tasted by The King before 253 bottles were filled and numbered by hand on November 14 2023, His Majesty's 75th birthday.

Article continues below

"The bottles feature a gold engraving of the Balmoral crest with His Majesty's Cypher at its centre. Further rooting this special whisky on Royal Deeside, each bottle is presented in a wooden case handcrafted from windblown larch from the Balmoral Estate and incorporating Balmoral Tweed.

"It also features an innovative material from a forest below the sea: zero-waste seaweed paper made by Notpla, a winner of The Earthshot Prize, of which Prince William, The Duke of Rothesay, is Founder and President.”

News.title: 'Andy Burnham has the public's attention - he must hold onto it when the honeymoon ends'
News.content:
It's been a dream start for Andy Burnham.

He pulled off a bloodless bid for the top job, avoiding a fractious leadership contest over the summer, and hit the ground running in No10 at a breakneck pace.

But his real win? The public are listening. Labour has seen a bounce in the polls and his actions so far seem to be landing with voters who feel he's looking at the right issues.

The bitter irony for Keir Starmer is that he tried to do similar things but the public had switched off.

‌



Burnham has their attention now, and intends to use it to sear who he is in their minds before the honeymoon period ends.

Andy Burnham hints carers could be exempt from visa crackdown with 'fairness' pledge READ MORE :

Burnham says more cost of living help on its way as struggling families in his sights READ MORE :

View 2 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaks to Mirror Political Editor Lizzy Buchan during a visit to BAE systems in Barrow in Furness (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

When I joined the PM to see the construction of nuclear submarines at Barrow-in-Furness this week, he was upbeat and fired up to get cracking.

He's clearly enjoying being Prime Minister - a prize he's long coveted - and he knows what he wants to do with power. But I was struck by the tension between his style of politics and the office he now holds.

‌



He's a great communicator, and is less guarded than his predecessor, engaging earnestly with questions about what he wants to do.

This can be risky, generating headlines and speculation before plans are nailed down. But the pay-off for speaking frankly is it shows he gets the issues people are worried about.

As Greater Manchester Mayor, he would pick up ideas from speaking to people in the pub and on buses.

Insiders joke with gentle exasperation about running on "Andy time" as he stops to talk to everyone despite the intensity of a PM's schedule.

‌



But he wants to do things his way - and that includes getting out there.

He wistfully quipped to me that he's fighting a one-man battle to remain in his seat to watch Everton. The reality of being PM - and the intense security that comes with it - means this will be a tough fight.

Much has been made of how normal Burnham is. It's won him fans on social media, where his team has been savvy in getting his message out.

And it's true in real life. He's the same off camera as he is on it, unlike Starmer who was much warmer and more normal behind the scenes.

‌



Burnham's challenge will be holding onto this when the pressures of PM begin to weigh on him.

The honeymoon will fade as he is forced to make difficult decisions over the same tangle of domestic and international problems as Starmer.

But if he can keep the public's attention and convince them he is on their side, maybe he can succeed where Starmer failed.

News.title: Andy Burnham hints carers could be exempt from visa crackdown with 'fairness' pledge
News.content:
Andy Burnham hints carers could be exempt from visa crackdown with 'fairness' pledge

EXCLUSIVE: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure 'fairness' in the rules for people who came to the UK in good faith to work in the social care sector

PM says he wants fairness for foreign born care workers

Andy Burnham has signalled he could exempt foreign care workers from immigration reforms as he praised the staff who care for his dad.

‌



The Prime Minister said he wanted to ensure "fairness" in the rules for people who came to the UK in good faith to work in the sector in his clearest sign yet that he could water down a visa crackdown drawn up by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood.

‌



The plans will make it harder for migrants to permanently settle in the UK, requiring overseas carers to wait 15 years to qualify for indefinite leave to remain rather than the current five years, even if they are already in the UK.

‌



The idea of applying the rules retrospectively to people who arrived on post-Brexit health and social care visas triggered a major backlash.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, a former carer, publicly criticised the idea on Thursday, while unions and care organisations have also warned that the sector is heavily dependent on international workers and the changes could worsen chronic staff shortages.

View Image Andy Burnham has vowed to fix social care (Image: JASON ALDEN/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

‌



Mr Burnham used a major speech on fixing social care this week to pay tribute to the overseas care workers who look after his dad Roy, who has Alzheimer's.

Asked if he was looking at how reforms applied to care staff, he told the Sunday Mirror: "I wanted to mention people who've come from overseas to work in our care system and in our health system as well. I see it in the social care system because of the times I visit my Dad.

"I don't think they hear people like me sometimes recognising the fact that they have come all this way and they are contributing so much. It felt right in that moment to recognise them specifically, as well as obviously care workers more broadly.

‌



"It's a challenging thing to do isn't it, to look after someone else's mum and dad. To me, it's like the highest calling you could answer.

"It's an amazing thing that they do that, and it's just not right is it that people who, in my view, should be the highest paid really in society get treated as they do.

"That's why social care is such as priority for me. But also, I do want to make sure we get fairness in the rules in relation to people who came here in good faith, and made a commitment, I will make sure that we do that."

‌



Pressed on whether he was looking at the idea of applying the rules retrospectively, he said: "There's a range of issues.

"Obviously, it's a sponsorship issue that caused some overseas care workers difficulties and there is an issue around indefinite leave to remain. There's other issues as well.

"What I'm saying is we have to have a firm approach to immigration. We have to ensure that we're managing access to public services properly, but at the same time, we also need to be fair and recognise the commitment people are making to this country."

Article continues below

The PM has backed Ms Mahmood's immigration reforms, and kept her in post when he reshuffled his Cabinet.

She has argued that migrants must earn the right to permanently settle in this country - and the Government previously said some 1.6million people would get an automatic right to settle in the UK by 2030 unless the rules are changed to apply retrospectively.

However the Home Office has consulted on whether there should be transitional arrangements for people who are already living in Britain, with a decision expected to be announced in the autumn.

News.title: Burnham says more cost of living help on its way as struggling families in his sights
News.content:
Burnham says more cost of living help on its way as struggling families in his sights

EXCLUSIVE: The new Prime Minister told the Mirror helping hard-pressed households would be his top priority in office, and signalled he could do more to bring down utility bills and rail fares

Andy Burnham confirms his #1 priority for the UK

Andy Burnham has said people struggling to take the kids out, to go to the pub, or to go on holiday drive his decisions as he promised more cost of living help is on the way.

‌



In an interview with the Sunday Mirror, the new Prime Minister said helping hard-pressed households would be his top priority in office, and signalled he could do more to bring down utility bills and rail fares.

‌



After a whirlwind two weeks in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said the concerns of voters on the doorstep were ringing in his ears as he gets down to the business of governing.

‌



Asked who he had in mind when he was making decisions, he said: "People on whose doors I was knocking only about five, six weeks ago... They did get over to me how tough life was. Can't go for drink anymore. Can't take the kids out. Not having a holiday this year.

"I heard those type of things being said throughout the campaign, and those comments were still ringing in my ears as I arrived in Downing Street."

Andy Burnham has charmed Donald Trump - but keeping him happy is a full time job READ MORE :

Chancellor John Healey announces date for first Budget under Andy Burnham READ MORE :

View 3 Images Andy Burnham said the concerns of voters on the doorstep were ringing in his ears as he gets down to the business of governing. (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



Mr Burnham used his first days in Downing Street to roll out a rapid-fire list of cost of living announcements. VAT will be slashed from electricity bills from October, bus fares will be capped at £2 and pubs, social clubs and live music venues will get a 20% cut to business rates from April.

He also took aim at some of the most intractable issues gripping the country - from rough sleeping to social care and the crisis of young people not in work, education or training.

But despite his packed in-tray, the cost of living remains at the top of his agenda. "It's about looking across the piece," he said. "Not giving people false promises, but being honest with them and saying, "Well, I'll do whatever I can in all of these different areas just to take a little bit of pressure down".

‌



He went on: "I think rail fares are too high, outrageously so in some instances. So that's something that's in my sights.

"I mentioned VAT and electricity bills. It's a short-term measure at this moment, but let's see where we can go with that.

"Water is an issue as well, where I think the public pay high bills and they don't see that money then going into infrastructure. There's another area that needs reform."

‌



But the PM's hopes of offering breathing space to struggling families risk being plunged into jeopardy by global turmoil.

The war in Iran triggered a spike in wholesale energy costs, sending household energy bills rocketing by 13% for millions of people in Britain at the start of July. The typical household that pays by direct debit saw the price cap increase from £1,641 to £1,862 a year.

Mr Burnham's Government will need to decide whether to intervene to help consumers this winter, when the price cap is expected to rise again and temperatures drop.

‌



View 3 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaks to Mirror Political Editor Lizzy Buchan during a visit to BAE systems in Barrow in Furness (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

The PM said the situation was being monitored, and said he had been urged to look at standing charges - a flat daily fee like a telephone line rental - which are added to bills regardless of how much energy is used.

He said: "We'll keep monitoring that situation and make sure we're doing everything that we can do. People have raised issues like the standing charges on bills, and they kind of pushed me to go further on that.

‌



"So I'll take a look at that issue, alongside other issues and other things that we might be able to do to help people with the cost of living.

"It remains a very tough time for people, and I know the main thing people would like me to do if I can do it is to ease that pressure a little bit."

Part of his pitch is to make Britain fairer - in terms of opportunity, geography, and living standards. He said: "I think too often the country's been run for some people, not all people. I definitely am somebody who wants to change that."

‌



Creating No10 North will be one of the defining changes, he said, ensuring "a feeling in all places that they are on the rise if you like, not going backwards".

He added: "I'm serious when I talk about giving Britain hope back. We haven't had enough to feel hopeful about recently." Asked if Britain could get it's mojo back, he joked: "Yeah, that's it. I'll try."

View 3 Images Andy Burnham and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, right, visit Submarine Academy for Skills and Knowledge (SASK) at BAE Systems, in Barrow in Furness, (Image: Christopher Furlong/Pool Getty v)

‌



But the other pressures weighing on the PM were brought home as he spoke to the Sunday Mirror in Barrow-in-Furness, where four new Dreadnought-class submarines are being built. The cutting-edge vessels will enter service in the 2030s, armed with deadly Trident missiles that act as Britain's nuclear deterrent.

The PM said the thing that had struck him most since entering No10 was "the fragility" of the global situation. He said: "Things can change very quickly, it feels, in the times in which we're living, and because of that, I think Britain really does need to regain its stability to be in a world like this, and drifting is not a good place to be."

As the sixth PM in 10 years, Mr Burnham said he was conscious that British politics hasn't been working. He said: "It's too much about point scoring and politicians doing what they like doing, rather than what the public want them to do. [Changing] that's a really important way of regaining stability.

‌



"The unpredictability, the volatility, the fragility of the world right now is the thing [that surprised him most]. I knew it was like that, but obviously, when you're in the position that I'm in, you really feel that, and I've got to do whatever I can to build some stability back into Britain."

But he added: "I do feel hopeful. I love this country, every facet of it, and I do feel hopeful about it because I talked about the fragility of the world, but you come into this role, and you just see the amazing strengths we've still got here."

Despite being Prime Minister, Mr Burnham wants to stick to his style of politics - picking up policy ideas from voters in shops, on the bus, and in the pub.

‌



"That's the way I've always done my politics, and I don't want it to change," he said. Just this week, he went to the theatre with his family and was approached by people. "I love that," he said.

He joked that he was infuriating his security by stopping to talk to people - and said he was fighting a "one-man campaign" to stay in his season ticket seat at Hill Dickinson stadium to watch Everton.

He said: "I'm not really winning it right now, but I'm still fighting the fight. But again, that's a chance for people just to say, 'you know what, you should do this, or you said this last week, don't say that.'

Article continues below

"I've always used that feedback as a politician to get my focus where I think people want it to be."

News.title: Mum and daughter, 10, killed in horror crash are buried together in same wicker coffin
News.content:
Mum and daughter, 10, killed in horror crash are buried together in same wicker coffin

Heartbroken loved ones have gathered to say goodbye to author Nell Raven and her daughter, Ira, both born in the UK

View 4 Images Former journalist and writer Nell (53) and Ira (10), lost their lives following the two-car collision on Friday, July 24. (Image: Anglo Celt)

A mum and daughter who were born in the UK before moving to start a new life in Ireland have been buried together in the same coffin after a tragic crash cut their lives short.

‌



Acclaimed author Nell Saffron Raven and her young daughter Irena, known as Ira, were killed in a two-car collision on Friday, July 24. Nell, 53, was a former journalist, and lived with her family. including 10-year-old Ira, in Gortnacleigh, Milltown in Belturbet, Co Cavan.

‌



Originally from the UK, Ms Raven had recently become an Irish citizen. An emotional funeral brought together the loved ones to celebrate the lives of the pair, including Nell's talents as a writer, her dedication as a mother, and her triumph over cancer. Ira was remembered as a "kind, creative and joyful little girl" who loved music, Irish dancing and life in Co Cavan.

‌



The fatal incident occurred on the R162 at Corclare, Sherlock. Ms Raven passed away shortly after the crash, while Ira succumbed to her injuries on Tuesday afternoon, July 28, at Children's Health Ireland at Temple Street Hospital.

A single wicker coffin carrying Nell and Ira was brought into St Patrick's Church, Milltown on Saturday morning to the strains of 'Hallelujah' by Leonard Cohen, a favourite song of Nell and her husband Alex. A framed photograph of the mother and daughter was placed atop their coffin, reports the Irish Mirror.

View 4 Images St Patrick's Church, Milltown in Co Cavan (Image: Google Maps )

‌



During the funeral Mass, mourners learned that Ira had posthumously given the gift of life to four children through organ donation. Among the chief mourners at the funeral Mass were Nell's devastated husband and Ira's father Alexandru, daughters and sisters Eveline Margalla Kemp and Violet Elizabeth Kemp, parents and grandparents Erik Raven and Christina Smith, and Nell's sisters Daisy Raven and Poppy Sharrock.

Struggling to contain his emotions, Alexandru addressed the mourners, admitting he was "not a storyteller", but his wife had always been one. He reminisced about meeting Nell in Oxford in 2013, witnessing their family expand, and ultimately settling down in rural Cavan, where they discovered friendship, community, and joy.

"When I met Nell, she already had two girls of her own, Eveline and Violet. They were very sweet kids, bright and gorgeous. It didn't take too long and soon after I became the fourth member of their family," Alexandru shared with those gathered.

‌



He revealed that in 2016, their daughter Ira was born at John Ratcliffe Hospital in Oxford, and spoke fondly of their blissful family life in Oxford and later near Southampton, until Nell expressed her desire to relocate to Ireland, believing it to be the ideal place for writers. Alexandru recounted how they all embarked on the ferry from the UK in 2019 and made the move to Ireland.

"It was very hard at the beginning but when the pandemic started in March 2020, we fell in love with a very old cottage in Cavan," he said.

"We didn't hesitate in buying it and we made it our new home and from there on, we had a very happy life together."

‌



View 4 Images Former journalist and writer Nell (Image: Anglo Celt)

Paying tribute to Nell as a talented writer, dedicated mother and cancer survivor, he portrayed Ira as a "kind, creative and joyful little girl who embraced music, Irish dancing and life" in Cavan.

Confronted with the incomprehensible loss, he confessed, "Is there any justice, or is there any meaning of what happened? I do not know.

‌



"But perhaps, like in all stories, not just the beginning, or the middle, or the end but the whole story is all that matters."

He concluded his tribute by reciting Dylan Thomas's Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night, a poem his wife had treasured.

Meaningful symbols and cherished belongings of Nell and Ira were placed upon the altar, including a George Orwell book, who served as Nell's greatest literary inspiration; Ira's beloved teddy, 'Ratty', her treasured comfort companion; a vase containing dried flowers that Alex had presented to Nell on Valentine's Day; and Ira's dancing shoes that secured her a spot on iconic Irish TV programme The Late Late Toy Show.

‌



View 4 Images Ira, 10, has been buried in the coffin alongside her mother (Image: Anglo Celt)

Ira's closest friend and classmate, Liam Connolly, reminisced about their cherished moments together, recalling how they attempted to construct a fort only to hurl stones at it afterward, their water pistol battles, and during sleepovers when they would launch their teddies as high as possible.

Liam also remembered their chess matches and how Ira concealed the king piece outside "because she was fed up playing chess with me.

Article continues below

"Ira was one of my best friends and I will miss her a lot," Liam told mourners.

Their coffin was carried from the church as Ira's beloved song 'Hey Brother' by Avicii echoed throughout.

The interment followed at Drumlane cemetery.

News.title: Wildfire expert delivers sobering warning about impact of climate change
News.content:
Wildfire expert delivers sobering warning about impact of climate change

EXCLUSIVE: Andy Elliott spoke out after a spate of blazes in recent days, including in Suffolk, where firefighters tonight continue to tackle flames for a fourth successive day

View 4 Images Emergency services near the scene of the wildfire at Dunwich Heath, Suffolk (Image: Humphrey Nemar/PA Wire)

Devastating wildfires are set to become the new normal, a top consultant has warned today.

‌



Andy Elliott, who has 35 years experience as a firefighter and consultant, says conditions across the UK are becoming very challenging and the government can do more to help land managers and the fire service, including by providing better personal protective equipment.

‌



The alert comes after blazes ripped through Suffolk and other parts of the country in recent days. Mr Elliott told the Mirror: "Compared to 20 years ago, it will be much more frequent. It's likely to happen almost every year. This will be the new normal.

‌



"They are going to become much more frequent. There will be years when we get the odd wet summer, but we can expect to see more flooding in the winter and more frequent hot periods, resulting in drought conditions in the summer."

Met Office names 29 areas facing heavy rain on Monday – see full list READ MORE :

UK drought maps turn red but temperatures set to drop after record dry July READ MORE :

View 4 Images Two fire service workers being driven away from the site covered in soot (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily mirror)

Increasing threat to life

Speaking about the threat to human life, he added: "We should expect to see an increase in wildfires and we should expect to see loss of life. The risk to human life increases all the time.

‌



"We only need to look at France and Spain where people have lost their lives - they're fighting very similar wildfires. The British public need to be aware of that. It's very challenging."

Mr Elliott spoke out as firefighters today continue to tackle the Suffolk wildfire, on Dunwich Heath, close to Sizewell B nuclear power station, for a fourth successive day. At its height, it was estimated to span 370 acres – the size of about 220 football pitches.

View 4 Images Cottages were saved despite the landscape around them being burnt to the ground (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Suffolk wildfire continues

Around 200 families, including residents and holidaymakers staying in caravans and lodges near the heath, were evacuated around two miles to a pop-up rescue centre at Westleton Village Hall late on Wednesday night after police banged on their doors telling them they were in danger.

The National Trust, which have been caring for Dunwich Heath since 1968, have launched a public appeal for donations to help restore the site to its former glory. There were also other ongoing blazes yesterday, including across Europe.

Speaking about the Dunwich Heath fire, a Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service spokesperson said: "The situation remains stable, although firefighting operations continue and crews are responding to hotspots where they emerge.

‌



Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service and supporting agencies have the resources they need on scene and work continues to create a large firebreak around the perimeter of the site.

A Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue spokesperson said their teams expect to carry on working alongside firefighters until Monday night at the earliest. They added: "The main tasking is focused around using drone technology to identify hot spots and areas of reignition.

"We are in awe of the efforts of the firefighters, who are working relentlessly around the clock, and we are grateful to have the drone capability to be able to assist their work."

‌



View 4 Images Greek firefighters try to extinguish a blaze in the area of Porto Germeno, some 70 kilometres (45 miles) northwest of Athens (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Western Europe ravaged by wildfires

There have also been wildfires across Europe in recent weeks, again following huge rises in temperatures. Firefighters held a vast wildfire inside its perimeter in southwestern France today, allowing about 198,000 people to return home after what may have been the country’s largest peacetime evacuation.

But other fires have forced thousands from their homes elsewhere in France and Greece. In the Mediterranean Var, a fire thought to have stopped advancing raced across 10 square kilometers (4 square miles) in six hours on Friday.

Article continues below

The opposing movements — mass returns in France's Gironde region, renewed displacement in the Var and boat evacuations from a Greek resort — underscored how quickly days of firefighting progress can be reversed. At their peak, fires in France and Spain alone drove a third of a million people from homes and vacation sites, stretching firefighters, aircraft and emergency services across simultaneous crises.

News.title: William and Kate bring children to Commonwealth Games
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have brought their three children to watch some of the final sporting events at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Cheering crowds at the city's OVO Hydro were treated to exhilarating performances in the netball semi-finals where the family watched New Zealand's 61-54 win over England.

Known as the Duke and Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland, the couple also spent time meeting athletes, staff and volunteers during a slightly blustery visit to the venue on the River Clyde.

They then made their way to the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome - where they chatted to British cyclist Laura Kenny and sat one row behind Olympic cycling champion, Sir Chris.

News.title: Sir John Curtice: The 'Burnham bounce' is real but it's not massive
News.content:
But with still no more than a narrow lead over Reform, it is unsurprising Burnham has ruled out an early election. In any event, Reform's displacement from first place in the polls for the first time in over a year appears to owe more to its own difficulties than it does to Labour's new-found popularity.

Reform has been dogged in recent weeks by questions about the legality of the source of some of its funding and about whether Farage should have declared to the Commons authorities some of the funding he received before being elected an MP. Following these allegations, Farage announced on 7 July that he was standing down and putting himself again before the voters of his Clacton constituency in a by-election now scheduled for 13 August.

This move appears to have backfired. Immediately before Farage's announcement, Reform's average poll rating stood at 27%. In the polls conducted immediately after Farage's announcement, it fell by three points to 24%, the level at which it still stands now, and the lowest it has been for 15 months. At the same time, Farage's personal poll ratings are now the worst they have been since he returned as Reform's leader during the 2024 election campaign.

News.title: He thought a fitness supplement was safe, but it sent him into psychosis
News.content:
Daniel Murphy thought he was taking a safe and tested dietary supplement that would help him put on muscle in the gym.

But over the following two years, his mental health spiralled to such a degree he ended up in a state of psychosis in which he believed his wife was trying to steal his business and his mother-in-law was going to kill him.

Unknown to Daniel, the daily pills he had been taking had been mixed with testosterone.

The 32-year-old is one of 54,000 consumers listed in a case against a multimillion-pound peptide company based in the US, which sold its products around the world.

The owner of Paradigm Peptides, Matthew Kawa, was jailed for five years and 10 months on Thursday after he admitted deliberately selling unapproved medicines, trying to deceive people about what they were and illegally bringing the products into the country.

His sister, Jennifer Stechkober, who also pleaded guilty to selling unapproved medicines, was sent to prison for a year and four months.

Both admitted they had lied about where the pills were sourced, their purity and their company's testing procedures. Despite claiming the supplements were manufactured in the US, they were actually imported from China, India and several other countries. The pair also faked certificates of analysis, the documents that prove the safety and quality of a product.

Paradigm Peptides' website had stated it "stringently" tested all their products to ensure "efficacy, purity and potency", but the pair admitted not testing or analysing any of the products they sold, so they had not been aware they had been mixed with testosterone.

News.title: The five dramatic days that shook Infantino and world football
News.content:
The question many have asked around Infantino's plan is tied into a separate - but critical - aspect of the fundamental reasons behind this week unravelling.

Fifa is a not-for-profit organisation. It has huge financial reserves - over $2bn (Â£1.48bn) - and is expected to announce record revenues of about $15bn (Â£11.13bn) in relation to this summer's World Cup.

Given that backdrop - and the reality some countries simply did not need the extra $40m (Â£29.67m) being offered for football development initiatives if they signed up to Infantino's plan by 19 September - many wondered why private investment was needed in the first place.

It was a question that needed to be asked. But that did not happen in public - or, it has become apparent, privately in Fifa's corridors of power.

Many of Fifa's most senior people - from vice-presidents to special advisers and executives - did not have a chance to ask any questions, simply because they had no clue the plans were being drawn up.

Uefa had strongly opposed the plans from the moment they became public. When they were dropped, its response was damning.

"The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family," it said in a statement.

"When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa's member associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said: 'Of course we have to be transparent.'

"He told the assembled stakeholders: 'The money of Fifa is your money. It's not the money of the Fifa president. You are the national associations and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.'

"On both these promises, he has failed to deliver."

It was not the first time a lack of transparency had been highlighted.

Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa - president of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), and one of eight Fifa vice-presidents - referred to it too.

He said any future plans that may impact global football should be presented to members "in a timely, transparent and meaningful manner".

"The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game," he added.

Football Australia chair Anter Isaac said trust was earned "not simply through good decisions, but through the integrity of the processes that lead to them".

"Football has never stood still, nor should it," he said.

"Some principles, however, should never change. Integrity. Independence. Good governance. Transparency. Meaningful consultation. Due process. These are not constraints on progress."

News.title: Faisal Islam: Four reasons why the World Cup plan never stacked up
News.content:
In the slides, Fifa's central argument was that football does not raise enough cash in relation to its fan base, that "Fifa has been under-monetised versus other leagues" and so "global football development gets squeezed".

It did this with reference to a comparative chart showing annual revenue as well as revenue per fan for Fifa, the Uefa Champions League, Premier League, US baseball and NFL American football.

On the face of it, Fifa is the poorer cousin at just $1 per global fan, compared to NFL's $52.80. But this measure is rather suspect.

The World Cup is not an annual competition - it happens once every four years. If instead this was done on revenue per World Cup 2026 match, Fifa makes multiples of the Premier League, perhaps more than three times as much.

As important, football is decentralised globally, so more of the revenues go to individual leagues, such as the Premier League or Champions League. Fifa was effectively arguing it wanted to keep more of that overall football pie.

Football's fans are also spread across the globe, in rich and poor countries alike. NFL has a much smaller base concentrated in the US and is pretty much the whole of American Football.

Finally, about half of NFL's revenues are paid out as wages. Fifa does not pay Erling Haaland or Lionel Messi or Vozinha. Profits would have yielded a rather different result than the chartâs focus on revenues.

News.title: Infantino on the brink? Who might replace him if he goes?
News.content:
Life moves fast for Fifa president Gianni Infantino.

It was doing so last month as he was zig-zagging across the United States in a private jet to make him virtually omnipresent as the World Cup reached its crescendo.

On 19 July he must have felt on top of the world as, together with US President Donald Trump, they handed the trophy over to Spain.

Less than two weeks later, Infantino is in a lonely place after scrapping controversial plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investment.

Condemned by UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, castigated by fans of the game he professes to want to protect. These can easily be deflected as hazards of the job.

Less so the threatened boycott of Fifa competitions by European governing body Uefa, and its subsequent stunning statement in which it declared it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership.

Concacaf (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and the AFC (Asia) also - in their own ways - have offered withering assessments of how Fifa is being run under Infantino.

"This issue extends far beyond a single proposal," said the AFC. "Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed."

Sources say, in addition to rejecting Infantino's plan, the vast majority of the Concacaf members are either losing faith in the Fifa president's ability to govern the game, or have lost it altogether.

On top of that, Carlos Cordeiro, special adviser to Infantino and appointed by Trump as senior adviser to the White House Task Force on the 2026 World Cup, has resigned.

Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to Associated Press that Fifa's own administration was "deceived" about the project.

BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

It feels as though the walls are closing in on Infantino.

But if this is the beginning of the end of his tenure, who takes over?

News.title: What is Iran's Pickaxe Mountain and why does Trump say he wants to bomb it?
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to bomb a suspected underground nuclear site in Iran known as Pickaxe Mountain, where recent satellite images appear to show construction work taking place.

Pickaxe Mountain is one of the few Iranian sites linked to the country's nuclear programme that has not been the target of US and Israeli strikes. There have been unproven claims that some of Iran's stock of highly enriched uranium may be kept there, which could be further enriched for use in nuclear weapons.

"We'll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily," Trump told reporters on 21 July. And on 28 July he said: "I know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe. It's not a big problem - we took out their nuclear sites, and we'll have to take out Pickaxe if we don't make a deal."

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said on 22 July that "no nuclear activity is taking place" at Pickaxe Mountain, and described US threats as "a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage".

BBC Verify and BBC Persian have spoken to experts and analysed satellite imagery to piece together what we know about the site, and the potential impact of any strike.

News.title: Decades-long search ends with discovery of new marine species
News.content:
The Great Barrier Reef might be the world's most famous underwater ecosystem, but hidden in UK waters lies an ancient marine world you may not have heard of.

Known as maerl beds, these carpets of coral-like seaweed create some of the richest habitats in the sea.

And 40 years ago, while studying one such bed for her PhD, Prof Christine Maggs found a fragment of pink-striped seaweed living on maerl she had never seen before.

The discovery would become a lifelong obsession and a decades-long scientific puzzle.

News.title: Greater Manchester mayor says Burnham's new powers will change lives
News.content:
Greater Manchester's new Mayor Bev Craig has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham's move to give the regions more power could "change our lives".

The Labour candidate claimed victory in Thursday's by-election after securing 309,525 votes over Reform's Sian Astley, who won 157,178.

The 41-year-old will succeed Burnham as mayor, after he stood down to run in the Makerfield by-election in June. The pair appeared together at a Labour rally in Manchester after Craig's election win.

Craig said: "For a prime minister two weeks in, to start giving powers out of Whitehall and putting it in the places that can make a difference - that can change our lives."

She added: "I will rise to his challenge about taking the power and control that he is offering mayors like me to make our regions better.

"Because that is what it is all about."

News.title: Soap star Shane Richie facing drink-drive charge
News.content:
EastEnders actor Shane Richie is to appear in court charged with drink-driving, police have said.

Essex Police confirmed it was called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the Church Langley Way area of Harlow, shortly before 23:20 BST on Wednesday.

A force spokesman confirmed the 62-year-old, of Tadworth, Surrey, was arrested and a charge of drink-driving had been authorised against him.

It added Richie, real name Shane Roche, was due to appear at Colchester Magistrates' Court on 9 September.

Richie plays Alfie Moon in EastEnders, making his first appearance in the BBC soap in 2002.

The Sun reported he was arrested, external at a Tesco petrol station forecourt.

Essex Police said: "Officers were called to reports of a suspected drink-driver in the area of Church Langley Way, Harlow, shortly before 23:20 on Wednesday, 29 July.

"On arrival, officers arrested a man.

"A charge of drink-driving has subsequently been authorised against Shane Roche, 62, of Tadworth, Surrey."

Richie's representative has been contacted for comment.

Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.

News.title: Greek police fast-tracking tests to find out how British woman found in suitcase died
News.content:
Police investigating the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase in Greece say they could determine how she died "in the coming days" as they are fast-tracking toxicology tests.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in an abandoned building in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, reportedly by a homeless man.

The 38-year-old, known to her family as Lisa, is thought to have travelled to Greece from Edinburgh in late June, and went missing on 15 July.

Greek authorities are also looking to trace Lisa's American friends, who they said were also staying in Kypseli.

News.title: Suffolk fire 'stable' and fundraiser set up
News.content:
The blaze that has devastated heathland in Suffolk is now "stable" but crews have continued to tackle hotspots on what is the fourth day since the flames took hold.

The fire affecting RSPB Minsmere and Dunwich Heath started at about 17:00 BST on Wednesday and engulfed 371 acres (150 hectares) at its height - equivalent to the size of 210 football pitches.

Wildlife habitats of some of the UK's rarest species have been destroyed.

The National Trust has launched a fundraiser to help the habitats "recover and thrive in a changing climate".

Meanwhile, some local people have started returning to normal life.

A scheduled market went ahead at nearby Westleton earlier, which an organiser said was the chance for people to take their minds off recent events.

News.title: Manhunt after prisoner escapes from van outside court
News.content:
A manhunt is under way after a prisoner escaped from a van taking him to a court appearance.

Stephen Grzyb, 22, was being transported by contractor GEOAmey from Belle Vale custody suite to Liverpool Magistrates' Court to face burglary charges on Saturday.

As the van arrived outside the court building, at around 10:00 BST, Grzyb was able to flee and ran off down Red Cross Street towards the Strand.

Merseyside Police said: "Assisting him in any way will bring police to your own door, so it is not an association worth keeping."

News.title: Stick to spending limits, PM and chancellor tell ministers in joint memo
News.content:
Healey said the budget would "meet our fiscal rules" and "give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future".

A report in the Times says the joint letter told ministers they must work "within the budgets they have already got" even while "pay[ing] for new things they want to do this year and next".

While the ongoing war in Iran is pushing up inflation and borrowing costs, senior Treasury sources confirmed that the government was determined to stay "well within the fiscal rules" inherited from Sir Keir and Reeves.

But Burnham has said his government will stick to Labour's fiscal rules on spending and borrowing as well as the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase income tax, VAT or National Insurance contributions.

He also said he will honour the fiscal rules imposed by Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

An influential think tank said earlier this week that the prime minister only had a small margin of error to do this and that Healey may have to cut spending or raise taxes to meet Burnham's policy priorities, such as extra defence spending and better social care.

Healey was defence secretary under Sir Keir but resigned after a row over defence spending commitments, saying he was "certain" that Britain should lift its spending to 3% by 2030.

Questioned about funding on Thursday, Burnham's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting repeatedly refused to commit to that target.

"Before we set out specific spending commitments, we will also set out how we pay for them at the same time," he said.

Reeves left a Â£22bn buffer in her last Budget, but persistent inflation due to the Iran war could have eroded that.

On Friday, the PM said he would give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his efforts to move power away from Westminster.

Reeves had previously said that regional mayors could be given control of some tax revenue to spend on their local priorities.

Labour pledged to devolve more powers to local councils and mayors in areas such as housing and transport as part of its 2024 election manifesto.

More details of Burnham's plan are expected to be announced in the Budget, but the government said the rate of income tax will not change as a direct result of the reforms.

AJ Bell public policy director Tom Selby said Healey "doesn't have the luxury of pointing the finger of blame at the last administration".

"Healey will likely spend a chunk of his time leafing through the thesaurus looking for new ways to rephrase the 'tough choices' message of his predecessor," he said.

Shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the announcement of the budget date meant "89 more days of unfunded spending commitments and damaging tax speculation until we get some details".

"Eighty-nine more days for Brits to wait before they know how much their taxes are going to go up to fund Burnham's spending addiction," he said.

News.title: Police arrest men over alleged modern day slavery
News.content:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of modern day slavery and money laundering offences.

Dorset Police said the 20-year-old from Sussex and a 22-year-old from Buckinghamshire were arrested during an investigation into suspected exploitation, immigration and financial offences.

Officers made the arrests after raiding a business premises in Gillingham, Dorset, it added.

Three further men were also arrested for immigration offences, the force continued.

Dorset Police said the raid followed intelligence from the community and detailed enquiries.

The force added that the "day of action" had led to a number of individuals being safeguarded.

News.title: King's Theatre in Edinburgh re-opens after £41m refurbishment
News.content:
Edinburgh's historic King's Theatre has re-opened following a Â£41m refurbishment.

The 120-year-old venue has been closed for almost four years while the work was carried out.

The project has seen extensive modernisation work aimed at making the building more accessible.

First Minister John Swinney described the building as "an iconic landmark" and a "prized part of Edinburgh's identity and heritage".

"Its reopening will strengthen the city's vibrant cultural sector, draw in tens of thousands of visitors and support jobs and businesses across Edinburgh and beyond," he said.

Members of the public will be able to tour the theatre on Saturday and Sunday before performances begin on Friday.

News.title: Donald Trump’s intervention in the Ceuta crisis is a distraction from the serious issue of migration
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging.
