Sports.title: There can be no letup. Humiliated Infantino must stand down at Fifa or be removed | Nick Ames
Sports.content:
There is no time to dance around the subject. Gianni Infantino must stand down as Fifa president or otherwise be legally removed. No fresh chances can be made available for an official who has demolished trust in football’s integrity and governance, trashing all remaining credibility of the body that oversees the world’s most-cherished sport.

Infantino was forced into a humiliating climbdown on Saturday morning when he accepted the failure of his plan to sell off portions of the World Cup to private investment. He resolved to resume dialogue about football’s growth “in the spirit of shared interest in our game”. But such a naked attempt to save his own skin cannot hold. Every day Infantino remains in power is a fresh stain on an institution whose reputation is on the floor.

The overreach involved in unilaterally launching the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme – with its vision to place huge influence on football’s future in the palms of venture capitalists – would be enough to bring down most leaders. But Infantino’s rap sheet goes far beyond that. He has routinely made a mockery of Fifa’s own statutes and governance regulations, so nobody should be surprised that patience has finally snapped in corridors of power globally. Fifa’s “football unites the world” slogan has never looked more empty.

Article 10.3 of those regulations, which specifically pertains to the presidency, requires the incumbent to ensure “Fifa’s objectives, mission, strategic direction, policies and values are sustainably pursued, protected and implemented, and that a positive image of Fifa is fostered”. It stipulates “promoting friendly and peaceful relations within Fifa”, which is a nonsense given the degree to which federations and senior personnel have distanced themselves from Infantino in recent days.

The rules give no green light to the pursuit of multiple private projects that, most recently in lockstep with the current US administration or its tributaries, have been tabled with scant appetite for oversight or explanation.

Where to begin? The Folarin Balogun saga tipped many leading figures in football, particularly in Europe, towards the edge. There had already been widespread bafflement and disgust at Infantino’s presentation of the new Fifa peace prize to Donald Trump in December, with little background given about the process and highly contestable information provided about the US president’s qualifying achievements. Stakeholders were frustrated by a lack of consultation about the introduction of “hydration breaks”, which fundamentally toyed with the fabric of matches at this summer’s World Cup.

View image in fullscreen The saga involving Folarin Balogun after his ban for a red card was suspended tipped many leading figures in football towards the edge. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

The bizarre expedited bidding process for the 2034 tournament, which resulted in Saudi Arabia’s candidature being waved through in December 2024, also brought widespread criticism. This list only covers the past 20 months of controversies inflicted by Infantino, capped on Friday by revelations that plans for a 64-team World Cup are in full swing.

When a scathing statement from Uefa on Saturday called for an end to “secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game”, it was not only referring to the FFE project and its casual sidelining of other decision makers within Fifa.

A critical mass has been reached. Uefa took a decisive lead in following more than a year of harsh words with strong, united action in pledging to boycott future Fifa tournaments if Infantino did not withdraw his plan. It undoubtedly influenced the outcome and the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, secured an achievement that may define his own reign. But it will mean nothing if Infantino, who is understood to have deployed a major consultancy to smooth relations with federations in recent days, is given the oxygen to dangle fresh promises and turn heads back towards the status quo.

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino’s rap sheet goes far beyond attempting to launch the Fifa Forward Enterprise unilaterally. Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPA

There is an acknowledgment within Uefa and beyond that the pace must not let up. Senior figures are adamant Infantino must not survive the current scandal. Some insiders feel a crucial next step will be for member associations, the overwhelming majority of whom had formally pledged their support for Infantino’s re-election next March, to recall those letters.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Doing so requires a request to Fifa but could, in sufficient numbers, be a de facto vote of no confidence in Infantino. Fifa had lobbied aggressively for those submissions but many FAs would now be red faced if their expression of fealty towards Infantino was more widely publicised.

Member associations have a duty not to shrink in staving off existential threats to their sport otherwise they, like Infantino, are doing it an egregious disservice. Backing away now would mean leaving the job half done at best.

Uefa have pledged to devise a new method for distributing Fifa’s wealth, delving into its multibillion cash reserves without “selling the family silver”. Behind the scenes it continues to work with other confederations in an effort to find credible candidates for Infantino’s replacement, with a view to running in the election should the Swiss hold on until then. The present crisis can be used to reshape football for the better but only if Infantino is not in situ to impose the final say.

The alternative is that Fifa, and by extension the game, continue lurching from one disaster to the next. It is no laughing matter when the public conversation around football centres on one man, his ego and brazen ventures.

In December Zvonimir Boban, a former sidekick to Infantino as Fifa’s deputy secretary general, told the Guardian that “the way is lost” after the peace prize award to Trump. Fifa will not find a route back until Infantino plays no further part in its operation.

Sports.title: Transfer news: Welbeck joins Chelsea, Brentford complete record Sangaré deal
Sports.content:
Chelsea have signed Brighton’s veteran striker Danny Welbeck in a deal worth a reported £5m. Welbeck has agreed a two-year contract and will link up with Xabi Alonso’s squad on their pre-season tour.

The 35-year-old’s move to Stamford Bridge is a break from Chelsea’s policy of signing younger players with the potential to be developed. It is the first time they have paid a transfer fee for a player over the age of 26 since they signed Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang from Barcelona in 2022 when the striker was 33.

“When you hear of interest from Chelsea, it’s something that fills you with such immense pride. Knowing the history of Chelsea, it’s a club that wants to win trophies and is pushing to do that every single season,” Welbeck said.

“I’m really honoured to come to a club of this stature at what feels like a really exciting time. I know a few of the boys already and I’ve had fantastic conversations with the manager and already feel that connection. I’ve got that fire in my belly and I’m ready to give it everything for this club to make everyone at Chelsea, and the supporters, proud.”

Alonso was keen to add experience to his squad after last season’s disappointing 10th-place finish in the Premier League. He opted for Welbeck after the former Manchester United and Arsenal forward enjoyed a memorable campaign with Brighton.

Welbeck, who has 42 caps for England, scored 13 goals in 37 Premier League games last term after netting 10 times in 2024-25.

Welbeck’s arrival in west London will raise questions about the future of Chelsea striker Liam Delap, who signed from Ipswich last season, as well as fellow forwards Nicolas Jackson and Marc Guiu.

Welbeck is the latest player to move from Brighton to Chelsea in recent years after João Pedro, Moisés Caicedo, Robert Sánchez and Marc Cucurella, who joined Real Madrid earlier this summer.

Chelsea spent a British record £117m to sign the England forward Morgan Rogers, 24, from Aston Villa in July. They also secured the France defender Maxence Lacroix, 26, from Crystal Palace for £52m earlier this week and signed Atalanta defender Marco Palestra, 21, for £43m.

Brentford seal record Sangaré deal

Brentford have signed the Mali international Mamadou Sangaré from ⁠Lens for a club-record fee, reported to be £39m. Sangaré, 24, joins Brentford on a five-year contract, with ⁠the option to extend for another year.

“Mamadou ​is someone ‌that we’ve tracked ‌for quite some time. He’s been on ‌our radar and was a player we were really keen to bring in,” the Brentford head coach Keith Andrews said. “He’s a humble young man, but he’s equally as ⁠determined to succeed in his career. He ​fits ​everything we want from ​a Brentford player, on and ​off the ‌pitch.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Sangaré left Austria’s Rapid Vienna to ‌join Lens last year, and featured prominently as they won the ​French Cup for the first time and finished second in Ligue 1.

View image in fullscreen Mamadou Sangaré has swapped RC Lens for Brentford in a £39m move. Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/Reuters

Bournemouth have announced the signing of António Silva from Benfica for a fee believed to be in the region of £25m. The 22-year-old defender becomes new manager Marco Rose’s second signing of the summer after the arrival of Álvaro Rodríguez earlier this week.

Silva made 235 senior appearances for Benfica and collected six major honours during his time in Portugal. He told the club website: “I am very happy to be here. It’s a pleasure to play for Bournemouth and in the Premier League.

“The mentality is always to win. I will try my best, and I will play for the fans. We have everything here that helps us perform on the pitch, and I can’t wait to get started.”

Sports.title: Women’s football continues to be used as a pawn in Gianni Infantino’s Fifa tenure | Suzanne Wrack
Sports.content:
Despite not having been deemed worthy of more than a single mention in Fifa’s 25-page sales deck to its 211 member associations on its doomed proposal to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, now very expensive waste paper, it was women’s football that had found itself on the frontline in the fight for the “soul of football”.

Uefa’s statement that European national teams would not “participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership”, was a bold, necessary and effective declaration of war against the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino.

However, with the Under-20 Women’s World Cup being held in Poland next month; the Under-17 Women’s World Cup and Uefa’s qualifying playoffs for the senior tournament both beginning in October; and the big one, the Women’s World Cup itself, taking place in Brazil next summer, women’s tournaments would have been the first test cases had a boycott gone ahead.

There was no further detail on the FA’s plans for England’s two-legged World Cup playoff against Greece, but Uefa’s call for a boycott would have had an impact on the women’s game in September.

A boycott of the Women’s World Cup would have been catastrophic and yet that was the likely consequence of Infantino’s deadline. The 2023 Women’s World Cup was the first to break even after generating more than $570m (£424m) in revenue and Fifa said in May 2025 it is targeting $1bn in revenue from the 2027 edition.

The women’s game is so desperately reliant on international competition for accelerating its growth that the knock-on impact of having no World Cup would have set progress back far more than four years.

However, Uefa was not wrong in its stance and the subsequent collapse of Infantino’s masterplan after the almighty fallout from demonstrates as much. It was not European football’s governing body that engineered the timeframe that put women’s football on the frontline and it was correct not to exclude women’s football, or youth football, from its arsenal in the fight back against Infantino’s attempt to steamroller through his plans.

View image in fullscreen England’s dream of avenging their World Cup final defeat in 2023 was thrown into doubt by Gianni Infantino’s proposals. Photograph: Zac Goodwin/PA

The blame for the threat posed by a boycott on women’s football lay squarely at the feet of Gianni “I have four daughters” Infantino, who was praised in February by Jill Ellis, Fifa’s chief football officer and twice a World Cup-winning coach, for his “commitment to accelerating the women’s game and increasing women’s influence in shaping its future” and under whose leadership “investment has moved from rhetoric to action”.

To an extent Ellis is right – Infantino is the Fifa president who has done the most for the women’s game. But when his predecessor is Sepp Blatter, a man who said in 2004 that “tighter shorts” was the way to get more people watching the women’s game, the bar is staggeringly low.

Yes, under Infantino Fifa has invested more in the women’s game than ever before, but it has been a pawn in his tenure: initially useful for showing just how progressive and in tune with modern society he and Fifa are, and now useful because it presents an opportunity for medium- to long-term financial gain as one of the fastest growing and least‑tapped areas of the game.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Step behind the rhetoric and handouts and Infantino’s real attitude to the women’s game is evident. In 2023 Sky News reported the Fifa president had left the Women’s World Cup for Tahiti after less than a week, before returning later in the tournament. By contrast, he went to at least some part of every one of the 64 games of the 2022 men’s World Cup and at times appeared at two a day during the latest men’s edition despite the huge environmental impact of using a private jet.

View image in fullscreen The 2027 Women’s World Cup in Brazil starts in less than 11 months. Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters

Perhaps Infantino waited until the beginning of a new four-year men’s World Cup cycle to try to limit the impact of any backlash on the showpiece event, but in doing so he added to the pile of evidence demonstrative of real attitude towards women’s football, with women’s edition of the tournament on the imminent horizon.

It would have been oddly fitting, then, if the women’s game had become the sun that melted his Icarus wings. Luckily, women’s football didn’t have to pay that costly price. However, this episode must act as a warning, both to those who care about the development of the women’s game and its future and those who care about the future of the men’s game.

The reality is that the European Super League debacle and this latest and most blatant of attempts to hand the wealth of football to private finance vultures show that private finance will keep coming back as they search for ways to get a piece of the pie.

Sports.title: Amanda Staveley consortium set to buy Gold family’s 25.1% stake in West Ham
Sports.content:
A consortium led by Amanda Staveley has reached an agreement to buy a ‌25.1% stake in West ⁠Ham after Vanessa Gold, daughter of the former chair David Gold, ⁠agreed to sell ⁠her ​family’s shares in the Championship club.

The move by the businesswoman who helped lead the Saudi consortium takeover of Newcastle comes after a previously agreed sale to fellow shareholder and Czech businessman ⁠Daniel Kretinsky fell through.

The Gold family ​trust owns the 25.1% stake in West Ham, ‌who were relegated from the Premier League last season just two seasons after winning the Europa Conference League in 2023. However, current shareholders will also be presented with the chance to buy out the Gold family under an ongoing process.

Gold said in a statement: “As the daughter of David Gold, it was a great honour to step into a joint chair and director role at the club following his passing in 2023. Whether as a youth team player, a lifelong fan or an owner, my father’s priority was always to champion and protect this great club. Over the past three years I have taken huge personal pride in continuing that legacy and will always be hugely grateful to the staff, players and fans who allowed me to do so.

“On June 12, Daniel Kretínsky and I agreed a sale that would have made EP Group the single largest shareholder in West Ham. Unfortunately, since that time, the original deal and other alternatives that we have discussed could not be brought to fruition.

View image in fullscreen West Ham were relegated from the Premier League last season. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/Reuters

“In light of this, I have now reached an agreement to sell my family’s shareholding to a consortium led by Amanda Staveley, Mehrdad Ghodoussi and PCP Capital Partners. This sale remains subject to a pre-emption process, under which existing shareholders have the option to buy the shares instead.

“While the process has not yet concluded, I wanted to be open with our fans about where things stand and my intentions. My ambition throughout this process has been to ensure the club has the right leadership and ownership to enable West Ham to achieve its potential and return to its rightful place in the Premier League.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Amanda Staveley, Mehrdad Ghodoussi and PCP Capital Partners will bring deep experience and understanding of what it takes to lead a successful football club, and I have every confidence in what she and her partners can bring to West Ham. While the sale process proceeds, I will continue to act in the club’s best interests, as my father did and would expect of me.”



Staveley brokered the deal which allowed a Saudi-backed consortium to buy-out then Newcastle owner Mike Ashley in October 2021, and she and Ghodoussi oversaw the club’s rise from Premier League relegation candidates to Champions League participants and, after their departure during the summer of 2024, Carabao Cup winners.

The Hammers dropped out of the top flight at the end of last season and will begin the process of attempting to secure a swift return at Burnley on 16 August.

Sports.title: De Zerbi wants ‘lovely guy’ Richarlison to stay at Tottenham after winner sinks Chelsea
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi wants Richarlison to stay at Tottenham, but says the striker, who has been linked with a move away, is still unsure about his future.

The Brazilian scored a last-gasp winner as 10-man Tottenham defeated Chelsea 2-1 in a pre-season friendly in Sydney, with Kevin Danso sent off just minutes after coming on as a half-time substitute.

Speaking after the game, De Zerbi said Richarlison had not clarified if he was going to depart this summer. “I don’t know, I didn’t understand well, because sometimes he said to stay, sometimes he leaves, we have to speak. Anyway, there is not any problem, he’s a lovely guy. All of us love him, the teammates, the club, the staff, because he works hard every day.”

Richarlison has less than a year left on his contract after joining Tottenham from Everton in 2022. He has struggled to find consistent form during his time in north London but De Zerbi said it would be difficult to replace his goals.

“For me he’s still an important player because it’s not so easy to find another striker as Richarlison, because Richarlison scored goals and he knows the way. The new striker, we don’t know, the other striker, we don’t know. He [Richarlison] scored 12 goals last season, not for luck, because he feels the way to score.”

Richarlison bagged a 92nd-minute winner for Tottenham against Chelsea in front of more than 80,000 fans at Sydney’s Accor Stadium. The Brazilian was the first player to react after Jamie Donley’s shot came back off a post, prodding the ball into an empty net to avert the need for a penalty shootout.

It was the first time that the two sides have met outside the UK and the match started in the spirit of a true London derby. Conor Gallagher flew into a challenge on Dário Essugo after 10 minutes, picking up a yellow card and a fair few heckles from the largely Chelsea-supporting crowd. Jan Paul van Hecke clattered into João Pedro, while Dominic Solanke and Levi Colwill tussled off the ball.

This fixture has had its fair share of red cards over the years and there was another one to add to the list, after Danso was sent off three minutes after coming off the bench. A poor surface got the better of the Spurs defender as he failed to control a backpass, allowing João Pedro to run on to the ball and through on goal. Danso lunged headfirst into the Chelsea forward, with the referee reaching straight for his pocket.

View image in fullscreen Kevin Danso is shown a red card three minutes after coming on as a substitute. Photograph: David Neilson/EPA

De Zerbi said the sending off made the game harder for both sides. “It was worse for us and for Chelsea, because if you consider the condition of the pitch, very bad. And if you consider we are starting from two weeks, maybe less than three weeks, the second half you start the fatigue and playing, attacking against 10 players behind the line of the ball is tough for every team.”

De Zerbi’s side were on top in the early stages and took a deserved lead on 17 minutes when the new signing Sandro Tonali scored his first goal for Tottenham. The midfielder’s side-footed effort from outside the area took a deflection, wrong-footing the Chelsea goalkeeper Teddy Sharman-Lowe before nestling into the bottom corner.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Spurs were only ahead for four minutes, as Estêvão Willian got the better of Andy Robertson to head home at the back post after some good work from Jamie Gittens down the left.

The game lost its competitive edge in the second half with both sides making a flurry of substitutions, before Richarlison settled it at the death.

Chelsea will now head to Hong Kong where they will be joined by Mykhailo Mudryk, who has been cleared to play again after the Football Association and the World Anti-Doping Agency resolved his appeal against a ban for failing a doping test. The Ukrainian winger was suspended for four years after failing a drug test in 2024. De Zerbi, who managed Mudryk at Shakhtar Donetsk, said he viewed the player as one of his “sons”.

“I’m very happy – he deserves to play, he’s a good guy, top player. Hopefully he can show what he suffered in the last two years, in the next season, maybe not against Tottenham, but he’s a lovely guy and he’s a very, very good player.”

Sports.title: Faster, faster: Iraola in a rush to plug Liverpool gaps before Premier League starts
Sports.content:
“Faster, faster,” bellowed Andoni Iraola throughout the open training session Liverpool held in Chicago on Friday. His first pre-season tour as Liverpool head coach ends at the city’s famous Soldier Field Stadium on Sunday, with a friendly against Leeds, and “faster, faster” could apply to all aspects of the club’s preparations for a new Premier League campaign that begins in three weeks’ time.

Iraola was in his element as he immersed himself at the centre of every training drill that Liverpool performed at Chicago Fire’s Endeavor Health Performance Center, their base for the past two weeks in the US. “Faster, faster” was the new head coach’s instruction to his players as three teams of seven worked on their pressing games. He also shouted it when they walked over to a different pitch, recently vacated by Robert Lewandowski and his new Chicago Fire teammates, to work on offensive and defensive set-piece routines. Sprints were demanded following every rondo.

There is an urgency to Iraola’s situation at Liverpool as he works towards his first season in charge, not only to his style of football. Post World-Cup holidays have deprived him of eight first-team players so far, injuries of a further six.

It was telling that, after Liverpool’s open training session had ended, many of the fans invited headed to the gym for a look through its glass windows. Jérémy Jacquet, Liverpool’s £60m recruit from Rennes, was inside working on his recovery from a shoulder problem.

He was joined by Giovanni Leoni, who is rehabilitating from an anterior cruciate ligament rupture and appears to have doubled in chest size since sustaining the injury on his Liverpool debut last September. Nearby was Joe Gomez, who pulled up with a muscle injury eight minutes into the first friendly of the tour. All central defenders, all out.

The concentration of problems in one particular area was a recurring theme under Arne Slot last season and has not eased yet. Two 18-year-olds, Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, have impressed in their absence but Liverpool are looking to loan out the latter next season having been unable to secure a work permit.

Among the observers on Friday was Mike Gordon, the president of Liverpool’s owners, Fenway Sports Group, who has returned to a more hands-on role at the club after the departure of Michael Edwards as FSG’s chief executive of football.

View image in fullscreen Teenage defender Ifeanyi Ndukwe is likely to be loaned out by Liverppool. Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty Images

Gordon is expected to be in attendance at Soldier Field on Sunday when Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak should feature for the first time in pre-season. FSG will not be the only ones at Liverpool looking for a return on their combined £241m investment in the pair.

“We need a very good version of Florian,” Iraola said this week, when confirming he intends to play the Germany international “in that position behind the striker” rather than on the left, where he operated without reward at the World Cup, or in the variety of roles that Slot tried without success.

Wirtz supplying Isak and/or Hugo Ekitiké was always the intended plan of attack for Liverpool last season. The trio ultimately played only 119 minutes together as injuries struck. That stat was never lost on Slot as he was ushered to the exit after a turbulent and toxic campaign.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Liverpool need a very good version of Isak, too. The excuse of playing catch-up having missed pre-season, or almost four months of the season due to a fractured ankle and fibula, no longer washes for a striker who featured in all four games of Sweden’s World Cup. Isak has looked sharp in pre-season training. He not only has to sustain that sharpness next season but convince he is a suitable fit for this Liverpool team.

View image in fullscreen Florian Wirtz will be used behind the striker this season under Andoni Iraola for Liverpool. Photograph: Becky Oliver/LFC/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

Iraola’s options and vision for Liverpool will improve as senior names return but he undoubtedly requires more help through the transfer market. Work is under way on a move for Bradley Barcola, who is open to leaving Paris Saint-Germain for Anfield, but a deal for a winger who the European champions value at £145m is yet to be struck.

A lack of defensive cover cost Liverpool last season and remains a glaring issue, and there are doubts over the futures of Curtis Jones, Federico Chiesa and Harvey Elliott, among others.

Liverpool’s head coach has admitted he “hates this month of August” because of the uncertainty that surrounds players while the season starts. “It’s difficult to build a proper team with a lot of question marks,” he added. Between Soldier Field on Sunday and St James’ Park on 23 August, the building work must accelerate.

Sports.title: Have you ever switched allegiance as a football fan? You are not alone | Luke McLaughlin
Sports.content:
“I was fanatically pro-German when the Germans were here to protect us against the Americans, and now that Americans are here to protect us against the Germans, I am fanatically pro-American … you and your country will have no more loyal partisan in Italy than me – but only as long as you remain in Italy.”

This passage from Joseph Heller’s Catch-22 – as an old Italian man explains the logic behind his fickle wartime expedience to a naive American soldier – plays with the question of what constitutes true strength. Universally perceived as weak, Italy are in fact the strongest nation in the second world war, according to the old man. And that, sort of, explains my feelings on football fandom.

My dad was passionate about cricket and chess. But I was a football-mad kid, and he dutifully escorted my brother and I to watch West Ham v Nottingham Forest at Upton Park in November 1987. Dad naturally knew about Brian Clough and correctly predicted it would be an entertaining game: the hosts won 3-2.

After that ridiculously exciting day as a 10-year-old, and despite living in south London, I became a Forest supporter, despite photos existing of me in Everton and Tottenham kits earlier in childhood. My mid-1980s decision to support Everton, for clarity, had been pure, unadulterated glory-hunting. Why I then decided to switch to Tottenham, I don’t recall, but it may have had something to do with Paul Gascoigne’s unique ability.

Geographically I should have supported Crystal Palace or Millwall given I was brought up between their grounds: I vividly remember visiting the Den with a Swindon-supporting schoolmate during the era of Terry Hurlock.

As a cricket fan, I have stuck with Middlesex since childhood, but there was never any familial impetus to support a football club. My brother became an Arsenal fan and when I was old enough to regularly attend games alone I started following Forest around London, including a draw at the Den in 1993-94 marred by post-match violence after a Stan Collymore equaliser ended Millwall’s playoff hopes.

When Forest sank into the doldrums after the magical mid-90s, I started to pay less attention to them in classic fairweather-fan fashion. Recently, when living in Somerset, I dabbled with being a Yeovil supporter. Now back living in London I am a regular patron at the Den and have begun to follow Millwall’s results more than Forest’s.

It’s not unusual to support an overseas club either, and after a formative experience watching Napoli lose to Chelsea in 2012 a passion for the Italian club emerged. I’ve visited Naples several times, made good friends there and seen a few games. The most memorable trip was in May 2023 when the Serie A title was sealed under Luciano Spalletti. I didn’t have a ticket but ultimately didn’t need one: the entire city was electrified by their (our) third scudetto.

View image in fullscreen ‘As a teenage follower of Forest, I felt my personal fortunes were linked to the club’s.’ Bayern Munich’s Jürgen Klinsmann takes on Steve Chettle in 1996. Photograph: Lee Beskeen/Action

For some people switching, or even mixing, football allegiances remains taboo. Devoted supporters of a single club may regard my experience as a sign of weakness, or at least exceptional fickleness. But “fan” is short for “fanatic”, and I am no longer convinced so much emotional energy should be invested in supporting any club. Why, after all, would I associate my happiness and sense of fulfilment with something I can’t control? Was the obvious and sustained misery of Arsenal fans as they edged nervously to the Premier League title worth the payoff? Perhaps it was, but there is clearly something unhealthy in that level of obsession.

It is possible, after all, to be too emotionally invested in a certain outcome for your own wellbeing. As an avid teenage follower of Forest, I felt my personal fortunes were linked to the club’s. I regarded one particularly inept late-90s defeat by Wimbledon as a personal tragedy that raised serious questions about my future happiness. I still love football – I am just more ambivalent to its outcomes.

Not only is it acceptable to switch allegiance, it actually makes more sense to base your support on what’s going on in your life at the time. If professional athletes can represent more than one country, let alone several clubs, why shouldn’t fans switch teams?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The disparity between mercenary players and loyal fans grows ever bigger and more grotesque. The players earn obscene amounts of money, and wield a disproportionate amount of power, but often show zero loyalty to a club and its fans when a better offer appears. How can any of this make sense for the lifelong supporter?

And being a diehard fan can be a compromising position in so many ways, frequently leading to defending the indefensible, from unethical petro-state sportwashing and financial doping to obvious on-field foul play and even spying. If you are a glory-hunting Manchester City devotee with a hidden Manchester United-supporting past, or have ever done a football-supporting switcheroo of any kind, do not be ashamed. There is help available. There are people who understand.

Since becoming a regular attendee at Millwall, I’ve enjoyed watching matches with one of my oldest friends and his son. A tight, noisy, old-fashioned ground, no video assistant referee, close to home … have I finally become a real fan?

As long as I live in London I will enjoy following Millwall … with Forest and Napoli thrown in. Not forgetting Dulwich Hamlet. Should I ever return to Somerset, though, I’ll be Yeovil till I die.

Sports.title: Marketing stunt or ‘extraordinary’ transfer? Ravenna fans ride wave of the Ronaldinho Effect
Sports.content:
On a scorching summer afternoon in Ravenna, a city far better known for its fifth-century Byzantine mosaics and Dante’s tomb than for footballing glory, eyes are peeled in the historic centre for one of world football’s most recognisable figures – a man who featured in the World Cup final half-time show alongside Madonna and Ronaldo: Ronaldo de Assis Moreira, better known as Ronaldinho.

“We haven’t seen him yet,” four Ravenna supporters sitting at a cafe say with dry irony as they flip through La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy’s famous pink sports daily. They are undeniably sceptical, viewing the signing as a purely commercial operation, yet deep down they still harbour the dream of seeing the 2005 Ballon d’Or and 2002 World Cup winner wear their yellow and red shirt.

It is a small, surreal glimpse into the whirlwind that has engulfed this quiet corner of Emilia-Romagna, thanks to the business instinct of Ignazio Cipriani. Heir to the Venetian hospitality dynasty behind the renowned Harry’s Bar, Cipriani took over the club in 2024 when they were in Serie D, the fourth tier of Italian football. A native of Ravenna, he is the grandson of Raul Gardini, the Italian chemicals tycoon and sailor who steered Il Moro di Venezia to the 1992 America’s Cup final.

In his first year as president, Cipriani oversaw victory in the Serie D Cup and promotion to the professional ranks of Serie C. But that is merely the first step in a long ascent, he says: “It’s not a provocation. Serie A is the goal I declared from day one because I intend to reach it. And the Champions League remains the ultimate horizon we want to walk towards, step by step. I made this statement because I like working with my back against the wall: when you have no way out, you are forced to find solutions instead of excuses. I prefer to remove every alibi from the beginning.”

And this summer, Cipriani pulled off a surprise move – so surprising that anyone reading the headlines assumed it was a prank: bringing the 46-year-old Ronaldinho back as a player.

View image in fullscreen Ronaldinho holds up a Ravenna top with Ignazio Cipriani, the club president, after the surprise move was announced in Miami in June. Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/AP

“We met through Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida,” Cipriani says, “two people who worked for over 20 years at AC Milan and had Ronaldinho as a player. The idea of involving him was a dream I cultivated as soon as I bought the club. Thanks to Lorenzo and Ariedo, we met, started talking, and a genuine friendship grew. From that relationship came many ideas for the club’s growth. And to the question everyone is asking, I am happy to answer: Ronaldinho will wear the Ravenna shirt as a player, and he will try – maybe scoring the last goal of his career with us!”

Meanwhile, a dedicated website has already put a special-edition shirt on sale featuring the “R10” logo – the Brazilian’s personal brand – which sold out within a few hours. It represents a striking collision of high-end global branding, small-town football, and brilliantly executed marketing stunt.

“If someone had told me three years ago that Ronaldinho was coming to Ravenna, I would have sent them straight to the psychiatric ward,” says Fabio laughing, a lifelong supporter. “The night the news broke, international headlines everywhere read ‘Ronaldinho to Ravenna’. It was an extraordinary operation.”

Ravenna is no footballing giant. Plagued by bankruptcies in 2001 and 2012, the club has spent decades bouncing around the lower tiers, with seven seasons in Serie B the highest point. Historically a volleyball stronghold, the football scene was accustomed to modest budgets and regional rivalries.

View image in fullscreen Ronaldinho will be aiming to wow the crowds at Ravenna’s Stadio Bruno Benelli this season. Photograph: Roberto Salomone/The Guardian

“Ronaldinho is a unique icon,” Cipriani says. “His way of playing made my generation fall in love with the game. We want him today to make the next generation of fans, in Italy and around the world, fall in love with Ravenna . It’s not just a visibility stunt; it’s about building a bridge between different eras of football and growing a truly global fanbase around it.”

To support this ambitious sporting and industrial project, the club is working with the municipality to renovate the Stadio Bruno Benelli, increasing its capacity beyond 6,300. But the president’s ultimate dream is a new multi-purpose venue open seven days a week, featuring retail spaces, concert facilities, and an integrated Hotel Cipriani linked to the city’s international tourism expansion.

For Ravenna’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, the arrival of a world-famous figure fits neatly into a broader strategy to promote the city globally. In recent years, Ravenna has been expanding its international reach beyond traditional beach tourism and commercial ports. The city is enjoying renewed ties with the Anglo-Saxon world, highlighted by a recent visit from the British royal family and the opening of the Lord Byron Museum.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Ronaldinho brings a whole new level of global fame,” Barattoni says. “When the news broke, my phone exploded with messages from former schoolmates. For younger kids today, he might be someone to discover on YouTube, but the fascination remains intact.” With a smile, the mayor adds that, schedule permitting, he would be delighted to personally guide Ronaldinho on a tour of the city’s cultural heritage.

However, Barattoni is quick to clarify the institution’s role: “Our common ground with the club is internationalisation: bringing Ravenna’s image to the world. Ronaldinho has been a global ambassador for countless brands. There is an overarching project that can bring great visibility to the team and allow the city to showcase its initiatives beyond standard routes.” He adds: “Even before Ronaldinho’s arrival, the club did a fantastic job engaging younger generations. The average age in the stands is lower, more vibrant, and more engaged than ever before. A genuine sense of community is forming.”

View image in fullscreen Alessandro Barattoni, the mayor of Ravenna, is confident the Ronaldinho transfer will be positive for the Italian city. Photograph: Roberto Salomone/The Guardian

Yet, fears of a hyper-commercialised image linger among traditional supporters. In the Curva Mero, such marketing moves are approached with caution. “There is a certain reluctance among some factions,” Fabio admits. “Modern football pushes values that many don’t share: rising ticket prices, losing accessibility for lower-income families. As a result, visibility and marketing stunts risk being viewed sideways.”

Cipriani demonstrates an acute awareness of these dynamics: “Without roots, no global project makes sense,” the president says. “Ravenna is not a brand we are building from scratch; it’s a history and an identity that existed before us. Tradition isn’t a brake on ambition: it’s the foundation. A club without its people is worth nothing.”

“I’m 50 years old and I’ve been coming to the stadium since my school days,” says Giovanni, another fan. “I’m rediscovering the enthusiasm of the past. If it takes an icon like Ronaldinho and a local entrepreneur to make us dream of Serie A, then so be it. The important thing is never to forget the people in the stands.”

Riding the wave of the “Ronaldinho Effect”, the season-ticket campaign has just launched with a target of selling 2,800. Ticket prices have risen by an average of about 12%, with variations across different stadium sections.

For now, Ravenna is soaking up a dizzying, galvanising atmosphere. On the pitch, the club is assembling a squad to win the league; off it, the city awaits 20 August, when Ronaldinho is expected to appear during a three-day summer festival in nearby Marina di Ravenna, organised in signature Cipriani style.

Sports.title: Freddie Potts in line for West Ham exit after joining club 17 years ago as a five-year-old
Sports.content:
Freddie Potts in line for West Ham exit after joining club 17 years ago as a five-year-old

West Ham have reportedly agreed to sell academy graduate Freddie Potts to Club Brugge in a deal worth just over £10million.

The 22-year-old was expected to be a key member of the Hammers' squad in their upcoming Championship season, as they seek an immediate return to the top flight.



5 Freddie Potts looks set to depart West Ham after making 32 senior appearances Credit: Getty

But Potts - the son of club icon Steve - now looks set to end his 17-year association with the club he first joined as a six-year-old.

According to the Daily Telegraph, Belgian side Club Brugge have agreed a deal worth €12m (£10.2m) for the midfielder.

Despite a move appearing close, Potts was named on West Ham's bench for their final pre-season friendly against German second division side FC Magdeburg.



The young Englishman did not feature in the clash though, as the Irons rounded off their season's preparations with a 1-1 draw.

And the east London outfit now look to have been dealt a late blow ahead of their campaign, with Potts seemingly destined to leave.



If his move to Brugge goes through, the midfielder will be swapping the Championship for Champions League football, after the Belgian giants qualified by clinching league glory last term.

According to the report, Potts is being lined up as a replacement for Raphael Onyedika.



The Nigeria international is closing in on a move to Bundesliga outfit Eintracht Frankfurt for a rumoured £7.6m fee.

Pott twist

Potts' anticipated West Ham exit comes just as he looked to set to play a greater role for the club in the Championship.

The local lad made 22 Premier League appearances last season, starting 12 times as the Hammers were relegated on the final day.

5 Potts captained West Ham in 1-1 draw with Rangers in pre-season Credit: Getty



5 Potts' dad, Steve, made over 500 appearances for West Ham in 17 years at the club Credit: Getty

But having spent the 2024/25 season on loan at Portsmouth in the second tier, he was expected to feature more in the upcoming campaign.

The departure of key man Mateus Fernandes to Tottenham in a £85m deal appeared to pave the way for this.

Potts wore the captain's armband during West Ham's pre-season friendly draw with Rangers in July, suggesting he would be among Nuno Espirito Santo's starting midfielders.



It appears Potts himself even expected this, having recently shared his plans to become an established player at the London Stadium.

In an interview with BBC Radio London, he said: "I want to play as much as I can for West Ham this season.

"I want to show that I've got the experience in the Championship from before with previous clubs. I'm excited for the challenge that comes ahead."

5 Potts has never played outside of English football in his fledgling career Credit: Getty



Potts also spoke of the desire throughout the club to bounce back to the Premier League at the first attempt following relegation.

He added: "I think it's going to be a very good season for us."

"We can see the love for the club from the fans, and we want to replicate that on the pitch.

"We're very confident going into this season that we can achieve the goal that everyone wants to achieve and no doubt the fans will back us."

End of the road?

Should he finalise his departure, Potts will leave West Ham having made 32 first-team appearances.



He made his senior debut in a 1–0 loss against Dinamo Zagreb in the Conference League in 2021, with his Premier League bow coming last August, coming on as a half-time susbtitute in a 5-1 loss to Chelsea.

5 Nuno Espirito Santo is looking to win promotion from the Championship for the second time in his career with West Ham Credit: Getty

West Ham will play their first competitive game of the season next week, as they host league rivals Portsmouth in the Carabao Cup first round.

They will then get their league campaign underway a week later with an away trip to fellow relegated side Burnley on August 16.

Sports.title: West Ham co-owner issues strongly-worded statement as Amanda Staveley agrees stake purchase
Sports.content:
Daniel Kretinsky has hinted towards instability at West Ham United in response to Amanda Staveley agreeing to purchase a minority stake.

In a statement, the daughter of the late David Gold confirmed that the former co-owner's shares will be sold to a Staveley-led consortium.

3 Staveley has agreed to purchase a stake at West Ham Credit: GETTY

The ex-Newcastle United chief is set to purchase the 25.1 per cent stake currently owned by Vanessa Gold on behalf of the Family Trust.

"I have now reached an ​agreement to sell my family's shareholding to a consortium of ⁠PCP Capital Partners, led by Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi, in ​partnership with Ashland Forest Capital Partners," she said.

"This sale remains subject to a pre-emption process, under which existing shareholders have the option to buy the shares instead.

"While the process has not yet concluded, ​I wanted to be open with our fans about where things ​stand and my intentions."

West Ham confirmed this later on Saturday, saying: "West Ham United can confirm it is aware of the announcement from Joint-Chair Vanessa Gold that she has reached a provisional agreement to sell her shares to a consortium of PCP Capital Partners, led by Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad Ghodoussi, in partnership with Ashland Forest Capital Partners.

"The proposed transaction will now be subject to a pre-emption rights process. This provides all existing shareholders with the opportunity to acquire their proportional percentage of shares in round one, and any remaining shares in round two. This process will take approximately two months and, until it is completed, nothing will change regarding the ownership structure of the Club.

"West Ham United would like to assure supporters that the day-to-day running of the football club is in no way affected by this situation. Preparations for the new season continue to take shape with diligence and focus, and we thank all fans for their continued loyal backing at this time.

"The Club will be making no further comment while the pre-emption process runs its course."

Last month, the Gold family agreed to sell a 16 per cent stake to Kretinsky after David Sullivan stepped down as the club chairman.

The Czech billionaire would have seen his overall stake rise from 27 to 43 per cent, making him the majority owner at West Ham.

3 Kretinsky looked set to become the majority owner at West Ham Credit: Getty

However, the Premier League club's ownership has now been thrown into doubt amid the agreement with Staveley.

In a statement of his own, Kretinsky said that as a current stakeholder at West Ham, he will look to fight off the outside interest.

"The agreement we had reached with the Gold family in June provided stability for the club at a crucial time. Today's announcement does the opposite," Kretinsky said.

"We will always act in the best interests of West Ham United and are reviewing all of our options, including exercising our pre-emption rights in full."

Kretinsky, whose stake is named under 1890s holdings, has been at the club since November 2021.

talkSPORT understands he pushed for Nuno Espirito Santo to stay as head coach after their relegation to the Championship.

3 West Ham say the shares process could take two months Credit: Getty

Espirito Santo was widely expected to leave, and Sullivan was inclined to make a change, but the Portuguese remains in charge.

Kretinsky also wanted captain Jarrod Bowen to stay and lead their promotion fight in the new season, and the winger has signed a revised contract until 2030.

Sports.title: Phil Collins’ son secures move to German fourth-tier club
Sports.content:
Music legend Phil Collins' son Mathew has signed for German side 1860 Munich.

The 21-year-old midfielder, born in Switzerland, has spent the majority of his senior career in Austria, spending last season with second-tier side Austria Salzburg.

2 Collins has featured for clubs in Austria and Germany Credit: WSG Tirol

1860 announced the signing on Friday, with Collins penning a one-year deal at the Grunwalder Stadion.

Collins' new club play in the Regionalliga, the fourth tier of German football.

1860 finished eighth in the third-tier 3. Liga last term but were relegated after failing to obtain a licence for the upcoming campaign.

Established as a multi-sports club way back in 1848, they added a football department in 1899.

Founder members of the Bundesliga in 1963 – unlike city rivals Bayern – they enjoyed their finest hour when they won the 1965/66 title.

1860 have also lifted the DFB-Pokal (German Cup) twice and reached the 1965 Cup Winners' Cup final, losing to West Ham at Wembley.

After spells with German outfits Astoria Walldorf and Hannover 96 as a youngster, Collins moved across the border to Austria to join WSG Tirol in 2023.

Collins even featured for the club in a pre-season fixture against Bayern, where he came up against Harry Kane.

He made four league appearances for Austria Salzburg in 2025/26 and featured once in the domestic cup.

Collins linked up with his 1860 ahead of the campaign-opening 2-2 draw away to FC Schweinfurt.

2 The Collins clan has churned out several famous faces Credit: @mcollins0112 - Instagram

His move comes after completing a trial at 1860.

Phil your boots

Mathew is the youngest of Phil Collins' five children, with his brother Nic also born in Switzerland.

Phil Collins shot to fame as the drummer and later lead singer of rock band Genesis in the 1970s.

He then went on to have a hugely successful solo career with hits such as 'In the Air Tonight' and his cover of the Supremes' 'You Can't Hurry Love'.

Collins was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame earlier this year.

He had previously been inducted as a member of Genesis in 2010.

Mathew's other sibling are actress and model Lily Collins, drummer and singer Simon Collins, and producer and actress Joely Collins.

Sports.title: Arsenal immediately sanction midfield exit with Bruno Guimaraes deal close
Sports.content:
Christian Norgaard is reportedly set to sign for Everton from Arsenal.

Norgaard only joined the Gunners from London rivals Brentford last summer in a £15million deal.



2 Norgaard is set to leave Arsenal just a year after signing Credit: Getty

The Denmark international made seven appearances in their Premier League title-winning campaign and started on just one occasion.

He also featured just 20 times in all competitions amid competition with Declan Rice, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi.

Now he looks on course for a move to Merseyside, as The Athletic say Everton have reached an agreement in principle for his signing.



The deal is said to be worth £7m, and the 32-year-old will undergo a medical next week.

Norgaard will be Everton's second midfield signing of the summer after Hayden Hackney joined from Middlesbrough for £25m.



Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Merlin Rohl and James Garner are among the midfielders already at the club.

One out, one in

Although Arsenal are set to make a loss on Norgaard, they are close to completing a move for Bruno Guimaraes.



talkSPORT understands the Gunners are closing in on a deal to sign the Newcastle United captain for more than £75m.

A formal bid is expected once a full verbal agreement is in place.

The move will come as a huge blow to Newcastle, who have already lost Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali.

2 Guimaraes is on his way to Arsenal this summer Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Eddie Howe, who led the club to their first trophy in 56 years, has also left the club.



Arsenal will be welcoming a signing who has made 153 appearances in the Premier League, scoring 30 goals and assisting 26.

Guimaraes will likely be their fourth signing of the summer after deals for Piero Hincapie, Illan Meslier and Christos Tzolis.

The Premier League champions could also be set to sign Vinicius Jr from Real Madrid.

Arsenal have been weighing up a move for the Brazilian, who has one year left on his deal at the Bernabeu.



However, they have not yet submitted a bid to Madrid.

Sports.title: Lucas Herrington in line to become most expensive Australian ever in Premier League move
Sports.content:
Lucas Herrington in line to become most expensive Australian ever in Premier League move

Premier League newcomers Hull are poised to sign Australia World Cup star Lucas Herrington.

The 18-year-old centre-back, currently playing his club football for MLS side Colorado Rapids, was one of the breakout stars of this summer's World Cup.

2 Herrington featured in the 2026 MLS All-Star Game as one of the league's standout players Credit: Getty

talkSPORT understands Hull are in advanced talks about a deal to bring Herrington to the Premier League.

The Tigers are ready to pay more than £20million, which would be a record for an Australian player, and Herrington is keen to join.

Harry Souttar previously held the record from his £14.5m move from Stoke to Leicester.

Herrington's Socceroos defensive teammate Harry Souttar currently holds that record after joining Leicester from Stoke for a reported 26m Australian dollars (£15m) in 2023.

Born in Brisbane, Herrington came through the ranks at local A-League club Brisbane Roar.

Last summer, he agreed a deal to join Colorado Rapids ahead of the 2026 MLS season, making his MLS debut in February.

But, helped by his impressive showings in Australia's run to the World Cup last 32, he appears set to make the biggest move of his career yet.

Herrington has earned six caps for his country since making his senior debut in March.

He previously starred in Australia's 2025 AFC U-20 Asian Cup triumph.

Herrington became the Socceroos' youngest-ever World Cup starter in their final group game against Paraguay.

2 Herrington achieved his ambition of representing Australia at the World Cup Credit: Getty

"I can't really describe it," he said after that game. It means everything to me to represent the Socceroos at a World Cup.

"I've been dreaming of it since I was a kid, and to be able to do that today, it's so, so special."

Herrington also featured in the last-32 defeat to Egypt, agonisingly missing a penalty in the shootout, drawing praise from Zlatan Ibrahimovic for 'showing a lot of courage' to step up to the spot.

Tigers continue to gear up for Premier League return

Hull are preparing for their first Premier League campaign in almost a decade after returning to the top flight as last season's Championship play-off winners.

Sergej Jakirovic's men have made four signings so far this summer as they aim to secure survival.

Former England goalkeeper Jack Butland and Ecuadorian midfielder Oscar Zambrano have arrived from Rangers and Maribor respectively, with left-back Matt Targett and Japan midfielder Hidemasa Morita heading to the MKM Stadium on free transfers.

Hull kick off the 2026/27 campaign at home to Manchester United on August 22.

Sports.title: UEFA president calls for blanket withdrawal of Gianni Infantino support with FA in talks to join mass protest
Sports.content:
UEFA president calls for blanket withdrawal of Gianni Infantino support with FA in talks to join mass protest

Gianni Infantino's future as FIFA President remains in serious doubt, talkSPORT understands.

It follows the shelving of plans to form a subsidiary body called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) that would have been part-funded by private equity and promised federations $40m each to join.

4 Infantino's time as FIFA president may be nearing its end Credit: AFP

Infantino sensationally backed down from the contentious project admitting it had 'created divisions', and off the back of UEFA threatening to boycott FIFA competitions if FFE got off the ground.

Infantino also lost the support of lead financier Joshua Kushner and JP Morgan in an embarrassing 48 hours where his grip of FIFA weakened.

Senior FIFA advisor Carlos Cordeiro also stood down, while FIFA COO Kevin Lamour issued a statement saying Infantino had 'deceived staff'. And British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called Infantino the 'wrong man' for the job.

Gianni, you've got mail

talkSPORT can reveal that UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin is discussing whether to ask all UEFA members that have backed Infantino in writing, a number believed to be above 40, to revoke their support.

UEFA declined to comment when approached.

Some senior figures in the English FA, speaking on condition of anonymity, have already discussed whether to remove their formal endorsement given to Infantino ahead of the World Cup.

The FA also issued a formal statement on Saturday calling for urgent change.

"It is time for a full and robust review of FIFA’s leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently, for the benefit of all 211 member nations and with the long term stewardship of football at its heart," the statement read.

talkSPORT understands the German FA remain opposed to Infantino standing, while the Norwegian, Polish, French, Swedish, Belgium, Canadian, Mexican and Jordanian federations will all hold meetings to discuss their stance.

How do FIFA presidential elections work?

It is also understood Infantino could face an emergency FIFA council meeting in which he will be asked to resign or remove his candidacy for 2027.

4 UEFA president Ceferin has lead the charge against Infantino's latest idwa Credit: AFP

Concacaf issue statement as FFE proposal withdrawn Concacaf and its 41 Member Associations welcome the withdrawal of the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). The Confederation also commends its 41 Member Associations and the wider football family for the courage and unity they have shown this week. At a moment that demanded principled leadership, our members stood together in defence of football’s long-term interests and the principles of good governance. That unity has prevailed. Concacaf would also like to acknowledge and commend the role of the media in bringing this issue out of the shadows and into the light. The events of recent days have exposed something that cannot now be set aside: the future of the FIFA World Cup, the greatest asset in world football, was advanced outside every established governance framework, without transparency, consultation or due process. A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place. This concern is not Concacaf’s alone. It is shared across many confederations, Member Associations and those who serve and love the game. When people entrusted with protecting the game conclude they can no longer do so from within, the football family is entitled to ask how such a proposal was allowed to proceed, and who bears responsibility for it. FIFA is not a private enterprise. It is a body held in trust for the game and its members. Those appointed to serve it carry a fiduciary duty, a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional. As mandated by our Member Associations, Concacaf’s FIFA Council members will engage directly, and through the FIFA Council, to ensure that questions of governance, accountability and leadership are addressed properly through the institutions and procedures established under the FIFA Statutes. They will also work within that same framework to determine how existing vast reserves can be dispersed to our membership via the FIFA Forward funding for football development across our region, without compromising our shared future. We are all simple custodians, serving a game that belongs to us all. The unity demonstrated by our Member Associations this week has reaffirmed that when guided by courage, integrity, and sound governance the game will remain where it belongs: in the hands of football - not a single individual.

There is a strong preference from several UEFA federations for Infantino not to stand again in 2027 and a willingness to block a vote against him if he does. UEFA carries 55 votes with 106 needed to win.

Concacaf also rejected Infantino's FFE plan and their president Victor Montagliani has aspirations to be FIFA President.

"He has always been focused on Concacaf re-election next year," said a senior source familiar with Montagliani's thinking.

"It is quite interesting that Concacaf and UEFA voting together only take a candidate 10 short of a winning a FIFA presidential election."

The election actually works with a candidate needing a two-thirds majority in the first round - 141 votes - but if a second round is needed then a simple majority is enough for victory.

Who are the candidates that could replace Infantino?

Plenty of UEFA federations would also back Nasser Al-Khelaifi to stand, even though a source close to the PSG president has insisted 'he has zero ambition to do so'.

4 Despite the likelihood of being a popular candidate, Al-Khelaifi is not gunning for Infantino's role Credit: Getty

Gianni Infantino's timeline of controversies 30 April, 2026: Gianni Infantino confirms at the FIFA Congress in Vancouver he'll stand for re-election in March 2027 30 April: Infantino tries and fails to orchestrate a handshake between the Palestinian Football Association’s President Jibril Rajoub and Israel FA’s VP Basim Sheikh Suliman 5 December: Infantino awards Trump the inaugural FIFA Peace Prize at the World Cup draw, an award seemingly created for the US President in light of his Nobel Peace Prize snub 7 June: Iran land in Mexico after moving their training base from America following rising tensions 8 June: Former UEFA president Michel Platini files a criminal complaint in France against both Infantino and FIFA alleging a smear campaign preventing him from succeeding Sepp Blatter as FIFA President 8 June: Somali ref Omar Artan is barred from entering the US with FIFA insisting they couldn't intervene, while Andrew Giuliani repeatedly accuses Artan of "talking to bad people" without elaboration 8 December: FairSquare make a complaint to FIFA’s Ethics Committee that Infantino has breached political neutrality 10 June: Infantino tells his critics to "chill, relax" 13 June: Trump doesn’t attend the USMNT's World Cup opener against Paraguay or any other game until the World Cup Final 2 July: Trump calls Infantino and asks him to review Flo Balogun's red card sustained against Bosnia 5 July: Balogun's red card is suspended by FIFA's disciplinary committee despite FIFA insiders originally claiming there were no grounds for appeal 19 July: A 27 minute and 22 second World Cup Final half-time show that Wayne Rooney called "crap" 19 July: Infantino and Trump present Spain with the World Cup trophy with the US President remaining on the podium for the lift 27 July: Infantino tells his critics to "pray, meditate or watch football" in a 15-slide Instagram statement 28 July: Infantino pitches FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) blindsiding confederations in the process 28 July: Sepp Blatter calls the relationship between Infantino and Trump "deeply damaging" 29 July: Infantino tells FIFA's 211 members they have 53 days to vote on FFE and offers each $40m if they join 30 July: UEFA reject FFE plans and threaten a boycott of all FIFA tournaments if they pass 30 July: Concerns over the project are raised by JP Morgan and private investor Joshua Kushner 31 July: Concacaf and the AFC reject FFE, senior FIFA advisor Carlos Cordeiro quits, FIFA COO Kevin Lamour says Infantino "deceived" staff and British PM Andy Burnham calls on the FIFA President the "wrong person for the job" 1 August: Infantino scraps FFE plans at 00:30 due to "divisions" but falls short of re-sign

Highly-regarded FIFA General Secretary Mattias Granström would prove another popular option.

The Swedish executive is not viewed as tarnished by Infantino's failed project and is believed to have been totally blindsided by it.

Within FIFA's currently divided leadership, there are prominent voices who want Infantino to quit now and Granström to take interim charge, potentially positioning him to stand next March.

Legia owner Dariusz Mioduski is another favoured name within UEFA, as talkSPORT revealed last month.

Those close to AFC President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa insist he does not want to go head-to-head against Infantino, despite a strong AFC statement also rejecting FFE.

Multiple AFC and FIFA sources have told talkSPORT that privately there isn't the same unanimous position among all Asian federations as other confederations. Sheikh Salman would likely only consider whether to run if Infantino removes himself from the ballot.

4 The AFC President would only seek to take Infantino's role so long as he doesn't run for re-election Credit: Getty

talkSPORT has learned CAF President Patrice Motsepe also wants to be FIFA President one day, but as a close ally of Infantino sources believe he is currently more inclined to throw his support behind the current FIFA President doing one final term.

What is Infantino's current stance on re-election?

Those familiar with Infantino's thinking insist he has no plans to resign and is hoping plans to expand the World Cup to 64 teams, potentially as early as 2030, prove to be a vote winner.

Yet Infantino is in danger of a mutiny from some of his closest allies. As with FFE, if it becomes apparent another candidate has enough votes to defeat him, the FIFA President could yet walk.

Further emergency meetings are set to take place between Infantino and his inner circle to determine a path forward. His intent is to battle on, but a unified way forward under his leadership is not guaranteed if confederations and federations continue to vocally call for change.

Infantino is reliant on the fact that, as of now, he has 200-plus votes in writing, but there is nothing to stop federations transferring their support. The deadline for another candidate to come forward is November 18.

Montagliani appears to be the most viable candidate between now and then especially if he garners UEFA backing.

Sports.title: Ashley Williams reveals Robin van Persie refused apology over incident which ‘could have killed him’
Sports.content:
Ashley Williams has revealed Robin van Persie blanked his apology after he infamously kicked the ball at the Manchester United hero's head.

Back in 2012, Williams found himself the major talking point after a clash between Swansea and the Red Devils, when he launched his clearance into the back of Van Persie's head.



6 William's 2012 incident involving Robin van Persie was one of the most high-profile moments of his eight-year Swansea career Credit: Getty

The Dutchman was lying on the ground after being tripped outside the box, before Swans captain Williams blasted the ball at him from just yards away as referee Michael Oliver blew the whistle for a foul.

A furious row broke out with both players being booked, but that wasn't the end of the matter.

Fergie's fury

While the match ended 1-1, all the talk afterwards revolved around Williams, not least after a fiery post-match interview from Sri Alex Ferguson.



The legendary United boss famously said that the Welsh defender 'could have killed' Van Persie with his actions.

Ferguson fumed: “He could have been killed [Van Persie], I think the FA has got to look into it.



"I think irrespective of him having a yellow card, he should be banned for a long time because that was the most dangerous thing I've seen in a football field for many, many years."

The Scot insisted Williams had acted deliberately, and continued to call on the FA to ban him retrospectively.



He added: “Absolutely deliberate. Absolutely no question. The whistle's gone, the game has stopped, and he's done that right in front of the referee. Two feet from the player.

"He could have really killed the lad. It was a disgraceful act by the player. He should be banned for a long, long time.”

Ultimately, Williams received no further punishment for the incident, while Ferguson's comments have lived long in the memory of fans.

6 After Williams booted the ball at his head, Van Persie immediately jumped to his feet to confront the Swansea man Credit: Getty



6 Sir Alex Ferguson pulled no punches as he slammed Williams in his post-match interview Credit: YouTube/Sky Sports Retro

'I did try and hit him'

14 years on from the infamous incident, Williams was given a chance to share his side of the story on Friday's talkSPORT Drive.

And while the former Wales international revealed he had intentionally kicked the ball at Van Persie's head, he insisted there had been a huge overreaction to this, especially from Ferugson.

On the incident, he told co-host Ade Oladipo: “[Ferguson] He said that's the most dangerous thing he's seen on a football pitch.



"Did he see the Eric Cantona thing [kung-fu kick]? He didn't see that?”

Explaining his thought process at the time, Williams admitted he instantly regretted his split-second decision.

Asked if he felt bad at the time, he replied: “Yeah, I've spoken about this before. What happened was the ball came, and it was a little bit like when you're a kid and you go, ‘Oh, should I?'

6 Neither Williams nor Van Persie backed down in the aftermath of the Swansea captain's actions Credit: AFP



6 Van Persie had to be held back as he was left furious Credit: AFP

“And then I just hit it. And then once it hit him, instantly I was like, ‘hmm [that was a mistake]’.”

The 41-year-old added: “It wasn't a full punt. And I did try and hit him - there's no way around it.

“But I instantly regretted it and did apologise to him after that as well, so it was wrong.



"But I think it was just completely blown out of proportion. There were people on the news like the Monday, like neurologists and doctors saying how dangerous it was.

“I was like: ‘Hang on a second. I get paid to put my head in front of shots every single day, so it can't be that bad’.

“But it was one time, it was out of order. It was wrong. And it was one of the things that I definitely did [wrong]."

6 Williams revealed his attempts to make up with Van Persie were rebuffed Credit: Getty



Unforgivable?

Despite confessing to meaning to kick the ball at Van Persie, Williams then revealed he tried to make amends during their next encounter.

He shared that he had apologised to the 144-goal Premier League icon, but revealed that the Dutchman was having none of it.

Williams explained: "The next time I played against him, I apologised and he shrugged it off. He didn't really accept it.”

It's fair to say no lasting damage was done to Van Persie though, who went on to fire Man United to Premier League glory that year with 26 league goals, which also clinched him the Golden Boot that year.

Sports.title: Four new Premier League managers tipped to be sacked this season
Sports.content:
Four new Premier League managers tipped to be sacked this season

Half of the Premier League's eight new managers could lose their jobs before the end of the season.

That's the view of talkSPORT's Tony Cascarino, discussing the record number of changes in the dugout.



3 Chelsea's Xabi Alonso is among the eight new Premier League bosses already appointed Credit: Getty

Nine of the 20 top-flight teams will begin the 2026/27 campaign with a different manager from the one who ended last term in charge.

Eight clubs have already moved to appoint new bosses, with Newcastle searching for Eddie Howe's successor after he stepped down on Friday.

Premier League clubs with new managers for 2026/27

Bournemouth Marco Rose Chelsea Xabi Alonso Crystal Palace Pierre Sage Fulham Alvaro Arbeloa Ipswich Gary O'Neil Liverpool Andoni Iraola Man City Enzo Maresca Newcastle Matthias Jaissle (unconfirmed) Nottingham Forest Oliver Glasner

The previous record for coaching changes between the end of one Premier League season and the start of the next campaign was seven in 2016/17.



And Cascarino feels that with the managerial merry-go-round turning at full speed, chances are not all eight new starters will still be in charge come next summer.

"Now, out of that eight, you probably could say it’s very likely that half of them will be gone by the end of the season," the former Chelsea and Republic of Ireland striker told Shebahn Aherne on the talkSPORT Weekend Sports Breakfast.



Asked if he really thought that, Cascarino continued: "Well, if you just look at the numbers game… yeah, it’s very likely that out of them eight managers, four of them could be gone."

As such, he expects there to be opportunities for Howe to return to Premier League management sooner rather than later.



"Yeah, he’ll get offered jobs without a doubt," Cascarino said.

"How long he takes off, we don’t know that…I’m sure he’ll want to get back into football.

"He’s still, like you said, what, 48 he is – so he’s still a very young man in many ways as a manager.

3 Howe left Newcastle after the best part of five years in charge, during which he ended the Magpies' 70-year trophy drought by winning the 2024/25 Carabao Cup Credit: Getty

"And Eddie did a great job [at Newcastle], and I think if opportunities – like they always do – come up, Eddie…I guarantee he’ll be the bookmakers’ favourite about five times if he doesn’t take a job by Christmas, because there’ll be four or five managers that probably go by then."



However, talkSPORT understands Howe is in no rush to get back into management.

Newcastle, meanwhile, are expected to name Matthias Jaissle as Howe's successor.

The German is currently head coach of Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli, having previously led Red Bull Salzburg to two Austrian Bundesliga titles.

The managerial merry-go-round never stops turning

There were a whopping 11 managerial changes in the Premier League during the 2025/26 season, with Nottingham Forest sacking both Ange Postecoglou and Sean Dyche.



Arsenal's Mikel Arteta is still the league's longest-serving boss and one of only three who have been in post longer than three years, along with Aston Villa's Unai Emery and Leeds' Daniel Farke.

3 Arteta has been in charge of Arsenal since December 2019 Credit: Getty

The new Premier League campaign gets underway with Arteta's title-winning Gunners hosting newly promoted Coventry on Friday August 21.

There are five rounds of fixtures between then and the first international break at the end of September.
