World.title: Germany's small islands: nature and slow living almost on your doorstep
World.content:
Germany's lesser-known islands offer exactly what many people are looking for today: less hustle and bustle, more nature and authentic experiences. Whether it's the Wadden Sea on the North Sea coast, a Baltic Sea beach or quiet countryside, for a short break it is often the smaller islands that provide the greatest relaxation.

 

Hiddensee: Baltic Sea island made for slowing down

Hiddensee in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may no longer be a real insider tip among island lovers, but it is still far less well known to many travellers than Rügen or Usedom. The island in the Baltic Sea is only about 17 kilometres long, car-free and best explored by bicycle, horse-drawn carriage or on foot.

The long sandy beaches, dune landscapes and the Dornbusch in the north with its lighthouse are particularly appealing.

The west coast of Hiddensee Sebastian Negraszus, Wikimedia Commons

Ummanz: Island feeling without the island stress

Ummanz lies to the west of Rügen, also in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and is one of the quietest islands in the German Baltic Sea. It is linked to Rügen by a bridge, which makes it especially easy to visit for a short stay.

The flat landscape of meadows, salt marshes and small villages is a paradise for nature lovers and photographers. In autumn, thousands of cranes stop here to rest – a spectacular natural spectacle.

Poel: Baltic Sea holiday without mass tourism

Poel lies between Wismar and the island of Rügen and is often underestimated. This Baltic Sea island offers wide beaches, small villages and a laid-back atmosphere.

Cycle tours along the coast, walks along the cliffs and visits to the historic lighthouse in Timmendorf are particularly popular. Poel is a good alternative for anyone wanting the Baltic Sea experience while avoiding the hustle and bustle of larger resorts.

Timmendorf on the island of Poel at sunset. Daniela Kloth, Wikimedia Commons

Vilm: Germany's little nature island

Vilm, off the coast of Rügen, is one of Germany's most strictly protected islands. Only a limited number of visitors are allowed ashore each day. The island is known for its ancient beech forest, untouched nature and its status as a nature reserve. Visits are only possible on guided tours.

Vilm Island nature reserve M. Anarbaev - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php

Neuwerk: Island holiday in the middle of the Wadden Sea

The small island of Neuwerk belongs politically to Hamburg, but lies around 100 kilometres away in the Wadden Sea off the coast of Lower Saxony. It forms part of the Hamburg Wadden Sea National Park.

At low tide, the island can be reached on foot or by horse-drawn wagon across the mudflats. The historic lighthouse dating back to the 14th century is Neuwerk's landmark. Anyone staying overnight experiences something special: almost complete silence at night and a spectacular starry sky.

East Frisia: A nature paradise with plenty of peace

Baltrum is the smallest of the inhabited East Frisian islands and is often referred to as the "Sleeping Beauty of the North Sea". With an area of less than seven square kilometres, it is easy to explore entirely on foot.

Palisade wall as coastal protection on the East Frisian island of Baltrum. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/

There are no cars here; instead, bicycles, horse-drawn carts and the sound of the sea set the pace. Walks across the mudflats, long strolls along the beach and sweeping views over the North Sea make Baltrum an ideal destination for a short escape.

Langeoog is one of the better-known East Frisian islands, but still feels much quieter than the big North Sea hotspots. The car-free island offers endless sandy beaches, dunes and a rich birdlife.

A short trip to Langeoog is particularly worthwhile in spring or autumn, when there are fewer visitors and walks by the sea are especially impressive.

Spiekeroog is one of the quietest of the East Frisian islands. The car-free island is known for its unspoilt dunes, old lime-tree avenues and its kilometre-long sandy beach. Unlike some of its neighbours, Spiekeroog relies less on large holiday complexes and more on nature, peace and relaxation. Walks through the dunes, mudflat excursions and bike rides are especially popular.

Wangerooge is the easternmost of the inhabited East Frisian islands and is ideal for a long weekend. The island is car-free and, alongside its beaches, offers protected natural areas where you can see seabirds and seals. A particular highlight is the journey on the island railway from the harbour to the village.

Juist, at around 17 kilometres long, is one of the longest East Frisian islands but only a few kilometres wide. With horse-drawn carriages instead of cars, it is wonderfully quiet. Its wide sandbank, the Wadden Sea and endless horizons make Juist a favourite with nature lovers.

The Foto Fitti, Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported license.

Arngast is no longer a classic holiday island, but it is an intriguing destination for outings. The former island in the Jade Bay near Wilhelmshaven is best known for the Arngast lighthouse, which stands in the middle of the Wadden Sea. At low tide, you can discover this unique landscape on guided mudflat walks.

Islands in southern Germany: Time out on Lake Chiemsee

It's not only the North Sea and Baltic Sea that offer island experiences. Southern Germany also has some remarkable islands – right in the foothills of the Bavarian Alps. The Chiemsee islands show that you don't necessarily have to head to the sea for an island escape.

Fraueninsel: Monastery, gardens and Bavarian island charm

Fraueninsel is probably the best-known island on Lake Chiemsee and also one of the most atmospheric. Covering just 15 hectares or so, the island is car-free and easy to explore on foot. Its centrepiece is the historic Benedictine convent Frauenwörth, usually called Frauenchiemsee Abbey, which is still home to nuns today. Founded in 782 by Bavarian Duke Tassilo III, it is one of the oldest surviving convents for women in Germany.

Frauenchiemsee Abbey Allie Caulfield, Chiemsee, Schliersee 025, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php

Alongside the convent, small gardens, old fishermen's houses, narrow paths and numerous arts and crafts shops shape the island's appearance. The combination of lake, mountains and historic architecture gives Fraueninsel its very special atmosphere.

Krautinsel: The quiet nature haven on Lake Chiemsee

Krautinsel is the smallest and at the same time the most original of the three main Chiemsee islands. It is uninhabited and serves primarily as a natural habitat. Its name goes back to its former use: vegetables – especially cabbage – were once grown here to supply the inhabitants of the neighbouring islands.

Today, Krautinsel is above all a retreat for plants and wildlife. The flat, green island with its meadows and reed beds offers a glimpse of how pristine the Chiemsee landscape once was. Landing on the island is not possible – the best way to see it is from a boat or by circling it during a trip on the lake.

It shows that island experiences do not always have to be about beaches and swimming.

Herreninsel: Royal history and nature trails

Herreninsel, at around 230 hectares, is the largest of the Chiemsee islands and is famous for Herrenchiemsee Palace. The Bavarian King Ludwig II began building the palace in 1878, modelled on Versailles – a homage to the French King Louis XIV.

Ferry landing stage on Herrenchiemsee Island By Jannis Raabe - Own work, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=64923231

Away from this main tourist attraction, large parts of Herreninsel are covered by forests and meadows, criss-crossed by quiet walking paths. Anyone who leaves the main routes behind will find peaceful spots with views over the lake and towards the Alps.

World.title: Hamburg celebrates Pride with increased security one week after deadly Berlin attack
World.content:
Hamburg celebrated its annual Pride event, one of Germany's biggest, with increased security on Saturday, one week after a deadly attack near Berlin's pride parade that shocked the country.

 

Organisers expected around 250,000 people to attend the parade, which this year has the motto "Queer in solidarity. Take a stand — for a future without fear."

A late addition to the trucks taking part was one representing the Berlin Pride event — or Christopher Street Day, CSD for short, as the parades are known in Germany. People on that truck were asked to wear dark clothing as a sign of respect for the victims of last week's attack, where one person was killed and 29 others injured.

A reveller holds a placard during the Hamburg Pride 2026, the Christopher Street Day (CSD) parade, in Hamburg, Germany, Saturday Aug. 1, 2026. Georg Wendt/dpa via AP

Late on July 25, a man plowed a van into people a few hundred metres from the closing party of the Berlin Pride event before cutting others with what appears to have been a machete.

The 21-year-old suspect, Abdul Ballout, was killed in a confrontation with police on Sunday. Investigators later found a video in which a person believed to be the suspect claimed responsibility and pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group.

Prosecutors have said Ballout, who was born in Germany and has Lebanese roots, travelled to Lebanon in 2025 with the goal of going to Syria to join IS. He made contact with several people who were presumed members.

Hamburg's police chief said earlier this week that roughly twice as many officers as last year would protect the Hamburg event.

A police officer stands on Steindamm at the edge of Hamburg Pride 2026, the Christopher Street Day (CSD) parade, in Hamburg, Germany, Saturday Aug. 1, 2026. Georg Wendt/dpa via AP

“After the brutal attack on the CSD in Berlin, many are unsure in the queer community but also in society whether here and today is the right place,” Hamburg's deputy mayor, Katharina Fegebank, told RTL television.

“I say, now more than ever, let’s all take to the streets, stand up for diversity, for freedom, for an open society, and above all, in full solidarity with and for the queer community," she added.

"Well, when something like that happens, we all have to show that we’re not afraid, that we won’t let it get us down," said Petra Schwab, who was attending Saturday's Pride in Hamburg.

World.title: Wildfires in Europe: blazes continue to spread in France and Greece
World.content:
A wildfire in France's Provence region continued spreading on Saturday as overnight efforts successfully stopped the blazes from reaching the nearby towns of Correns and Montfort-sur-Argens.

 

Some 1,300 firefighters have been deployed to tackle the blaze, which has flared up again in the Gros Bessillon area, burning approximately 1,250 more hectares since Friday. By the end of the week, authorities said a total of 4,500 hectares had been burnt.

Despite the difficulties, 2,500 people were still unable to return home.

Meanwhile, authorities say France's largest wildfire in 70 years has been brought under control near the southwestern city of Bordeaux.

The Gironde fire has burned 420 square kilometres of pine forest west of the city, an area four times the size of Paris.

Firefighters said it remained contained within that perimeter Saturday, meaning flames had not broken beyond its existing boundaries. But it had not been declared “fixed” — the point at which crews determine that a fire is no longer advancing — and active sectors and buried hot spots persisted.

Twenty French departments were under an orange heat warning Saturday, mostly in the east and southeast. Temperatures of 35 to 39 degree celsius were forecast around the Mediterranean, while eight departments faced a high forest-fire risk.

Residents evacuated in Greece

In Greece, hundreds of firefighters on Saturday were battling to save a popular coastal resort northwest of Athens as violent winds lashed the country, hampering operations.

More than 400 firefighters, backed by several dozen specialised aircraft, were battling blazes in the area of Porto Germeno, the country's fire department said.

According to meteo.gr, the weather service of the National Observatory of Athens, winds up to 130 kilometres per hour were recorded Saturday.

The fire broke out Friday near the neighbouring coastal village of Agios Vasileios. Residents initially ignored a civil protection call to evacuate, and some 300 people had to be rescued by sea.

Wildfires have flared in several parts of the country this week, including on the popular island of Crete, and three firefighters have so far lost their lives.

World.title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed with all members of expedition in Pakistan avalanche
World.content:
Renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja has been confirmed dead in an avalanche accident in Pakistan, his climbing company Elite Expeditions said in a social media post on Saturday.

 

The avalanche struck on Thursday, cutting off contact with the international expedition led by 43-year-old British-Nepali climber Purja on Broad Peak in northern Pakistan.

"It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak," Purja's company Elite Expeditions said on social media.

"We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive," it added.

The remains recovered so far, flown by helicopter to a hospital for formal identification, included an American woman, an Omani woman and a Nepali man, the regional government said in a statement released on Friday night.

Lost contact since Thursday

The team lost contact with their base camp Thursday after an avalanche struck Broad Peak as they attempted to scale the mountain, said Karrar Haidri, vice president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan on Friday.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah offered his condolences over the "tragic" deaths of Purja and the other climbers, which he said "has shocked us".

"The physical journey of all the deceased climbers... has been interrupted, but the history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," Shah said in a statement on social media.

Broad Peak Illuminated at Daybreak, from Concordia Camp, Pakistan. Anne Dirkse via Wikimedia Commons

Police in the mountainous northern Gilgit-Baltistan region said in a statement that high-altitude porters and rescue teams were carrying out a second day of the operation on Saturday after the search was paused due to difficult weather conditions a day earlier.

Rescuers and military helicopters had been scouring the area and teams stayed at the base camp overnight, according to the regional government.

"The rescue operation is being conducted under extremely challenging terrain and high-altitude weather conditions by the Pakistani army in coordination with local high-altitude climbers and rescuers," it said.

Powerful avalanche

The avalanche struck while the mountaineers were on a mission to summit Broad Peak 8,047 metres on Thursday and while the team was ascending at an altitude of around 6,600 metres, according to regional authorities.

The expedition comprised 10 people, including Purja, five Nepalis, a Pakistani, an Omani, an American, and a climber from China.

"Data from their tracking devices indicates that they were thrown hundreds of metres down the mountainside," Naila Kiani, from Pakistan's Alpine Club, told Le Monde newspaper.

Elite Expedition announced death of Nirmal Purja in avalanche in Pakistan this Saturday. Elite Expedition social media post

Fida Ali, a climber in the area who worked closely with Purja since 2023, said their focus for the climbing season was summiting Broad Peak, but they had first tackled another mountain, G2, in harsh weather.

Ali also joined the expedition to Broad Peak in its initial stages but returned early to accompany a Russian climber who was feeling the effects of exhaustion - narrowly avoiding the fatal avalanche.

"I wanted to go with him (Purja) but couldn't and came back with her. I was part of the team but survived," he said.

Record high peaks climb

Purja had written on X this week that he was close to becoming the first person to climb all 14 "super peaks" twice without oxygen.

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down," he wrote.

He had climbed all 14 "eight-thousanders" (peaks above 8,000 metres) in six months and six days between April and October 2019, then a record.

Broad Peak is the world's 12th highest mountain, located in the Karakoram range in northern Pakistan, and is regarded as one of the toughest and most technical climbs of all the 8,000-metre-plus ascents.

World.title: Lithuania moves to tighten curbs on pro-Kremlin Russian and Belarusian figures
World.content:
Lithuania is proposing to tighten restrictions on Russian and Belarusian nationals by barring pro-Kremlin figures from carrying out public activities in the Baltic country and further limiting their ability to acquire property near strategically important sites.

 

The measures (link in Lithuanian) put forward by the Foreign ministry as amendments to Lithuania's Law on Restrictive Measures in Response to Military Aggression against Ukraine, would prohibit individuals and legal entities from Russia and Belarus from conducting public activities in the fields of education, science, culture, sport, the arts and entertainment if they have supported Russia's war against Ukraine, worked in occupied Ukrainian territories, backed repression in Russia or Belarus, or refuse to sign a declaration condemning Moscow's invasion.

According to the ministry, the changes are intended to prevent Moscow and Minsk from using cultural, educational and sporting activities as instruments of "soft power" to spread propaganda and influence public opinion.

"Establishing these restrictions would prevent situations where cooperation in the fields of education, science and studies, culture, art, and entertainment could be exploited to foster a favorable view of ongoing aggression, disseminate the ideology of aggressor states, and legitimize the politicized and manipulative activities of the Kremlin and Minsk regimes,” the Foreign ministry spokesperson told Euronews. The measures would also "enhance the resilience of Lithuanian society against information threats," the spokesperson added.

The ministry says the legislation would provide authorities with a clearer legal basis for taking consistent decisions based on objective criteria rather than ad hoc assessments.

The proposals also tighten existing restrictions on property ownership. Under current Lithuanian law, Russian citizens without a permanent or temporary residence permit are already barred from purchasing real estate. The amendments would extend the restrictions to Russian citizens who do hold residence permits, but only for properties located near facilities deemed critical to national security or close to military training areas. The same restrictions would apply to Belarusian citizens.

According to Vilnius, the objective is to “significantly” reduce the risk that property near sensitive sites could be used for intelligence gathering, surveillance or other hostile activities.

Lithuania would thus join several neighbouring countries that have introduced similar restrictions.

Estonia already restricts third-country nationals, including Russians and Belarusians, from acquiring property in certain areas important for national security. Latvia has adopted a prohibition on Russian and Belarusian citizens purchasing real estate anywhere in the country, while Finland has, since 2025, prohibited Russian and Belarusian citizens from obtaining permission to acquire property.

If approved by Lithuania's parliament, the Seimas, and signed by President Gitanas Nausėda, the amendments would enter into force on 1 January 2027.

World.title: Sánchez slams Europe's lack of solidarity over Ceuta in letter to von der Leyen
World.content:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has lamented what he describes as a lack of European solidarity over the Ceuta crisis in a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, in which he points to misinformation, prejudice and petty politics.

 

The letter, sent on Saturday and seen by Euronews, comes after Sánchez described the arrival of 50,000 migrants from Morocco in Ceuta in a single day, after the double-fenced border was breached, as an "attack" and a "violation of Spain's territorial integrity".

Pedro Sánchez's letter to Von der Leyen over the Ceuta crisis Pedro Sánchez

In the strongly worded letter, Sánchez describes the response from some EU partners as "rather asymmetric".

While breaches of national borders are always swiftly condemned by member states and often portrayed as hybrid attacks, several EU countries instead called for tighter controls on Spain, urging Madrid to restore order rather than expressing solidarity.

"Most have shown us their support and solidarity, and have offered their assistance," the Spanish premier writes in the letter.

"Others, however, have chosen to attack Spain and to call for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen Area," he continued, in an apparent reference to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government, which on Friday announced it would suspend freedom of movement with Spain, even as migrants were returning to Morocco.

It remains unclear what the measure would mean in practice.

Sánchez also appeared to hit back at Italy over irregular migration, arguing in the letter that Spain has "one of the least porous external borders of the European Union," citing Frontex data.

"In the current international context, the European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction," he added.

Madrid defends track record

Sánchez has come under scrutiny from conservative and right-wing governments over plans to regularise the status of 500,000 people living in Spain without legal permits.

Madrid has defended the decision, which was not consulted with the EU, arguing that these are people who already live and work in Spain and should be granted social rights. The European right has criticised the move as reckless, arguing that it would inevitably lead to a surge in irregular arrivals.

Still, Spanish sources say that conflating the regularisation process with the irregular crossings into Ceuta is short-sighted, arguing that the two episodes are unrelated. Madrid described the events in the enclave as an attack on its territorial integrity, rather than as a migrant crisis.

In his letter, Sánchez also defended the government's response to the crisis.

He said border control had been restored within 48 hours, humanitarian assistance had been provided to those who crossed, and almost all those who entered irregularly had been returned. On Friday, the EU said no illegal crossings had been recorded out of Ceuta into mainland Spain, and therefore the rest of member states.

Sánchez said these measures were carried out in coordination with the Moroccan authorities, with limited assistance from other European countries. The EU said Friday it was ready to deploy more means through Frontex, although this was not requested.

He added that Spain's had shown solidarity to EU countries facing similar challenges, including during the 2021 border crisis involving Belarus and several Eastern European countries, and the surge in migrant arrivals on the Italian island of Lampedusa in 2023.

It remains unclear what prompted the mass crossing of around 50,000 people from Morocco into Ceuta on Thursday, as border controls collapsed. Rabat has denied any instrumentalisation of migration for political reasons, although similar incidents have occurred in the past during periods of diplomatic tension between the two.

Even as border checks became overwhelmed, the EU praised Morocco's cooperation in managing migration flows. Spain said it had agreed with Rabat to accelerate returns. Footage from Ceuta showed many young Moroccans returning voluntarily on foot, as the city was practically put on lockdown and the Spanish army patrolled the streets.

Emergency meeting

Sánchez has formally asked the European Council to urgently convene a video conference of EU interior ministers. He said the meeting should aim to establish a common European response and to reaffirm the protection of the EU's external borders.

He said that is a shared responsibility, not just those on the front line in the south.

The Spanish prime minister ends the letter by calling on European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to show leadership and ensure that the European Union responds to the situation in Ceuta "swiftly, effectively and in a coordinated manner."

While European Council chief Costa expressed solidarity with Spain, von der Leyen focused on returns, calling the scenes in Ceuta "unacceptable" and blaming human traffickers.

Separately, a group of 22 member states, led by Italy and Denmark, issued a letter on Saturday asking for emergency talks after the Ceuta crisis. They urged more common action to strengthen Europe's external borders, with internal checks if necessary.

Portugal and France, Spain's direct neighbours, did not adhere to the letter.

This story has been updated to reflect a new letter sent by a group of EU countries.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: Germany's long road to equality for same-sex couples
World.content:
In 2001, same-sex couples in Germany were able to register a civil partnership for the first time. The Civil Partnership Act was a crucial step toward "marriage for all," which was introduced in 2017.

August 1, 2001, marked a turning point: with the Civil Partnership Act, same-sex couples in Germany gained a legal framework for the registration of their partnerships. However, another 16 years would pass before marriage itself became an option.

"The Civil Partnership Act was a milestone for the legal recognition of same-sex couples in Germany and laid the foundation for opening up marriage," Alexander Vogt of the national board of "Queere Vielfalt e.V. " (Queer diversity) told DW.

"It introduced a legally secure partnership with rights similar to those of marriage — such as inheritance, maintenance, and residency rights — though it remained discriminatory in many areas – like adoption or tax law. Nevertheless, it gave us a foot in the door — a solid base from which further rights could be secured, usually by appealing to the Federal Constitutional Court."

Reinhard Lüschow (r) and Heinz-Friedrich Harre were the first same-sex couple in Germany to register under the new Civil Partnership Act Image: picture alliance/dpa

Public opinion was ahead of the political establishment

The legislation was preceded by a fierce political debate. The opposition bloc of conservative parties, the Christian Democratic Union and the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), denounced it as an "unconstitutional attack on marriage and the family." Lawmakers from the ruling center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, described the law as "a long-overdue act of redress."

"There was strong conservative opposition, for instance from churches and civic groups," Alexander Vogt noted. "The debate reflected the classic culture war between traditional and progressive values."

Backed by the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens, the majority of Bundestag lawmakers voted in favor of the Civil Partnership Act in November 2000, despite opposition from the CDU/CSU and the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP).

German public opinion was already a step ahead: A 1999 survey showed that 55% of respondents were already in favor of the Civil Partnership Act.

However, Germany was by no means a pioneer. Denmark was the first country in the world to introduce civil partnerships for same-sex couples, doing so as early as 1989. Norway, Sweden, and Iceland followed in the mid-1990s, with France following in 1999.

Two fathers, two babies To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'We simply wanted equal treatment'

Twenty-five years ago, Reinhard Lüschow and his husband Heinz-Friedrich Harre — who has since passed away — became the first same-sex couple in Germany to tie the knot at a registry office under the new Civil Partnership Act. They had spent the preceding decade fighting for legal recognition as a couple.

As early as 1992, they had made a public statement by applying to register their marriage — in a coordinated move by 250 male and female same-sex couples across Germany. When their application was rejected, they took the case all the way to the Federal Constitutional Court. "We simply wanted to be treated equally," Lüschow recently told the Protestant Press Service (epd).

Although the court ruled at the time that marriage was a union between a man and a woman, it also mandated that the legislature ensure same-sex partnerships were not discriminated against. When the Bundestag implemented this requirement through the Civil Partnership Act, Lüschow and Harre reacted immediately.

Hard-won changes

The Civil Partnership Act regulates matters such as the use of surnames, mutual financial support, and inheritance rights. In the years that followed, the scope of civil partnerships was gradually expanded — first in 2004 to include stepchild adoption, and later to achieve tax equality following several rulings by the Federal Constitutional Court.

What do weddings look like in Germany? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Civil Partnership Act was merely the first step toward equality. The decisive step did not come until October 1, 2017, with legislation that introduced so-called "marriage for all."

This, too, was a hard-won victory. The conservative parties had come to power again in 2005. They blocked the legislation until Chancellor Angela Merkel authorized a vote free from party-line constraints, meaning lawmakers were to follow only their consciences; this is how the majority was secured in 2017. Angela Merkel and current Chancellor Friedrich Merz voted against the legislation.

Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile were the first same-sex couple to marry. Reflecting on the 2001 Civil Partnership Act, Mende later told DW: "It was a second-class partnership." Although there were few legal restrictions, the status lacked the standing of a conventional marriage.

Married partners enjoy more rights — for instance, regarding naming laws, child adoption, and the equalization of pension rights. Marriage also carries greater recognition internationally.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 108,000 couples had availed themselves of this new option by 2025. At the same time, approximately 24,000 registered civil partnerships remain in existence; these can be converted into marriages upon application.

Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile (r) were the first same-sex couple to marry in Germany in 2017 Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa-Zentralbild/ZB/picture alliance

'Marriage for all' does not amount to full equality

Differences remain between same-sex and opposite-sex couples. Alexander Vogt of the association Queere Vielfalt cites an example regarding the law of parentage: "If a child is born into a family with two mothers, the non-biological mother must first go through an adoption process to establish legal parenthood. This is not the case for heterosexual couples."

Reflecting on societal developments, Vogt observes: "Acceptance of same-sex marriage has clearly increased."

However, he adds: "We have become more visible in recent years, but not safer; violence and hate crimes — particularly against queer people — have risen sharply. The figures have increased tenfold since 2010! The attack in Berlin represents a tragic peak in this trend, one that has garnered significant public attention."

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan
World.content:
Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. Faridoon Tofan, who is currently in deportation detention, fears the same fate.

Things would likely have turned out very differently had Faridoon Tofan not taken the bus to Italy. He had intended to go on a short trip to Rome. The 46-year-old — who had fled the Taliban to Germany just under four years ago and had since been working and learning the language — was detained during a border check in mid-April and taken directly to a deportation detention center in Munich.

The reason: Tofan did not have the legal right to leave Germany. His asylum application had been rejected; he held only a temporary residence permit, which does not protect against deportation. He could now be sent back to Kabul, even though he is neither a convicted criminal nor has he been classified as a security threat. His asylum application appeal was definitively rejected in July, and he is now to be deported.

Faridoon Tofan fled to Germany from Afghanistan four years ago Image: privat

Tofan's wife and six children are still living in Kabul. They were recently paid a visit by Taliban officials and say they've been living in constant fear ever since and the sons no longer dare attend school, Nina Alizadeh Marandi told DW. She is an asylum law expert at the human rights organization Amnesty International in Germany and in close contact with Tofan's lawyer.

The Taliban officials' interest in the Tofan family in Kabul came after Faridoon Tofan's meeting with Afghan consulate staff in Berlin. Both the embassy in the German capital and the Afghan Consulate General in Bonn are now under Taliban control — a state of affairs for which the German government has faced heavy criticism from the opposition and human rights organizations.

While the German government does not officially recognize the Taliban administration as the legitimate government of Afghanistan, it points to contacts maintained at a purely "technical level."

Deportation precedent

This week, another Afghan national with no criminal record was deported.

The flight — operated by Freebird Airlines using an Airbus A320-214 — departed Leipzig/Halle Airport in Eastern Germany at 1:43 a.m. on Tuesday, bound for Trabzon, Turkey, before continuing to Kabul, Afghanistan. The Afghan national with no criminal record was on the plane alongside 30 convicted offenders.

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests: 260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

The complicated matter of deportation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Luca Müller, spokesperson for the anti-racism group, also referenced the deadly terror attack on the Pride event in Berlin over the weekend: "While Islamist violence targeting Berlin's Pride celebration is being condemned from all sides, the federal government is supporting the Islamist Taliban through its deals," Müller said.

By "deals," Müller is referring to accusations leveled by many human rights organizations and the political opposition that the German government is de facto legitimizing the Taliban regime in Afghanistan in order to facilitate more deportations.

Interior Minister justifies the tough approach

What critics view as a breach of fundamental taboo, others see as nothing more than the swift enforcement of existing law. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt again told journalists this week, that anyone who has gone through an asylum process resulting in a rejection is therefore required to leave the country and must expect deportation if they do not depart voluntarily. Dobrindt, who is a member of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), stated that the federal government is simply pursuing its goals in migration policy, driving forward this "shift in migration policy" with "control, a clear course, and a firm stance," Dobrindt added.

Improved security situation in Afghanistan?

Since the resumption of deportations to Afghanistan in 2024, Germany has returned more than 200 individuals. According to Amnesty International, at least one of them was killed following his arrival in Kabul.

However, the German government points to assessments by the UN migration agency (IOM) , which considers the return of men to Afghanistan to be feasible again — in principle.

"The security situation in Afghanistan has improved significantly; that is simply an objective fact," Mihyung Park, the IOM's country chief in Kabul, told the media outlet Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland. Park added one caveat: "Under current circumstances, we would strongly advise women against returning to Afghanistan."

In general, however, UN agencies warn against involuntary returns, noting that the returnees heavily depend on support to settle again in their country of origin.

Amnesty International condemns the German government for increasingly toughening its deportation practices without regard for the catastrophic human rights situation in Afghanistan. Nina Alizadeh Marandi pointed out that the very day of this week's historical deportation happened to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the adoption of the Geneva Refugee Convention .

"Human rights standards must not be eroded simply because upholding them is politically inconvenient," Alizadeh Marandi said. "Amnesty calls on the federal government to refrain from further deportations and to monitor whether Afghans who have already been deported are able to live in Afghanistan without persecution or danger to life and limb," she added.

Under Taliban shadow, Afghans in Pakistan look to Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Opposition speaks of a 'dangerous wrong turn'

Germany's political opposition has also sharply criticized the first deportation of an Afghan national with no criminal record. "It is irresponsible that Alexander Dobrindt is now deporting people to Afghanistan who have done absolutely nothing wrong here," said Marcel Emmerich, the Green Party's parliamentary spokesperson on interior policy.

Emmerich said that Dobrindt's "dirty deal" regarding deportations strengthens the Taliban, "makes us vulnerable to blackmail, and undermines Germany's own security." He added that the federal government is taking a "dangerous wrong turn" with this Afghanistan policy.

Juliane Nagel, a lawmaker for the socialist Left Party in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony, called the flight "shameful" and demanded that Saxony's Leipzig/Halle Airport — which is largely state-owned — no longer be used for deportations to Afghanistan.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Famed climber Nirmal Purja among 10 killed in avalanche
World.content:
A major search was launched after an avalanche struck the expedition high on Pakistan's Broad Peak. The confirmation ended hopes of a rescue and marked the loss of one of the world's best-known high-altitude climbers.

Celebrated climber Nirmal Purja and nine other mountaineers have been confirmed dead after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak, his expedition company said on Saturday.

The confirmation came a day after rescuers located four bodies while searching for the 10-member expedition.

How did Purja and the other mountaineers die?

"It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak," Purja's company Elite Expeditions said in a social media post.

"We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive."

The climbers had been missing since Thursday, when an avalanche struck the expedition at around 6,600 meters (21,650 feet) on Broad Peak. The party is believed to have been swept away.

Two Pakistan Army Aviation helicopters joined the operation on Friday, while an experienced ground team was deployed to the area where the group was last believed to have been.

Pakistani security sources said four bodies had been located that day, although they had not yet been recovered.

The mountain is the 12th highest in the world and lies near Pakistan's border with China (file photo) Image: Photoshot/picture alliance

At the time, rescuers were still searching for the remaining members of the group.

The deaths of all 10 climbers were confirmed on Saturday.

The expedition included Purja and five other Nepalese climbers, including several Sherpa guides, as well as mountaineers from four other countries.

They were Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi, Omani climber Nathira Ahmed, US climber Mallory Geis and China's Wang Zhong.

Who was Nirmal Purja?

Nirmal Purja, widely known as Nims Dai, was a British-Nepali mountaineer who became one of the best-known high-altitude climbers of his generation.

The 43-year-old served with Britain's Brigade of Gurkhas and later the elite Special Boat Service before leaving the military to become a full-time mountaineer and guide.

Purja shot to international fame in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains above 8,000 meters in just over six months, dramatically beating the previous record of nearly eight years.

His feat was chronicled in the 2021 Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible," which helped bring him a global following.

In 2021, Purja was also part of the 10-member Nepali team that completed the first winter ascent of K2, the world's second-highest mountain.

Before the latest ascent, Purja had posted his hopes for the expedition on X, asking the mountain for safe passage.

What is Broad Peak?

Broad Peak stands at just over 8,000 meters in Pakistan's Karakoram range, close to the border with China. It is the world's 12th-highest mountain and lies only a few kilometers from the better-known K2.

Originally designated K3 during the surveying of the Karakoram, its more modern name refers to its unusually wide summit ridge, which stretches for roughly 1.5 kilometers (just under a mile).

The region contains five of the world's 14 peaks above 8,000 meters and attracts climbers from across the globe, although avalanches and rapidly changing weather make expeditions particularly dangerous.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic, Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'
World.content:
In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.

Observing recent heatwaves in Europe, one pattern has often been remarked on: More women appear to be dying than men. During Europe's then-record summer of 2022, a study found 56% more heat-related deaths among women than men, drawing on mortality data from 35 countries.

Germany, which has just logged its deadliest heat season since 2016, with close to 9,800 heat-related deaths by mid-July, according to the Robert Koch Institute, is seeing the same pattern again this year.

Are hormones making heatwaves more dangerous for women?

Some of the recent coverage has leaned on the hormonal reading that women's bodies simply aren't equipped for heat. They sweat less, carry more body fat, and progesterone nudges core temperature up.

But scientists who study the effect of heat on the human body say that's largely incorrect. "Overall, studies usually show only slightly more vulnerability to heat in women compared to men," saidAlexandra Schneider , an environmental epidemiologist and deputy director of the Institute of Epidemiology at Helmholtz Munich. "It's not really a very strong signal."

The small differences that do exist are real: Women do have a lower sweat rate, less skin area relative to body size, and fat distribution that affects thermoregulation. Hormones play a role too, but unevenly across a lifetime.

Schneider points to one group in particular: Women past menopause, when cardiovascular risk climbs. Older women with existing heart disease, she says, are probably at the highest risk of all.

But even in those cases, she doesn't think biology is the main cause for the extra deaths during a heatwave. "The living conditions, the social environment where women live, makes probably even more of a risk than just the differences in hormone status."

How to survive heat waves in the city To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A research gap, not a biological difference

Toby Mündel, a kinesiology professor at Brock University in Canada, who studies extreme human environments, says that the impact is "overstated," when asked whether there's a real biological basis for the claim that women are more likely to die in heatwaves.

The factors that most determine how a person copes with a heatwave, Mündel says, are age, body size, fitness and habitual activity, and not biological sex.

Sweating is one example. Even though women do sweat less, that doesn't make them more vulnerable, because they compensate in another way. "They send blood flow to the skin, vasodilation, much better than males do," Mündel says, meaning their blood vessels widen more efficiently, moving heat to the surface where it can escape.

Pregnancy, which many assume must be dangerous, is another example. "As a woman progresses through pregnancy, she actually becomes better at handling heat," Mündel says. He draws a clear line between physiology and circumstance: There are good reasons not to have pregnant women doing heavy outdoor labor in extreme heat. But their bodies aren't the reason.

Why does the data suggest otherwise?

Partly, Mündel's argument is based on what gets measured. Studies often count hospital and emergency admissions, and women are far more likely than men to seek medical help. "That is not a physiological thing," he says. "Are they actually struggling, or have they just sought help earlier?"

Underneath it all sits a research gap. "We have about a hundred times as much data and evidence on men. We have nearly zero on women," Mündel says. "It's like comparing cats and dogs."

Numbers from Germany point in the same direction. The Robert Koch Institute attributes the higher female death toll to the fact that women make up a larger share of the oldest age groups. Its estimates also break down deaths per 100,000 people, and by that measure, the picture flips.

In every older age band this summer, the male death rate is higher than the female one. In other words, more women are dying in heatwaves only because more very old women are alive.

In scorching Taipei, locals seek ways to survive urban heat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The real risk is exposure for women, not biology

If the gap isn't physiological, where does it come from?

Laurie Parsons, a researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, studieshow heat stress moves through the global economy in construction, garment factories, farming, driving, street vending.

Across the board, he says, women spend 30% to 50% more of their working time above heat-stress thresholds than men. In construction, when comparing men and women doing the same job, the figure rises to around 50%.

The reasons, he says, are structural. Women often wear more clothing for the same job. Men are more confident asking for breaks. And where men's work is visibly strenuous, it's recognized as a heat risk and rewarded with rest. But women's work is steadier, less obviously punishing, and gets no such relief.

Parsons compares it to the difference between a plane crash and asbestos exposure: One is a sudden, visible catastrophe, the other a slow, constant harm that's easy to miss. "Male heat stress tends to be this taller risk, where you get relatively visible moments of physical distress that can be managed," he says. "Female heat stress is constantly there, but much less visible, because it doesn't have those same obvious peaks in the working day."

Long working hours, limited breaks, and repeated exposure to heat - women often face greater burdens under these conditions Image: Aaron Favila/AP/dpa

Then the shift ends, he says. Men rest, but women cook, clean and care for children.

Heat also cuts into pay. Parsons says workers under heat stress are around 30% less productive in the garment sector, which he says is the easiest to quantify.

In formal jobs, workers make up for it with longer hours during the hottest part of the day, feeding what he calls "a vicious cycle" of worsening health and falling output. The self-employed have no such buffer. For them, heat stress just means less income, which ripples the wider family over time.

For Parsons, the starting premise is flawed. "Heat stress is not an atmospheric condition," he says. "It is a social condition, which happens within particular atmospheric circumstances."

Edited by Ben Knight

World.title: Iran warns neighbors against being US 'defensive shield'
World.content:
08/01/2026 August 1, 2026 Israel claims to have killed several Hezbollah fighters

Israel's military on Saturday said its forces killed several Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon. A post on the military's official X account said that one of its combat officers was injured during the armed encounter and had been hospitalized.

The post pledged that the Israeli military would "continue to operate to remove any threat its forces and will not allow the Hezbollah terror organization to harm the citizens of the state of Israel."

The incident came despite a ceasefire being in place between Israel and the Iranian-backed militants. While Hezbollah has formally denounced the deal, the group has not claimed any attacks since theUS-sponsored framework agreement was signed by Israel and Lebanon and then put in place in late June.

The agreement remains fragile, with Hezbollah refusing to disarm and Israel refusing to leave southern Lebanon — both points outlined in the agreement.

Despite the relative decline in violence in southern Lebanon, Israel has continued to conduct airstrikes and carry out other military operations.

Lebanon has condemned Israel's operations, saying that its continued military operations make it impossible to fully deploy the Lebanese army as outlined in the deal.

World.title: Greece battles wildfires, including near Athens
World.content:
Firefighters were battling blazes in over 70 locations across Greece. Strong winds continue to fan the flames, adding to the firefighters' struggles.

A raging wildfire has continued to engulf a popular coastal resort in Greece, even as hundreds of firefighters battle to put it out amid gusty winds.

The fire broke out on Friday near the coastal village of Agios Vasileios.

More than 300 firefighters have been deployed to control the wildfire, in an effort to prevent it from spreading to the area of Porto Germeno, some 70 kilometres (45 miles) northwest of Athens in the region of Viotia.

"The fire has reached the sea... homes have certainly been damaged," a fire department spokesman told the French AFP news agency.

The Greek fire brigade said it was at the maximum level of alert Image: Costas Baltas/Anadolu

"The winds are very strong. Aircraft are trying to operate as best they can, but some are unable to and have been transferred to another fire (in the Peloponnese) where conditions are milder," he added.

Winds up to 130 kilometres per hour, recorded on Saturday by the weather service of the National Observatory of Athens, have made the fire department's efforts more difficult.

"The environmental damage is huge," the mayor of Thebes, Giorgos Anastasiou, told Open TV.

Fire breaks out in several places across Greece

Wildfires have flared in several parts of the country this week, with more than 70 locations in Greece affected by Friday.

The Greek fire brigade said it was at the maximum level of alert, warning that the fire risk was particularly high in the Attica peninsula and in Evia, an island east ‌of Athens where fires are frequent.

Wildfires have flared in several parts of the country this week, including on the popular island of Crete Image: Costas Baltas/Anadolu

"The fire has reached the sea... homes have certainly been damaged," a fire department spokesman told AFP.

Theodore Giannaros, a wildfire meteorologist and senior researcher at the National Observatory of Athens on Saturday said the damage to the Porto Germeno area was "inconceivable."

Wildfires have raged in several parts of Greece this week, including the popular island of Crete, affecting some 5,000 hectares on the island. Three firefighters have lost their lives so far.

Several European countries have been battling savage wildfires this summer, amid extreme heatwaves and little rain.

New heat wave could worsen France, Spain fires To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: War in Ukraine: Why Crimea has become a strategic target
World.content:
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russian logistics centers and energy facilities in Crimea. What are the consequences for local supplies, and how does Kyiv hope this strategy will affect the course of the war?

In an attempt to isolate Crimea from the mainland, the Ukrainian armed forces have intensified their attacks on the peninsula, which was invaded and annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine is using long-range drones to attack transports on the M14 highway between the Russian city of Rostov-on-Don and Melitopol in occupied southern Ukraine. It is also targeting Russian shadow fleet ships in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, as well as energy facilities that supply the Russian military.

Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, commander of the Ukrainian forces for unmanned systems, says 196 Russian ships and more than 100 energy facilities have been hit in the past month alone. His figures cannot be independently verified.

Russia appears to be struggling to supply both its military and the civilian population in Crimea. Fuel coupons were issued at the end of May, but ran out after 24 hours, after which gasoline was being traded on the black market. A state of emergency was declared in Crimea, especially Sevastopol, in response to repeated disruption of the electricity and water supply, and of the internet and cellphone networks.

What are residents in Crimea experiencing?

Nina, a pensioner who lives in a village near Feodosiya, southeastern Crimea, told DW about the difficulties people there are facing: Residents there can't cook because of power cuts, and fuel shortages mean public transport only runs intermittently. Nina's worst fear, though, is not having electricity in winter.

Russian-occupied Crimea hit by fuel shortages and power cuts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The longest power cuts have been in the north of Crimea. This is where Ivan lives [name changed]. He tells DW that for some time, people were unable to get hold of fuel with either coupons or cash. The only exceptions, he says, were police officers, state officials, and doctors. For several days, everything collapsed: Cars ran out of fuel and simply came to a stop; people didn't know how they were supposed to get to where they were going.

Ivan said that most shops no longer stock perishable goods, because they can't run their fridges and freezers: "There are no milk products, or fish, or meat," he said. "There are only a few shops with electricity generators, but the prices there are much higher than before."

Some small, private, volunteer initiatives are trying to help. The blogger Olena Gerasimenko works with companies in Simferopol to bring drinking water to people suffering from power cuts, and to hospitals and kindergartens. In her blog, she reports that people are complaining about the lack of help from the Russian-installed "authorities" in Crimea.

On social media, people say that, because of the power cuts and having no means of communication, residents of northern Crimea are sending post by public bus. But the buses aren't running regularly either.

What are Ukraine's tactics?

Ukraine's efforts to block supply routes both in and to Crimea are directed primarily against the small Russian tankers and tugboats that transport oil to larger ships and fuel to the Crimean mainland. Parallel to this, it is also destroying transformer substations. But Commander Brovdi says Ukraine is deliberately sparing the Kerch Bridge, which spans the Kerch Strait, connecting the peninsula with the Russian region of Krasnodar.

In a recent interview with the Irish journalist Caolan Robertson , Brovdi said the road and rail bridge should be maintained as a corridor for people to escape from Crimea. The aim is not to destroy it, Brovdi says, but to cut off Russian troops from supplies and reinforcements. "We want to make it impossible for the Russian military machine to remain and continue to operate there."

Satellite photo of the Henichesk Bridge, damaged by Ukrainian attacks, and a new, alternative bridge connecting Russian-occupied southern Ukraine to northern Crimea Image: Vantor/REUTERS

The military expert Ivan Kyrychevskyi serves in a Ukrainian drone unit. Speaking to DW he emphasized how important the air attacks on Crimea are for the frontline on the ground. "To stop the Russians getting anywhere near Zaporizhzhia, they have to put pressure on their lines of communication in the occupied south of Ukraine. This applies above all to Crimea. The blockade of shipping traffic in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea essentially has the same objective," says Kyrychevskyi. "For far too long, Crimea has served the Russians as a tranquil harbor and unsinkable aircraft carrier from which to carry out their offensives in southern Ukraine."

Pavlo Narozhnyi, a Ukrainian military expert and founder of the charitable organization Reactive Post, describes Crimea as a massive military base. Russian troops in the regions of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia are heavily dependent on it. Narozhnyi says that for a long time Russian logistics primarily ran through the peninsula, but this supply source is now being cut off on two sides: On land by attacks on the M14 highway, and at sea by attacks on transport vessels near the Crimea Bridge. "This way we are not isolating only Crimea but also the Russian troops in the south of Ukraine," Narozhnyi told DW. His organization supplies life-saving equipment to Ukrainian artillery divisions on the frontline.

Situation 'no worse' than in Ukrainian cities3

Narozhnyi explains that, at present, up to three million people in Crimea depend on Russia for their supplies. "A thermal power station that provided up to 60% of Crimea's entire electricity supply has been destroyed. The supply of oil products has been interrupted. The population is already experiencing problems, even with everyday things." The military expert also warned that these problems will get even worse in the fall, when the weather turns colder and people want to heat their homes. "Putin will then have to deal not only with military problems, but also the problems of the population," Narozhnyi says.

People use flashlights to navigate a dark street during a power outage in Yevpatoriya, Crimea, in July 2026. Image: Alexey Pavlishak/REUTERS

According to Sidharth Kaushal of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in London, attacks on power stations do not automatically contravene international law, particularly if the facilities have military significance and the attacks comply with the rule of proportionality.

Ukrainian experts confirm that the targeted facilities primarily supply electricity for military facilities. Kaushal told DW that he assumed a large-scale blockade strategy by Ukraine could ultimately compel Moscow to negotiate a ceasefire.

Commander Brovdi is asking people to be patient. "I apologize to the residents of Crimea, the Ukrainians, for the current difficulties. They are experiencing restrictions of advantages they have enjoyed all their lives – the supply of energy, water, and communications. But they are in a situation no worse than that of people in Kharkiv, Dnipro, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Nikopol, Kherson, and hundreds of other cities that are targeted on a daily basis."

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

World.title: How crypto miners are stealing power in Southeast Asia
World.content:
Across Southeast Asia, illegal cryptocurrency miners are stealing vast amounts of electricity, straining national grids, and exposing links to organized crime.

A raid in Malaysia last week exposed how cryptocurrency mining is becoming entangled with electricity theft and organized crime across Southeast Asia.

In Malaysia's southern state of Johor, 71 cryptocurrency-mining machines had been running around the clock across four rented premises for about a month before police moved in.

During the raids on July 22 and 23, officers arrested three suspects and seized computers, routers and vehicles alongside equipment used to illegally mine Bitcoin.

Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said the syndicate bypassed electricity meters, leading to an estimated €14,500 ($16,600) in losses in about a month, according to local media reports. The machines were thought to be generating between €17,200 and €21,500 in monthly revenue.

The case was relatively small by Malaysian standards. Between 2020 and 2025, national utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) identified almost 14,000 premises linked to electricity theft for cryptocurrency mining. Its cumulative losses reached around €1.1 billion.

Recorded cases of such theft increased from 610 in 2018 to 2,397 in 2024, according to Malaysia's Energy Ministry, which has described illegal mining as a serious threat to public safety, economic stability, and the national electricity system.

"In Malaysia, thousands of incidents have triggered investigations into illegal mining for cryptocurrency purposes," said Sonny Zulhuda, associate professor at the International Islamic University Malaysia.

"This poses a huge problem for the security of electricity resources, economic sustainability, competition, and revenue loss," Zulhuda told DW. "Enforcement has been lagging behind, due to a lack of legislative preparedness and limited agency capability in enforcement and investigation. This is unfortunate because Malaysia is fast developing its digital infrastructure."

Where crypto mining meets organized crime

Cryptocurrency mining is not inherently criminal, but authorities are increasingly finding links between illegal crypto mining, online gambling, money laundering, and Southeast Asia's industrial-scale cyber scam networks.

Last October, the United States and the UK sanctioned the Cambodia-based Prince Group and associated companies, alleging that the network operated forced-labor scam compounds and laundered proceeds through cryptocurrencies and other assets.

US authorities also seized Bitcoin worth around $15 billion at the time from wallets whose private keys were held by Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi, describing the cryptocurrency as proceeds and instruments of fraud and money laundering.

Inside Cambodia's scam industry To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thailand's Department of Special Investigation has made the clearest connection between stolen electricity and transnational crime.

In 2025, investigators dismantled three major illegal crypto mining networks, seized more than 6,390 machines and estimated losses to the Provincial Electricity Authority at more than €24.9 million.

In one operation, authorities found around 1,900 mining machines at warehouse sites. The electricity authority estimated that the network was consuming power worth around €575,000 each month while paying only a fraction of the amount due.

Indonesia battles crypto mining crimes as well

Indonesia has seen similar cases. In December 2023, police in the province of North Sumatra raided ten sites and seized more than 1,100 Bitcoin-mining machines. State utility PLN estimated losses over six months at around €700,000.

Governments have responded with raids, tougher penalties and cooperation between police, utilities, regulators and anti-corruption agencies. Malaysia has created a multi-agency committee and deployed smart meters at substations to identify abnormal consumption.

But enforcement remains difficult. Equipment can be moved quickly, premises can be rented through intermediaries and meter tampering may involve organized networks or insider assistance.

Saaidal Razalli Azzuhri, a telecommunications expert at the University of Malaya, told DW that raids should be supported by transformer-level monitoring, mandatory licensing, disclosure of companies' beneficial owners, and investigations tracing bank transfers and cryptocurrency wallets.

"The objective should not be to prohibit blockchain technology, but to ensure that miners pay the full economic cost of their electricity and do not transfer their costs and infrastructure risks to the public," he said.

Zulhuda said that Southeast Asian governments need to deal with this issue properly so they don't send the wrong message to companies that want to invest in the region's growing digital sectors.

Malaysia has several laws to curb illegal cyber activities, including the Cyber Security Act 2024 to protect its National Critical Information Infrastructure and the recently enacted Cybercrimes Act 2026 to address digital system misuse and abuse, he added.

Laos pulls the plug

Laos shows that even legal, state-backed cryptocurrency mining can struggle to deliver the promised benefits.

Scam factory: Behind Asia's cyber slavery To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In mid-2021, the government authorized six companies to mine and trade cryptocurrencies. The plan appeared suited to a country that had invested heavily in hydropower and sometimes produced more electricity than its economy could absorb. Mining offered a way to monetize surplus energy.

At its peak in 2021 and 2022, the industry consumed around 500 megawatts. But the surplus proved unreliable.

Some miners accumulated unpaid bills. More importantly, officials concluded that the industry created few jobs and little demand for domestic suppliers compared with manufacturing or other commercial activities.

Deputy Energy Minister Chanthaboun Soukaloun said last October that the government intended to end electricity supplies to miners.

Laos wants to redirect the power towards metals processing, electric-vehicle manufacturing and artificial intelligence data centers, while increasing electricity exports to neighboring countries.

The experiment offered a broader warning. Cheap electricity can attract crypto miners, but it does not guarantee lasting investment or wider development. When operators steal power, or consume subsidized electricity without creating much value, the public is left carrying the cost.

Edited by Keith Walker

World.title: La desgracia sumergida en la frontera de Ceuta: “Hay más muertos en el mar”
World.content:
En pequeños racimos, debajo de un agua cristalina, se ven las siluetas de cuerpos sumergidos muy cerca de la frontera de El Tarajal en Ceuta. Dos de ellos están cogidos de la mano. Son la desgracia sumergida, y todavía por conocer, que ha dejado el cruce multitudinario de personas desde Marruecos de esta semana y de las numerosas entradas a nado que hubo en la segunda mitad de julio.

Dos días después de la gran entrada en la ciudad autónoma, cuando la mayor parte de quienes accedieron de forma irregular por los espigones ya han regresado a Marruecos, sigue acentuándose la cara más dramática de esa avalancha. Al menos 67 personas perdieron la vida en sus intentos de llegar a territorio español. “Hay más muertos en el mar”, se lamentaba este sábado una fuente policial. En la ciudad autónoma preparan una instalación con capacidad para conservar 200 cuerpos.

Frente a la frontera, por la mañana, el trabajo para colocar las barreras de contención acuática, una hilera de boyas de 500 metros y un mallado subacuático de hasta un metro de profundidad, se combina con la búsqueda de nuevas víctimas bajo el mar. Los agentes del Servicio Marítimo de la Guardia Civil y los buzos del Grupo Especial de Actividades Subacuáticas (GEAS) se afanaban en localizar y sacar del fondo a los fallecidos. Desde la playa, numerosos periodistas, muchos de medios internacionales, grababan las labores y retransmitían en directo la última hora de la ciudad. En los próximos días, los agentes de la Guardia Civil marcarán cuadrados e irán recorriendo todas las zonas. En la mañana de este sábado sacaron una decena de fallecidos y seguían marcando puntos en los que había más cuerpos. Es habitual que parte de las personas que mueren en los intentos de cruce a nado terminen en la parte marroquí por el viento y la marea. “Es arriesgado hacer una estimación de las víctimas totales”, puntualizaba una fuente conocedora de los trabajos. Al otro lado de la frontera, los agentes de Marruecos también estaban recuperando víctimas mortales en el mar, mantienen las mismas fuentes.

Ceuta se ha habituado en los últimos años al hallazgo en el mar de jóvenes fallecidos que intentaban cruzar a nado desde Marruecos. En 2025 terminó con 46 víctimas mortales, pero lo ocurrido esta semana ha roto con todos los registros. Al no tener infraestructura para soportar esta carga de cadáveres repentina, se han instalado cámaras frigoríficas modulares, como las que se montan en una frutería o una pescadería, en el antiguo Hospital Militar, señala una fuente de la Funeraria Cuatro Culturas, que está colaborando en estas tareas.

La identificación de cadáveres y restos humanos corresponde a los servicios de Medicina Legal y Ciencias Forenses, dependientes del Ministerio de Justicia, pero la ciudad autónoma está prestando apoyo con la logística. Entre otras medidas, han puesto a su disposición el antiguo hospital, una instalación municipal a la que se le dan múltiples usos, pero que conserva la sala de autopsias.

Al edificio, protegido por grandes verjas negras, accedían diferentes vehículos conducidos por militares y guardias civiles. También furgones de la funeraria con los cuerpos de los migrantes. En torno a las 17.00, dos empleados municipales impedían el acceso a personas ajenas al dispositivo. Lejos de los objetivos, un equipo de forenses trabajaba a esa hora con instrucciones de que el recinto estuviera cerrado a cal y canto.

Entre los cuerpos recogidos del mar hay muchos adolescentes, según la fuente de la funeraria que ha sido testigo de todo el proceso. “Hay un rango de 13 a 25 años y otro de 25 a 35, más o menos”, a falta de identificaciones más precisas. Hasta ayer, todos eran varones, menos una mujer. Hay “bastantes chiquillos de 12 a 14 años”, añade. Por el aspecto, la mayoría parecen marroquíes, pero hay otros de origen subsahariano, entre ellos algún niño de esta procedencia.

A media tarde de este sábado, ya estaban en cámaras frigoríficas cerca de 80 cuerpos, que es justo la capacidad de los módulos refrigeradores que se habían instalado, y se trabajaba para aumentar la capacidad hasta 200 cuerpos. Está previsto que los módulos queden listos el domingo por la mañana. “La capacidad que tienen las cámaras ceutíes de ordinario no pasa de 15 cadáveres”, ha explicado esta fuente.

Los agentes creen que la mayoría de las víctimas murió durante la estampida humana que se produjo desde Marruecos, bien aplastados o, en muchos casos, ahogados. “Se vio empujada al agua gente que no sabía nadar”, explican. Algunos de los cadáveres presentan un mayor grado de descomposición porque las entradas al mar llevan ya sucediéndose por espacio de dos semanas.

Una vez que los sacan del agua, el Laboratorio de Criminalística de la Guardia Civil les toma las huellas y elabora una ficha con datos que puedan ayudar a identificarlos en un futuro, como fotografías, la ropa que llevaban o muestras de ADN. Muchas ONG y la propia funeraria están ya recibiendo llamadas de personas que no tienen comunicación con sus parientes. Los familiares de desaparecidos también llaman al diario local El Faro de Ceuta, para que les ayuden publicando su falta. No es inusual que dos personas que hicieran juntas el mismo trayecto hayan corrido distinta suerte. En ese caso, pueden ayudar a identificar al amigo o compañero.

Si hay suerte, y la víctima está identificada, se pide permiso al juez para la repatriación. Si no se logra ponerle nombre y apellidos, terminan enterrados con un número.

World.title: Las mejores playas en los alrededores de Santander
World.content:
Los Tranquilos. La preciosa y relajada playa de Los Tranquilos –por algo su nombre– es, en realidad, la prolongación del arenal que a lo largo de seis kilómetros se extiende desde el Puntal, que penetra en plena bahía de Santander, hasta la localidad de Loredo después de pasar por el paraíso surfista de Somo. Los Tanquilos se encuentra, pues, al final de esta increíble franja de arena que permite el baño, bien en las calmadas aguas de la bahía o, hacia el otro lado, entre las agitadas olas del mar abierto, donde se ubica Los Tanquilos. La mejor manera de venir es también en una de las embarcaciones que comunican Santander con Somo y desde allí en un agradable paseo por la orilla. En un ecosistema dunar, las vistas a la inmensidad azul del Cantábrico y la isla de Santa Marina son un regalo añadido que quienes visitan esta playa por primera vez no podían imaginar.
