World.title: The one place to find phenomenal pho in Vietnam
World.content:
You are looking for this place, even if you don’t know it. You’ve surely come to Ho Chi Minh City in search of the perfect spot to eat pho, the Vietnamese noodle dish that is served all over the country, with slight variations and differing quality. After checking the blogs and doing a Google search, you’ve found tourist favourites like Pho Viet Nam, Pho Pasteur and Pho Phuong 25. All of these are great choices.



But I have tried them all, and my pick of the bunch by far is Pho Phu Vuong. There’s nothing fancy: it’s just stainless-steel tables and plastic chairs, a few bubbling vats of stock and meat out front near the parked scooters. But the pho is phenomenal. Arrive early in the morning, as the city wakes, grab a table and order a bowl. The soup is fragrant and perfectly balanced, a touch of sweetness with those distinctive spices. The noodles are fresh and slippery, the beef nicely rare, the emerald mountain of sawtooth coriander and basil the perfect accompaniment. Is this the best pho in Ho Chi Minh City? Who can say. But it’s the one you’ve been dreaming of.

Order this

Options at Pho Phu Vuong range from standard beef and tripe to additions such as oxtail or flank, or the choice of having soup without noodles, all in three sizes: regular, large, and “special”. First-timers should go for the classic, pho tai, with noodles and thin slices of rare beef.

World.title: Kayla eats her first meal at 4pm. A dietitian has plenty of thoughts
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessSunday Life Kayla eats her first meal at 4pm. A dietitian has plenty of thoughts Nicole Economos August 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the August 2 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Kayla Saito is a bar manager. The 33-year-old shares her day on a plate. Photo: Artwork by Eliza Iredale 7.30am A large glass of water, a few stretches, and a quick walk with my dog. 9am A decaf almond cappuccino. I’m preparing for the World Class Bartender Competition, so I’ve reduced my alcohol and espresso intake to stay focused and rested. Noon An oat matcha to keep my energy levels up through the afternoon.



4pm My first meal of the day is staff lunch of grilled barramundi on mixed rice with a radicchio salad. 8pm Dinner is couscous, braised tofu, mixed greens with yuzu vinaigrette, homemade pickles, zucchini and spicy purple cabbage. I have it with a glass of sparkling water and lemon. 9pm I practise making a few seasonal tequila cocktails and take a sip from each. 11pm Dark chocolate, strawberries and a cup of sleepy tea.



Dr Joanna McMillan says Top marks for… Giving your liver an alcohol break with mindful tasting of your cocktails. And while the timing is out, your meals are packed with colourful plant foods that deliver an array of nutrients and fibre, with fish and tofu providing quality protein. If you keep eating like this you’ll ... Continue to ask your body and brain to perform through a workday with very little fuel. The biggest risk in your regimen isn’t what you’re eating, it’s when. Going until 4pm before your first meal makes it harder to maintain concentration, support muscle recovery and meet your energy and nutrient needs, particularly in a physically demanding job. Why don’t you try… Whipping up a breakfast smoothie – your choice of fruit, nuts, seeds and oats with dairy or calcium-fortified soy milk or yoghurt – the night before, so you can drink it on the move. Carry other nutritious snacks such as a boiled egg, edamame, mixed nuts, dried fruit and cheese and wholegrain crackers so you can graze throughout the day. Kayla Saito will represent Australia at the Diageo World Class Global Finals in Scotland in October. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: As a stressed city-dweller, this Queensland escape gave me the fuel to survive winter
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life As a stressed city-dweller, this Queensland escape gave me the fuel to survive winter Jane Rocca August 2, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the August 2 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

You’re either a rainforest or reef person if you come up here,” says my driver, Michael, as he takes me from Cairns airport to Port Douglas, a 70-minute drive north along the iconic Captain Cook Highway. Michael relocated here from my home city of Melbourne 25 years ago, and the reasoning behind his decision to stay is obvious enough on this beautiful day. It’s June, and I’ve leaned into Far North Queensland’s dry season by swapping heavy coats for breezy resort linen. As we drive north, the Coral Sea and Great Barrier Reef sit to my right, but it’s knowing that the world’s oldest surviving rainforest, the Daintree, is a mere tree hug away on my left that fills me with all the emotions. At first, Port Douglas comes across like a less showy, more laid-back offshoot of Noosa or Byron Bay. Getty Images I’ve been avoiding mirrors, selfies and Insta posts since I arrived because the humidity has made my hair unruly, but once I quit the straighteners and embrace my curls, Port Douglas showers me with its greatest offering: a total unwinding that pulls at all the parts of you wrapped in city knots. No wonder it appeals to so many Australians from the southern states, especially during the cooler months. At first, Port Douglas comes across like a less showy, more laid-back offshoot of Noosa or Byron Bay. Sure, Christopher Skase made the town famous in the 1980s, but in 2026 it’s still attracting foreign travellers and younger Australians who’ve never heard of him, with FIFO workers and backpackers on working holidays only adding to the town’s hustle and bustle.



I’m staying at the Pullman Port Douglas Sea Temple Resort & Spa, a village of rooms and apartments, many with the added allure of their own outdoor hot tub, set around a lagoon-style pool. My fellow guests are a mix of baby-mooning couples, adventurers seeking reef thrills and families soaking up an off-peak break. In keeping with its pristine surrounds, the resort champions such sustainable practices as composting its coffee grounds, offering reef-friendly sunscreen by the pool and serving locally caught barramundi. There are refillable containers in the rooms, electric buggies to zip you around, and a hop-on, hop-off bus shuttle into town. As we arrive, low-lying storm clouds dissolve into torrential rain, but by the time the share plates are served on the verandah it’s back to normal programming. JANE ROCCA On day two, a group of us drive 30 minutes north for a stroll through Mossman Gorge. Dreamtime Walks was founded by Aboriginal elder Roy Gibson in 1986, and while visitors can go on self-guided hikes, having a connection to Country through storytelling adds an extra dimension. We are led by two Kuku Yalanji women on an enlightening dance through the forest, noting where their ancestors have walked, revealing sacred burial and birthing sites, and pointing out old red cedar trees that hold many secrets. We learn about trees that sting and plants that can leave you paralysed, and when I mistake a thunderous clap as a sign of tempestuous weather on its way, the guides tell me it’s actually the sound of a tree falling nearby.



A luxe lunch at the five-star Silky Oaks Lodge, set amid the rainforest, only adds to the day’s romance. As we arrive, low-lying storm clouds dissolve into torrential rain, but by the time the share plates are served on the verandah it’s back to normal programming. With the rainforest ticked off our list, we enjoy a late afternoon catamaran tour with Sailaway to the Low Isles – ideal for those who love to snorkel (you might even get the chance to swim with turtles) and with a picturesque sunset on the way back to the mainland an added bonus. Related Article Sunday Life More than 1000km from a capital city, I found one of Australia’s best cultural experiences Back in town, a 60-minute Rainforest Relaxation massage with mini facial at Kaia Day Spa is one of the best I’ve had thanks to clinician Teresa, who moved here from Taiwan to embrace the tropics. (Kaia Day Spa will move to the Sheraton Grand Mirage in the next 12 to 18 months, but for the moment it’s a mere 350-metre walk from Sea Temple.) Macrossan Street is the town’s main drag and it leads to Four Mile Beach, though it should be noted that it’s named after the Fourmile family rather than its length. The beach is a natural focal point for the town, and while swimming between the flags and within the area enclosed by a stinger-proof net is fine, most visitors opt for the pool at their resort.



Port Douglas also boasts plenty of coastal-inspired shops and Indigenous art galleries: perfect for sourcing a souvenir as well as investing in community projects. And when you’re done, go to the oyster vending machine near the main supermarket. You might have filled your social media with spectacular rainforest and reef pics, but eating a freshly shucked oyster straight from a machine is equally guaranteed to get a reaction. The writer travelled to Port Douglas as a guest of booking.com. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: Govt to spend $500,000 on environmental impacts probe into Whanganui's Balgownie Landfill
World.content:
.

The government is to contribute about a half-a-million dollars to help investigate the environmental impacts of a former Whanganui landfill that operated for more than 40 years.

Minister for the Environment Nicola Grigg announced the project.

"The allocation of $464,000 from the Contaminated Sites and Vulnerable Landfills Fund, combined with funding from the Whanganui District Council, will enable a comprehensive investigation and assessment of remedial actions of the former Balgownie Landfill," Grigg said.

The landfill operated between 1956 to 1995, with parts of it operating a further six years to 2001. Like many of the nearly 3500 former landfill sites across New Zealand, it was developed before modern environmental standards were introduced.

Grigg said the former landfill, next to the Kokohuia Wetland in the Castlecliff and Gonville area of Whanganui, did not have several features associated with modern landfill containment and risk management.

"This investigation will give us a complete picture of how any contamination and leachate from the site may be affecting surrounding waterways and wetlands, and what long-term options may be needed to protect the environment.

"This work will complement significant community-led restoration work already underway, including the Kokohuia/Titoki Wetland project.

Grigg said the investigation was an important first step in exploring ways to further restore the area's cultural and environmental values, and reflected a collaborative approach between Whanganui hapū, Mokoia Catchment Rōpū, Whanganui District Council and central government to secure long-term environmental benefits for Te Awa Tupua/the wider Whanganui Catchment.

Whanganui Mayor Andrew Tripe. RNZ / Robin Martin

Whanganui Mayor Andrew Tripe welcomed the funding which was in addition to $310,000 council was putting up.

"This investigation is about getting the facts. Before we make decisions about the site's future, we need to understand its condition and how it relates to the surrounding environment.

"Like many people who grew up in Whanganui, I have memories of visiting Balgownie as a kid and hunting for treasure. Looking back, I realise how much our understanding of waste and its impacts has changed over the years.

"While we can't change how things were done in the past, we can do our best to manage the site responsibly into the future. These investigations will help us do that."

Tripe said people could still visit the site.

"You can walk on it and it's accessible, but as far as what can be done on it is unknown. Obviously, there'll be methane gas sitting underneath it, which is an accumulation over the time since it closed.

"That's very common with landfills or retired landfills. At the end of the day, it's about, understanding what's going on top of the ground, but more importantly, what's going on underneath the ground."

He'd previously suggested putting solar panels on the land before being alerted to the possible dangers.

"Apparently even digging beneath there could be seen as dangerous, and it's kind of like potentially, you know, putting a pin in a balloon and it goes pop. So, we just don't know what's gonna happen, and that's what the investigation is about."

Mokoia Catchment Rōpū chair Ken Mair. RNZ / Leigh-Marama McLachlan

Mokoia Catchment Rōpū chair Ken Mair said understanding the landfill was important for the wider catchment.

"The waterways and wetlands in this area flow through to Te Awa Tupua, so this work is an important step toward improving the health of the Awa and surrounding environment.

"Looking at future options for the landfill will support a broader programme of work focused on the well-being of whānau, whenua and the river."

The project, which had a total cost of $774,000, started in June 2026 and was expected to be completed by October 2027.

Contaminated Sites and Vulnerable Landfills Fund was administered by the Ministry for Cities Environment Regions and Transport, and supported councils and agencies to reduce risks to human health and the environment posed by legacy contaminated sites and vulnerable landfills.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Jamaica knock out Australia, to face Silver Ferns in netball final
World.content:
The Silver Ferns have a prime opportunity to win their first Commonwealth Games gold medal since 2010 after one of the biggest boilovers at the pinnacle event saw Jamaica knock Australia out.

It's the first time the Australian Diamonds won't play for a Commonwealth Games gold medal after fourth-ranked Jamaica shocked the reigning champs 46-45 against all predictions early on Sunday morning.

The Silver Ferns booked their first Commonwealth Games gold medal match since 2014 after beating England 61-54 in Glasgow on Saturday night.

The Silver Ferns beat Jamaica 53-48 in their second pool game but the Sunshine Girls will have their tails up after their performance to beat world number one Australia.

Jamaica are slightly less potent on attack at this event without prolific shooter Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard, who gave birth a few months ago.

But the hugely experienced Romelda Aiken-George anchored the Sunshine Girls at goal shoot, while Jamaica's world-class defensive line came to life.

The Australian players looked shell-shocked as they walked off the court.

Australia players dejected after defeat in the Semi-Final match against Jamaica. Lintao Zhang/Getty Images

Sunday night's gold medal match will be the Silver Ferns' first final of a pinnacle event since winning the 2019 Netball World Cup.

A gold medal for the Silver Ferns would be the ultimate response to what's been one of the most difficult periods for the sport in New Zealand.

The Silver Ferns are playing against the backdrop of the potential demise of the ANZ Premiership. With the league running at a deficit of $3.7 million this season, its future is under serious threat and Netball NZ can't guarantee that there will be an elite domestic competition next year.

The other storyline at this event is that when Dame Noeline Taurua sat on the coaching bench for the Silver Ferns' opening match against Scotland, it was her first time in charge since October 2024.

Last September, one of the most damaging periods for the sport was set in motion when Taurua was suspended due to concerns raised from players about the high performance environment.

Taurua was eventually reinstated as head coach, but only got her hands on the team three weeks before the start of the Commonwealth Games when they came together for a camp.

Captain Karin Burger, who stood in as interim captain in the immediate aftermath of the Taurua suspension, said the team's resilience came through in their win over England.

"We've been working really hard for this, we've been through some ups and downs so to be able to be in this position and know we're prepping for gold is a really good feeling," Burger said.

"England had their crowd backing them but I think the strength of this New Zealand side is playing for and with each other on the court and not letting the outside noise infiltrate the way we play. Our focus over the last couple of days has to be tight knit."

Grace Nweke came out on top against defender Shamera Sterling-Humphrey in pool play. Jayne Russell / Photosport

Taurua was thrilled they had put themselves in the position to contend for a gold medal.

"It takes a long time to get here not only on court but also the work we've done off court. We've got to give ourselves a bit of a tick and a pat on the back and to be able to put that performance out there is something of a success already in our minds.

"But it's always such an honour to play in a grand final, we're going to give it everything we've got, this is what we've prepared for."

Earlier on Saturday, the Silver Ferns confirmed defender Catherine Hall had been ruled out of the Games after rupturing her ACL in the match against Wales on Thursday.

The Silver Ferns are reduced to 11 players, with Kelly Jackson, Karin Burger, and Carys Stythe having to take the load in the defensive end.

Georgia Heffernan, who sustained a minor ankle injury in the same game and missed the final pool match, was able to make the starting line-up at goal attack.

The only change Taurua made was bringing Amelia Walmsley on to replace Heffernan at goal attack for the last few minutes.

The challenge for the Silver Ferns will be to back their performance up a day later.

Silver Ferns coach Dame Noeline Taurua. Simon Stacpoole / Photosport

Despite relying heavily on a starting seven for the knock-out games, Taurua said the players had more in the tank.

"We've actually got a few more mileage in our bank, so our strength and conditioning coach is really happy about that, we know that we can run that physically," Taurua said.

Burger, who was part of the 2019 World Cup winning team, is the only current Fern who has tasted success at a pinnacle event.

She believes the Ferns can go all the way.

"One hundred percent, I've got full faith in this group, if we play the way we can and stay united the way we can, I think we're unstoppable," Burger said.

Jamaica made their first Commonwealth Games final in Birmingham four years ago, where they finished runners up to Australia. New Zealand and Jamaica have never met each other in the final of the Netball World Cup or Commonwealth Games.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Emma Foy and Jessie Hodges win second gold, take NZ's tally to eight
World.content:
Para cycling pair Emma Foy and Jessie Hodges have won their second gold medal of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

After their win in the tandem sprint on Friday, the New Zealand pair took out the final in the 1000m time trial final overnight.

Ellese Andrews bounced back from an underwhelming start to her Commonwealth Games to win bronze.

The Olympic champion finished third in the women's one kilometre time trial behind Wales' Emma Finucane and Australia's Claudia Marcks, after missing out in both the team and individual sprint events.

New Zealand's medal tally now sits at 27, including eight golds.

World.title: NPC: Mo'unga scores match-winning try for Canterbury against Auckland
World.content:
Richie Mo'unga has scored the winning try for Canterbury in his first NPC match since 2020, with the defending champions beating Auckland 38-31.

Mo'unga, who has spent the last three years playing in Japan, came on as a replacement in the second half on Saturday night, and while he had a few awkward moments, he turned on the class to split the Auckland defence in the 78th minute, when the scores were deadlocked.

The first half was helter-skelter, with Canterbury starting off where they left off last season, with early dominance at the breakdown seeing them score two tries in the first 11 minutes.

But Auckland stormed back when the red-and-blacks made a couple of errors, leaving a hole in their lineout for Sam Hainsworth-Fa'aofo to score and then gifting an intercept to Xavier Tito-Harris.

Canterbury then scored two more tries, but Auckland claimed one back to trail 26-21 at halftime.

There was a big cheer when Mo'unga took the field but he looked a bit rusty early, knocking forward a ball that bounced just in front of him and then missing a conversion he normally would have nailed.

Auckland had taken the lead for the first time in the 60th minute, but Canterbury hit back seven minutes later.

It was 31-all with 12 minutes to go and stayed that way, until Canterbury's forwards charged towards the Auckland line from a lineout after winning a penalty and Mo'unga got his hands on the ball playing halfback, fooling the defence with a dummy and scoring by the posts. He then converted it.

In earlier games today, Otago beat Southland 41-14, and Taranaki beat Counties Manukau 20 points to five.

On Friday night, Tasman pipped North Harbour 31-29 in Nelson, while Waikato opened the season with a 38-26 win over Bay of Plenty on Thursday.

World.title: Country Life: Hydroponics in Horowhenua
World.content:
There's no need for extra washing when it comes to these salad greens. The plants from Waikawa fresh are harvested straight from their trays where they're grown hydroponically.

"There's no bugs, there's no soil, there's no dirt. We don't clean these plants with any chemicals or chlorine, so we eat those lettuce straight out of the channels. They're just absolutely crispy clean ... and they haven't been touched by anyone the whole time it's been growing," Tony Dale-Low told Country Life.

He and wife Lisa Dale-Low made the move to growing salad greens and herbs almost a decade ago, trading in city life and corporate jobs for horticulture in Horowhenua.

Hydroponics in Horowhenua: Growing with water Country Life Download MP3 17m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The couple had no growing experience before starting.

They'd spent a couple of years travelling around the country in a bus with their three children before coming up with a checklist of what they wanted for their next chapter.

"We wanted to be doing something productive, rather than something paper or computer-based. We wanted to be rural and we wanted to have a bit more flexibility with the kids. None of that was really sector specific or even location-specific," Lisa said.

The couple grow fancy lettuces and other herby greens hydroponically. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Hydroponic growing systems work by replacing soil with a water-based, nutrient-rich solution. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The water sourced from the 4500m2 of rooves of the many greenhouses, and the recent addition of solar power is also helping cut down on energy bills. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

After narrowing it down to the North Island they came across an existing hydroponic growing business near Levin - hydroponic systems work by replacing soil with a water-based, nutrient-rich solution.

That was in 2018 and after learning the ropes from the previous owners they've made it their own.

They grow the plants from seedlings themselves, also using hydroponics on a 'flood and drain table'.

"So this is set up on a timer. It runs three times a day and these tables will fill with nutrients or liquid with some fertilizer," Tony explained.

Seedlings, like these little basil sprouts, are also grown hydroponically. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The seedlings are easily plugged into the next growing space. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

It sits there for a few minutes before draining. Being fully automated means the team don't need to do any manual watering.

He said it helps the plants up well - making them more resistant to diseases and pests.

"[It] all definitely starts here in the propagating house. If we get it wrong here, then we have issues later. If we get it right, then we have so much more success."

Once the seedlings reach about three weeks, they're transferred to larger growing trays called 'gullies'.

"They look like downpipes, which in fact I think they are, actually straight off someone's house," Tony told Country Life.

"They've been drilled with a lot of little round holes and we plant the plant inside the holes. The nutrients get pumped around the greenhouse through these small whiskers."

Among some of the 'fancy' lettuces they grow, the oak leaf in red and green varieties. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The couple learned the art of hydroponics from the previous owners. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Over the cooler winter months, it gets too cold to grow basil so they replace this with growing watercress instead. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

The system they use only requires liquid to be pumped to the top of the gully before gravity does the rest, drawing it down the channel, through the gutter back to the holding tank which is topped up with the water sourced from the 4500m2 of greenhouse rooves.

The water is reticulated meaning they only need to add more to account for evaporation or absorption by the plants.

In the central tank, a computer system checks to make sure the water has the right balance of nutrients and the right pH level - the acid or alkaline concentration - and runs a dosing system to adjust this when needed.

Tony and his green 'lettuce' Leaf - the old Nissan Leaf gets its power from solar panels on the farm and is used to run around the property for the many maintenance jobs. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Sustainability is a key part of Waikawa Fresh' operations.

The recent addition of solar power at the end of last year is also helping cut down on energy bills - it's even used to power an old Nissan 'lettuce' leaf they use on farm to run the maintenance gear around.

About two months after the plants have finished growing they'll be ready to be picked straight from the gullies with no extra washing required - "lovely and crunchy and and fresh".

From their hands where they're packed straight into bags, the harvested plants are taken straight to the chiller ready to be picked up by a truck that same day. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

Getting the product to the market as fresh as possible is a key focus. RNZ / Gianina Schwanecke

World.title: Four in custody after staff assaulted, haul of perfume taken, police say
World.content:
Police responding to a report of a perfume heist say they quickly were able to quickly "sniff out" the leads and detain four young people.

Just before 2pm on Saturday, Hamilton police were called to a report that staff at a store at The Base shopping centre "had been assaulted and thousands of dollars' worth of perfume had been taken," a Police bulletin said.

"No weapons were used, nor were there any injuries."

Senior Sergeant Pete Simpson said officers who responded were given details about the possible identity of the suspects, and video captured by a person at the scene.

By 2:25pm on Saturday, officers had found "a bag full of the stolen items" at a nearby address, Simpson said.

Four young people were taken into custody, and are expected to appear in court on robbery charges next week.

World.title: Two new Auckland stations part of $2.4b rail spend
World.content:
Two new railway stations in South Auckland are among the final elements of a $2.4 billion government investment in Auckland's network, Minister for Auckland Simon Watts says.

He was speaking at the formal opening on Saturday of the Drury and Paerātā stops.

The stations will serve Drury, Paerātā, Franklin and South Auckland, with each station providing two platforms, 350 car parks and bus connections.

Services begin stopping at the new stations on Sunday. During the week, peak trains will run every 10 minutes.

Rail Minister Winston Peters at the opening of the new Drury station. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Other speakers at the opening were Rail Minister Winston Peters, KiwiRail chief metro officer Bevan Assink and Franklin ward councillor Andy Baker.

Watts said that while much of the recent investment in the rail network had been about preparing for the opening of the CRL, "the extension of the overhead electrification from Papakura to Pukekohe and these new train stations represent something more".

"Trains stopping at Drury and Paerātā stations from tomorrow and Ngākōroa station when it opens next year will help open up this part of Auckland.

"Around 130,000 more people are expected to be in the southern part of Auckland over the next three decades. More than 40,000 new homes are expected to be built, a new hospital in Drury, a number of new schools, new roads, including in time the Mill Road extension.

"For locals, it means ... being part of an Auckland that is properly connected to the rest of the city... It will give people greater confidence to move to this part of Auckland, knowing that they will not be reliant on their cars, and overall it's a great choice about where people live and how they get around," Watts said.

Auckland's new Paerātā railway station. RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

KiwiRail's Bevan Assink gave the gathering some project numbers - 6500 cubic metres of concrete; 600 tonnes of locally sourced steel; 25,000 cubic metres of material moved to make way for the facilities.

"We've also planted around 40,000 trees and everything to beautify the area. Also there were 22 apprenticeships that were able to be enacted as part of this project and also 32 local companies were also involved in the project as well.

"So it just shows how broad and vast-reaching these projects can be in supporting the communities and everything around them," Assink said.

Franklin ward's Andy Baker told a story of two girls, aged 11 and 12, writing to him in 2011 to ask if Drury could get a railway station.

"They had done a petition here in Drury. They had hundreds and hundreds of signatures about wanting a park and ride and a station at Drury.

"One of those girls is here today - my daughter ... she may have had some egging on ... the other, the 11-year-old at the time ... is now an emergency doctor at Christchurch Hospital, so time has moved on.

"I did promise Emma it would be built before she left high school, which was 2015, but we haven't quite made that.

"But it shows that there's been a demand for this type of infrastructure in this area for a very, very long time. It is fantastic to see it today," Baker said.

RNZ / Pretoria Gordon

Rail Minister Peters echoed Watts' figure of 130,000 more people expected in the area over coming decades "and infrastructure must come before growth - not years afterwards, as too often happens in this country".

"These stations are here because we funded them when last responsible for rail, as part of our wider commitments to unlock capacity, lift train frequencies, invest more than $500 million to get the network up to standard, and enable electric trains from Britomart right down to Pukekohe.

"While others say nice words about rail, we fund it, deliver it, and on this happy occasion are still here to open it.

"We will keep advocating for rail because taxpayers have built an asset with real potential to move people and goods efficiently - and we intend to make full use of it."

In an earlier statement, Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the stations were among the final elements of a $2.4 billion government investment in Auckland's rail network.

"The Auckland Rail Network Rebuild has been completed in time for the City Rail Link to open soon. We're also replacing level crossings across the network to support more frequent train services.

"The Third Main Line is now open, separating freight and passenger rail services, while the rail line to Pukekohe has been electrified. Looking ahead, new rail stations at Ngākōroa are also set to open in 2027.

The work was about investing in infrastructure "that would help our largest city to grow".

World.title: Pure shock as Diamonds fumble Australia's most anticipated gold medal
World.content:
When Sophie Dwyer's shot bounced off the front right of the rim, the first look on her face was shock.

As she turned and was dragged into something vaguely resembling a hug by veteran centre Kate Moloney, Dwyer's thousand-mile stare was one of numbness and utter disbelief.

Australia had lost its semifinal to Jamaica by 46-45 and would miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time in history.

The Diamonds certainly didn't expect to lose this game, they never do, but when they were down by four with four minutes left, they probably didn't expect to be shooting for extra time with the clock at 00:00 either.

Moloney was at pains to point out how much went wrong before Dwyer, the second youngest member of the team, had to take a long shot to tie the game, rushing through the moment in an apparent attempt to give nerves no chance to set in.

"It's a full team loss today, it's not on one person," she said.

The Diamonds were this close to potentially saving themselves from disaster. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

It had been their worst performance of an otherwise cruisy tournament, culminating in a final quarter that started 35-35 but quickly ballooned out on the back of miscommunication with the ball in hand, leading to uncharacteristic and costly late turnovers.

To focus solely on Australia's errors would do a disservice to the Sunshine Girls' harrying defence, but Moloney admitted her usually nerveless Diamonds were nowhere near their best.

"We have the players to get the job done, but we just didn't do it today," she said.

Things turned frantic in the final quarter.

"We just couldn't execute at really critical moments, and that's really important. It's something we speak about all the time and there's a few errors I'm sure we wish we could go back and take again.

"Credit to Jamaica, but we needed to be better today."

In an Australian team full of expected gold medals, the netball felt like one of the most secure after four victories from seven straight finals.

We saw Nina Kennedy unable to live up to similarly lofty expectations, but fans were never actively rooting against her success.

Nina Kennedy is often superhuman, but in Glasgow she was a super human Nina Kennedy can measure success in a lot of different ways, and it wasn't necessarily in metres or centimetres in Glasgow.

Every one of the Diamonds' opponents became de facto hometown favourites at the Hydro, and it was again the case in their semi.

Moloney said they were used to having the crowd rooting against their success, in an apparent acknowledgement that it would mostly likely come regardless, but the support for Jamaica felt different.

Once it became clear that they might be able to not just make the presumptive and defending champions bleed a little, but actually take them down, the tone turned as much anti-Australia as it was pro-Jamaica.

Taking down the Australian giants guaranteed the Sunshine GIrls at least a silver medal. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

"We don't really notice that, we're pretty used to that," Moloney said.

"I think there were just critical moments today that we weren't able to nail."

And that didn't just start when the game was at its most tense.

High-risk calls don't pay off

Although coach Stacey Marinkovich ran her best seven, the Diamonds got off to a slow start.

With an almost entirely Melbourne Vixens' frontline, there was a clear mental hangover from the Super Netball grand final.

Sophie Garbin, Kiera Austin and Moloney were all part of the side that lost to the Adelaide Thunderbirds by a record margin in that decider, 61-40.

So it was no real surprise that once again, the very next time they met, Jamaican defenders Shamera Sterling-Humphrey and Latanya Wilson had them spooked.

All had been running smoothly in the pool stages with the team winning comprehensively by margins of 61, 19, 36, 10 and 61 goals.

But in the semifinal the attackers were stuck in their heads, second-guessing their connections and making rushed decisions that led to turnover.

Australia went down 13-10 at the first break and the margin got as big as five in the second period. They were on the back foot.

Maybe this failure to address these demons ahead of the Games will come back to bite Marinkovich? As might her changes in live play.

The first substitution of the night to bring Cara Koenen on in goal shooter was the right call. Koenen helped Australia win gold in Birmingham and despite only averaging about 25 minutes of play before the finals, her experience meant she was very much ready to go.

The defence by Shamera Sterling-Humphrey and Latanya Wilson was stifling.

With Koenen involved for 44 minutes, the Australians ground their way into the contest and managed to win the second and third quarters.

Koenen was so close to being the hero — turning herself inside out to make rushed and misplaced passes look good, trusting her hold and take when she was sandwiched by the defenders. She was steady and reliable under the post with 18 goals at 90 per cent.

The struggles continued at the other end of the court where Courtney Bruce, who has had a strong hold on the starting goal keeper bib, caught the eye of the umpires early and was often standing out of play.

Bruce did come up with a couple of crucial gains to help the team get back in contention, but her overall impact was limited due to so much whistle.

The highest penalised player on court (14 contacts, five obstructions) struggled to get off the body of goal-shooter Romelda Aiken-George, but she wasn't alone as Sarah Klau, Matilda Garrett and Jo Weston could not find a way to shut down Jamaican linchpin Shanice Beckford. They really needed to invest more of their time planning tactics in this area.

At the final break, the score was level 35-35.

For the first time in this campaign, young mid-courter Georgie Horjus was left on the bench all game. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Austin had been left on and managed to toil away alongside Koenen. By now fans were confident she could pull the side through. But midway through the final term, with just seven minutes to play, Marinkovich pulled Austin off and injected Dwyer.

We'd seen this change throughout the pool stages when the Diamonds were up by much safer margins, but the Dwyer-Koenen partnership was very much untested against Sterling-Humphrey, and it was a huge risk in a match of this nature.

Dwyer had a very difficult season with the Giants, winning just one game all year. Her confidence isn't at its peak and to come on cold like this and execute was a huge ask that she came within a missed shot of answering.

It was a huge call from Marinkovich at a crucial point Australia's first-ever Commonwealth Games semifinal loss. Less damaging decisions have cost other coaches more, and Marinkovich's contract is up after next year's World Cup, where the expectations will now be even greater than they were in Glasgow.

If the Diamonds weren't going to stick with Austin, then Georgie Horjus at least deserved a crack. Bizarrely, the country's most in-form domestic talent — off the back of winning a third Super Netball premiership, training alongside the Jamaican defenders in Adelaide for several years — was the only player that didn't hit the court in this semifinal.

This is not on Dwyer missing the final shot. This call is on the coaching staff.

How could it all go so wrong?

World.title: Gold medallist makes no apologies for 'selfish' racing in Aussie podium sweep
World.content:
You know what just rips? A little hike.

And it's all the better if you've got a few buddies with you.

Jemima Montag had two teammates alongside her in the race walk final in Glasgow, but once they hit the track, they certainly weren't mates.

The two-time gold medallist broke clear early in the 25-lap race around Scotstoun Stadium with fellow Australian Lizzy McMillen leading the way.

It looked like the pair might link up with some drafting techniques to avoid one racer getting buffeted by the Glasgow winds that have caused havoc on the track and field at these Games.

Instead, the younger racer in her Commonwealth Games debut sat out front with Montag nipping at her heels for the better part of 23 laps before Montag made her move.

Montag sat behind McMillen for almost the entire race. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

"It was pretty windy out there so having to cop the wind for a good 23 laps was a bit tough, certainly not my plan, but I'm proud of my efforts and I went as hard as I possibly could," McMillen said.

"What can you do? That's racing for you."

Men's gold medallist Isaac Beacroft was in a similar spot a day earlier and said silver medallist Stephen Kihu was regularly trying to encourage him to take a turn setting the pace.

He didn't have any intention to do so, executing his race perfectly with a late kick to explode past the Kenyan and claim gold.

McMillen said she was similarly keen to have Montag take some of the load out front, but to no avail.

Nina Kennedy is often superhuman, but in Glasgow she was a super human Nina Kennedy can measure success in a lot of different ways, and it wasn't necessarily in metres or centimetres in Glasgow.

"I did look back a few times thinking 'Are you gonna kinda help out here?', but no," she said.

"I was the rabbit today, so what are you going to do?"

Montag said she had the utmost respect for silver medallist McMillen and bronze medallist Bec Henderson, but there were no friends out on the track.

"Not in a race. In training, absolutely, but in a race you have to be selfish. Unfortunately it's an individual sport, not a team," she said.

"If it was cycling or something with drafting, where you do change the lead around, then absolutely.

"But as much as I would love to, sometimes you have to forget it's a teammate that you care about and just remember it's another competitor and it's another body that's in front of you and to ultimately be selfish."

Henderson said the plan going in was to complete the 1-2-3, but how that played out was always up in the air as all three executed their own race plans.

"All three of us have really different strengths in terms of racing and really different tactics in terms of how we like to do the race," she said.

"So I think it was best for us to all take our own tactics going into the race and hope that that worked out for us on the day."

World.title: Aussies reign supreme over Irish in AFLW international
World.content:
Australia has overcome some spirited early resistance from Ireland to score a convincing 50-point win in the first women's Australian rules international.

A burst of six straight Australia goals either side of half-time propelled the home team to a 13.13 (91) to 6.5 (41) victory in an entertaining AFLW international played before a capacity crowd of 9,017 at North Sydney Oval on Saturday.

Australia led at every break, by margins of 12, 30 and 41.

Ireland thrilled the crowd, which included a large contingent of their fans, with several fast, flowing passages of play In the first half, but couldn't stay the course against a polished and more consistent Australia.

The home team won the physical battle, tallying 35 more contested possessions.

Australian captain and North Melbourne star Jasmine Garner was named player of the match.

Ebony Marinoff topped Australia's possession count with 25, from Ash Riddell and Nina Morrison 21 each.

For Ireland, Erika O'Shea led their possession tally with 21, followed by skipper Orla O'Dwyer with 19.

North Melbourne players were leading goalkickers for both teams, with Tahlia Randall bagging four for Australia and Blaithin Bogue three for Ireland.

Australia piled on three goals in the first six minutes with Sydney's Zippy Fish kicking the first, but Ireland responded with three goals of their own either side of quarter time.

The home team kicked two goals early in the second and Ireland replied in kind, before another Australian surge proved decisive.

Ireland's goal-kicking accuracy kept them in the game for most of the first half, as they kicked 5.0 to Australia's 5.6, before the home team took over and maximised their opportunities.

The home team kicked the only two goals of the third quarter and two to one in the last.

Australian rucks Mim Strom and Matilda Scholz dominated the hitouts, giving Australia a whopping advantage in that area.

The home team dominated in the air, taking 38 more marks and limiting Ireland to just eight in the first half.

Ireland's Aine McDonagh left the field clutching her right arm late in the second quarter.

It wasn't all bad for the Irish, however.

Niamh McLaughlin (centre) kicked an amazing goal for Ireland against Australia but her team went down at North Sydney Oval. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

North Melbourne and County Fermanagh player Bogue proved almost impossible to stop early on, kicking three goals for the game.

She also set up the goal of the game in the final quarter, producing a World Cup-like cross from the right forward pocket for Niamh McLaughlin to get her foot to the ball and flick it casually over the Australian defence and through.

The Irish didn't give up, despite the lop-sided scoreboard, and another Kangaroos player Vikki Wall (County Meath) delivered a bump that drew gasps from the crowd in the final quarter as she dispossessed Australia's Ella Roberts in midfield before setting up an attack.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Live: Aussies chasing history in star-studded track and field finale
World.content:
(Getty)

Australia's track program has pumped time and money into their relays over the past few years and it's culminated in some excellent results, including bronze and a national record in the men's 4x400m at the World Athletics Relays earlier this year.

At that meet in Gaborone, Botswana, the men's 4x100m quartet missed a medal by just 0.24 of a second and three quarters of that team ran the heats earlier today, with Josh Azzopardi, Chris Ius, Calab Law and Rohan Browning hitting the track.

They will welcome back 100m silver medallist Lachie Kennedy on the lead-off in place of Ius, both elite out of the blocks, for the final (5:15am AEST) after what Josh Azzopardi described as "a training run" in the heat.

"I think it's almost a training run for us now just to get the baton around," Azzopardi said.

"It was really good, really clean, really comfortable. Coming into the final we'll throw a bit of caution to the wind and see how we go."

They were incredibly crisp with their changeovers as they finished third in their heat with a time of 38.69.

Browning, who fumbled the baton in the 2025 world championships final, said the biggest change he has seen is the depth on display, giving them the luxury of resting Kennedy in the qualifying run.

"There's so many guys we can call on," Browning said.

"We've got guys like Eddie [Nketia], at home guys like Gout [Gout], so I think the future of the team looks really strong, the stocks are really strong."

(ABC News: Che Chorley)

The women similarly finished third in their heat, running 43.52 without individual 100m bronze medallist and national record holder Torrie Lewis.

"We've done many, many camps over this season having to come off racing individually and then coming together as a team," Ebony Lane said.

"I honestly think that's made us push each other even more to run better times get more comfortable with each other, learn each other's strengths, and I think that's been a massive help for both the men's and women's teams."

Lewis will come back in for tonight's final (5:26am AEST), replacing Georgia Harris and anchoring the relay after Ebony Lane, Chloe Mannix-Power and Monique Hanlon.

In the mixed 4x400m final (6:20am AEST), Australia will be represented by Cooper Sherman, Mia Gross, Tom Reynolds and Jemma Pollard.

World.title: Dozens of greyhounds to land in Australia as NZ racing ban begins
World.content:
Chartered flights will ferry up to 150 greyhounds to Australia as trainers pivot from a racing ban coming into effect in New Zealand.

The ban, which was first announced in December 2024 and legislated in April this year, took effect on Saturday after years of animal welfare concerns.

Ten greyhounds were euthanised during New Zealand's final racing season, including one days before the ban began.

Heather Simpson, the Greyhound Transition Agency (GTA) head, said she was aware that Greyhound Racing New Zealand had organised charter flights for about 150 dogs to go to Australia to continue racing.

"There is nothing in the legislation that stops trainers choosing to export their dogs to Australia; some of these dogs actually will be partly owned by Australians," she told Radio New Zealand.

Greyhound ban legislation delayed until government gets support A bill to ban greyhound racing in Tasmania has been delayed until the government can secure enough support.

Greyhound racing remains legal in most Australian jurisdictions, banned only in the Australian Capital Territory.

Plans for an industry phase-out in Tasmania have stalled after the government pulled a bill from the upper house in April when it appeared not to have enough support to pass.

Word of the chartered flights first emerged through a leaked message from a private greyhound racing group, Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi told a Senate Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee hearing in April.

She said the move appeared "to be kind of a deliberate attempt to avoid" New Zealand's transition agency.

"If they survive, they will become the responsibility of Australians to rehome," she said.

"And you would know we're already in a rehoming crisis."

The greyhounds brought to Australia will be classed as "companion animals". (Reuters: Action Images/Scott Heavey)

Brant Smith, a senior biosecurity executive at the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, told the senate hearing the government had been working with New Zealand's Ministry for Primary Industries on the dogs' import.

He said they would be classed as "companion animals", but may be used for racing once in the country.

"As to how they are then used, that's not something that we have control over thereafter because they're being imported as companion animals like other animals … and this is not unusual," he said.

Mr Smith said a similar contingent of greyhounds was imported to Australia in April 2025.

"In the previous consignment, I think approximately 80 came similarly, and they were just imported under our normal conditions," he said.

It is estimated a further 1,400 dogs will remain in New Zealand and require rehoming by the GTA.

Ms Simpson said the rehomed dogs would be regularly checked under a welfare program.

World.title: Broncos to 'look after each other' as title defence comes to early end
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos coach Michael Maguire has said the playing group will need to "look after each other" as their finals hopes were officially ended on Saturday night.

The Broncos will become the first reigning premier in 20 years to miss the finals after going down at home to the Newcastle Knights 30-6.

Brisbane has just six wins this season, in a premiership defence that has been hampered by injuries and poor performances.

With any faint hopes of making the finals ending with a 24-point loss to the Knights, Maguire told media the club would need to rally around each other in the face of a disappointing campaign.

"It is tough, because I've got a high regard on how these boys go about things," Maguire said.

"You can't fault how they try. Unfortunately at the moment, we're not getting things going our way.

"I feel for everyone that's going through it at the moment.

"But they're a group that support each other, and that's what it's about now.

"We've got to make sure that we look after each other through this period."

Brisbane becomes the first reigning premier to not make finals since Wests Tigers missed the top eight in 2006 after winning the grand final in 2005.

Earlier, Penrith winger Tom Jenkins has become the first player in 72 years to score multiple tries in 12 matches during a season, as the Panthers hammered the Canberra Raiders 42-18 in Mudgee.

The New Zealand Warriors consolidated their place in the NRL top four with a commanding win over the Gold Coast Titans.

Relive all of Saturday's NRL action in the blog below.

World.title: Fraser sheds light on coaching call as Blues record monster win over Lions
World.content:
Carlton's interim coach Josh Fraser says he will decide this week whether to join the club's process to find its next full-time coach.

Fraser's candidacy received another major boost as the Blues recorded a thumping 24.10 (154) to 11.12 (78) win over the Brisbane Lions at Docklands Stadium in club captain Patrick Cripps's 250th career game.

While Fraser began his coaching tenure by stating he wasn't interested in the full-time role, a stunning 9-2 record has caused him to reconsider his original position.

Carlton's win also enhanced its bid for a wildcard spot, with the Blues in 10th spot on the AFL ladder, four premiership points ahead of the ninth-placed St Kilda and the 10th-placed GWS Giants.

The Giants overcame a gritty Port Adelaide side to claim a 10.15 (75) to 9.9 (63) win at the Adelaide Oval to stay within touch of the final wildcard spot.

Earlier on Saturday, Sydney recorded a comeback 16.11 (107) to 13.10 (88) win against St Kilda at Docklands Stadium, but lost Will Edwards to a horror injury, with the result dealing a blow to the Saints' wildcard bid.

Meanwhile, Hawthorn survived a stiff test against North Melbourne before running out 14.15 (99) to 12.11 (83) winners in Tasmania.

In a curtain-raiser for the AFLW season, Australia recorded a 13.13 (91) to 6.5 (41) win against Ireland at North Sydney Oval as Jasmine Garner was named the Player of the Match.

Follow the live blog below for recap of all of Saturday's football action as it happened.

World.title: Boxer earns Tuvalu's first ever Comm Games medal without winning fight
World.content:
A boxer from Tuvalu earned her tiny South Pacific nation's first ever Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight overnight.

Tarona Taafaki lost her only bout in the women's 75-kilogram class to India's Lovlina Borgohain, losing every round on all three of the judges' cards.

Because there were only five entrants, Taafaki received a bye to the last four, meaning she was automatically guaranteed at least a bronze medal.

Tarona Taafaki arrives at the Commonwealth Games during the opening ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

But her coach and father said the population of Tuvalu, an island south-east of Tonga, will celebrate the medal and use it to highlight a climate change emergency.

Badi Taafaki, whose son Pasoni competed earlier in the Games and lost his only bout at 70kg, told the British Press Association: "For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything.

"We're one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it's a stepping stone."

Tarona and Pasoni are the two eldest of eight children, all of whom are boxers. They are based in New Zealand in order to take advantage of better facilities.

"My children are very fortunate," Badi said.

"They have opportunities and facilities that I never had. Boxing is our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline."

Athletes on the island famously train on its airport runway, the most stable land mass on an island increasingly threatened by rising sea levels. Climate experts predict half of the nation's capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050.

A group of locals play volleyball on the airport runway in Funafuti, Tuvalu. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

"Yes, we train on the airport runway," Badi said. "When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.

"If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change.

"It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades. Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can't sleep if there's a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes."

Tarona is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia's Taylah Robertson picked up a bronze in the women's flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her bout to England's Lisa Whiteside.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Tech.title: Is this Billboard Hot 100 hit AI slop?
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Fenix Flexin is best known as a member of Shoreline Mafia, a rap duo from Los Angeles. But he’s recently found solo success with the track “Rubberz,” which has climbed to number 58 on the Billboard Hot 100. Almost immediately, though, questions were raised about the song’s origins, with many speculating that it was largely, if not entirely, generated by AI. Fenix has denied those accusations, but done little to dispel them.

Part of the suspicion is certainly due to the fact that the song is a dramatic left turn. Fenix has primarily trafficked in trap-influenced West Coast rap. “Rubberz,” on the other hand, is heavily influenced by ‘80s UK synth pop. The vocal melody is clearly influenced by Morrissey, with Fenix even adopting a fake British accent. But artists are allowed to evolve and experiment. That alone doesn’t prove anything.

Perhaps more telling is the simple quality of the recording. Close inspection reveals a number of artifacts and anomalies that are commonly found in AI-generated music. Hi-hats have a certain brittle quality, the chorus vocals sound like a low-bitrate MP3, and reverb tails haphazardly cut off.

Speaking with The Verge, songwriter and co-host of the Switched on Pop podcast, Charlie Harding, highlighted the giveaways. “Ghostly backing vocals duck in and out unexpectedly. The drum reverb is full of unnatural digital artifacting reminiscent of a 64kbps MP3 downloaded off of Napster. Because most generative AI companies have trained their model on low-quality MP3s of unlicensed copyrighted material, we hear audibly degraded instrumentation.”

Feeding the song into an AI music detector doesn’t deliver a smoking gun. I ran the track through five different tools, and they all said that there was between 20 and 30 percent chance that it was AI or at least AI-assisted. But those sorts of tools are not necessarily super reliable and advance much more slowly than music-making models themselves.

Some of the supporting materials, however, have tripped up AI detectors. The single’s cover art and a post celebrating its success were both flagged as being AI-generated with over 97 percent certainty by multiple AI image detectors. Similarly, I fed the lyrics into multiple AI writing detectors and Gemini, which agreed they appeared to be written by AI. Producer and YouTuber Curtiss King dropped the lyrics into Claude, and it also flagged multiple signs that the lyrics appeared to be AI-generated.

The lyrics are the sort of logical near-gibberish that AI often spits out. The rhymes are simple and clean in a way that you wouldn’t expect from someone who is a reasonably accomplished rapper. There are no near rhymes or internal rhymes. Instead, everything sticks to a basic AA, BB format that clearly prioritizes the rhyme scheme over actual meaning or narrative development.

Swipin’ cards and stackin’ chips, I saw you sinkin’ ships Left me standin’ in the pourin’ rain, now I bought a heavy diamond chain

Who is sinking ships? Are we the sinking ships? No clue, this idea never comes back up. Similarly, the individual lines of the chorus might make sense, but when combined are meaningless.

Bankrolls on the table Watchin’ local cable Hatin’ that I’m able Hatin’ that I’m able

Ignoring the “local cable” bit, which is just awkward (and nearly sent King into a rage spiral), what is Fenix able to do? Why does he hate it? The lyrics raise more questions than they answer.

The way the lines are delivered is also odd. Verse three seemingly ends mid-thought on the line, “Not the jewelry.” Harding noted that it has a “complete lack of flow.” He says that, “No half-competent rapper would ever sing the title line ‘I just let the rubber band snap’ in such an awkward manner. The syncopation is highly unusual, emphasizing all the wrong syllables.” He goes on to explain that, “by smashing so many syllables together, it forces the word the onto the downbeat, instead of the word rubber, forcing all of the subsequent syllables to accent with unnatural syncopation.”

Live “performances” of “Rubberz” haven’t done Fenix any favors. The first couple of in-studio appearances featured the rapper awkwardly lip-syncing. At times it seems like the awkwardness of the flow and the lyrics trip him up, as if he can’t remember his own song. Honestly, he’s not even trying that hard to convince anyone that he’s actually singing.

Things only get worse when Fenix actually does sing. It’s abundantly clear in multiple clips that he is incapable of recreating the vocal range and accent from the recording (and that he doesn’t know the lyrics). In many of the clips of live performances, even when he’s singing, they’re simply playing the original vocals over his. His real vocals are kept extremely low in the mix, and the DJ strategically drops out the backing track briefly in an effort to prove the authenticity of the song, but fails.

Fenix has defended himself, saying the difference between the recorded version and any in-the-flesh performance is down to vocal processing, including AutoTune. However, multiple people, including Harding, King, and Anthony Fantano, have disputed this assertion. King compares AutoTune to spellcheck, and that’s not a bad analogy. While yes, it can be pushed to its limits to create unique robotic textures, it’s designed to clean up errors — it would not extend a performer’s vocal range or introduce an accent, as Fantano points out.

Perhaps the most compelling argument for “Rubberz” being authentic is just how bad it is. Harding says, “I would assume it was written by someone who has never written a song using an ‘80s kids practice keyboard.” If the song was indeed created using generative AI, it was clearly made with an inferior model. “I am concerned that audiences find this song interesting when it is created by one of the lesser generative AI music companies with a terrible model. More sophisticated models have already made big improvements in the audible artifacts and awkwardly sung rhythms.”

Fenix has posted clips of what he says are Pro Tools session files. But that doesn’t actually prove anything. Unless he shares the original recording and project files publicly, it’s likely he’ll never shake the AI allegations. And I don’t see that happening anytime soon.

Tech.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day leak racks up millions of views
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A bootleg of Spider-Man: Brand New Day was up on X for over seven hours before eventually being pulled. During that time, it reached over 5.9 million accounts and accumulated over 143,000 likes. Other accounts have reposted the leaked film, but none have lasted particularly long, as Disney now seems to be on top of issuing takedown requests.

The leak is unlikely to slow down the box office juggernaut, which is already shattering records. It raked in $72 million in previews this week. The previous record holder was Avengers: Endgame, which grossed $60 million during its previews way back in 2019. Endgame went on to set staggering records for opening weekend, grossing over $1.2 billion worldwide and over $350 million in the US. Spider-Man: No Way Home currently holds the number two spot on the all-time US opening weekend list with $260 million.

Brand New Day could potentially usurp Endgame, though it certainly faces an uphill battle. Between previews and opening day, it’s already grossed $168 million, which puts it ahead of Endgame’s $157.4 million. Sony is keeping its estimates somewhat conservative, saying it expects the latest Spider-Man to pull in $325 million.

Tech.title: Trump blames Tim Walz for water hacks even though it’s probably Iran
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The FBI, the EPA, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) have stopped short of officially blaming Iran for a spate of cyberattacks on Minnesota’s water systems, but consensus is that Iran is likely behind them. That, of course, hasn’t stopped Donald Trump from sharing his own theory — that Governor Tim Walz is to blame and telling reporters that “I don’t think there was an Iranian cyberattack.”

Trump’s comments come shortly after the FBI issued a warning that the cyberattacks on American infrastructure were spreading to other states. In Minnesota alone, at least 30 community water systems had been targeted in what appeared to be a coordinated attack. The CISA has linked similar attacks earlier in the year to Iran, which has been the target of an on-again-off-again war waged by the US government. With limited military options, Iran has repeatedly turned to digital efforts to become a thorn in the side of the Trump administration and wage a PR war.

Trump has lashed out frequently at Minnesota and Walz during his second term and even threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act against it during a surge of ICE enforcement efforts in the state that left multiple people dead.
